During the year but one instance of confusion among the Craft has appealed to
me, which, in lily judgment, required the exercise of executive authority to restrain
It. Although the most disagreeable function of my station was called into requlal·
tlon, I believe the corrective remedy applied was received in the proper spirit, and
has been saving in its intl.uence. The lesson taught, that the Grand Lodge will not
permit personal feeling to enter a Lodge to mer the beauty of the lofty teachings of
Hasonry, and illuetrate by odious comparison the revolting contrast between onr
high and fraternal professions and the exhibition of ungoverned prejudices, will noi
soon be forgotten. In asserting these principles, and for good reason shown, I
arrested the charter of Sotoyome Lodge, No. 123, and suspended its operation by an
order which took elf;ct on the ninth of Morch last. Boon after, early In April, I visited
the jurisdiction of' the Lodge, and by personal lospectlon became satisfied that the
aevere lesson was being appreciated at Its full value; and I am gratfHed in believing
that the presence of supreme executive authority, to which respectful deference waa
p·ald, had the effect of composing differences and restoring calmness where excite·
billty of temper bed prevailed to a too great extent. Having held them on probation to tee~ the sincerity of their Intentions, and being satisfl ~d, I restored tho charter
by an order dated the twenty-third of April, and have reason to believe that its
honor will for the future be more carefully preserved from reproach. I refer yon to
the records of this office for details.

~hould be received kindly but firmly, and if they are not clearly in poss~ssion of
convincing evidence of their true fellowship, they should .be dismissed from our
portals. Pl'ivate examinations by individual members, without authority from the
Master, do not, as a matter of right, entitle a member of a Lodge to vouch for a vis·
itor. The Ma•ter himself is responsible for the admission of all visitors within the
Lodge which he governs. He specially makes a promise that "no visitors shall be
received into hi• Lodge without due examination and producing proper vouchers of
their having been initiated iuto a regular Lodge," and it is therefore his right and bis
duty to discriminate in favor of the most discreet and skilfull brethren as the pro1.er
persons to·conduct an examination, who, indeed, act as his proxy in such cases. It
is the installation charge whieh rests upon him, and he should never lose sight of it.
I am led to believe, from the experience of my station, that trouble frequently
arises in the Lodges from lack of correct knowledge of the laws and customs which
regulate the form of admission of' candidates. In the absence of such knowledge,
discussions are freqently entered into where the ballot has resulted unfavorably to
the petitioner, especially aft.er the Lodge has been closed. Such discussions tend
only to evil, and attack the motive of the Lodge which has refused to receive him.
I say motive of the Lodge, because when the result is announced by the .Master, it is
the action of the Lodge, and by fiction of custom every member may be said to have
cast the ballot which should be considered unanimous. Discussion, then, is unlaw·
ful; it is productive of discord, and i• a canvass of the integrity of individual action
which is guaranteed by the solemnity which surrounds the occasion. No member
has the right to declare how he voted, whether affirmatively or negatively, unless it
be to declare his own act to the Master, if he is satisfied that he has committed an
error of judgment, in order that injustice may be remedied. The knowledge of the
officers in such matters, acquired in the discharge of their duties, belongs to their
stations, and our Constitution particularly cautions the Master in the uso of the final
remedy, provided for the "purpose of correcting 11 possible mistake," that he shall
resort to it" without declaring the ·result" of the former ballot. Regard for these
principles, thus briefly stated, will dry up one source from which trouble springs in
our Lodges.
I again rest the executive authority of the Grand Lodge with you, and shall be
plea;ed to invest my successor with the symbol of power and authority which yon
entrusted to my keeping, and clothe him with the honor which you have kindly
conferred on me. While exercising authority I have been more than ever impressed
with the spirit of confidence and trust so freely reposed by the brethren in him upon
whom the honor fortunately falls of being chosen as the head of the Craft. If in the
course of my official connection with you I have illustrated the fallibility of human nature in the exercise of judgment-a circumstance not uncommon where prompt action
is required-'-! feel the same abiding confidence in the Craftsmen which they have
always shown to this exalted pli.ce, that they will ascribe to any such act, as an
offset to error that may have been made, an earnest intent and persistent purpose,
on my part, to advan<>c the glory, honor, and asefulness of our Fraternity.
I submit this record of official acts during the year, as required by our law, and
such reflections as have naturally been inspired by experience, for your consideration; and invoke the mighty favor of Him who rules us all, upon our deliberation•, that

He will guide us in counsel, preserve our association in harmony, and continue it in
usefulness
"Till each man find his own in all mens' good,
And all men work in noble brotherhood."
GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE,
Grand Master.

dred-a number amply sufficient at the time it first was ordered, but Inadequate now

subordmate Lodges; now tbere are one hundred and fifty-two. Then there were

No surrender of a charter has occurred dm1ng the past year, and it is not probable that such an event will occur often in the future. Population has become more
fixed and permanent, and, during the le.st few years, profiti.ng by earlier experience,
Lodges have been established only where there was apparently good assurance that
they would be lasting. Our registered numbers now reach one hundred and eightyone, of which thirty-four have been erased from the roll, for reasons stated In the
report of.last year; leaving upon the registry one hundred and forty-seven chartered
Lodges, besides the five called into existence by dispenAation during the cnrrent
year-an aggregate of <.ne hundred and fifty-two Lodges now in active existence.
The form for keeping records of Lodges which the undersigned was heretofore
requested to prepare fur the guidance of inexperienced Secretaries, has been completed, and, in accordance with the directions of the Grand Lodge, has been printed
for distribution among the Lodges of the jurisdiction. In its inception it was intended
principally ns a guide to the Secretaries of new Lodges, that they might so commence
their record books e.s to show a full and complete history of the proceedings antecedent to the establishment of their Lodges, as well as a concise st11tement of their
transactions afterward. To this has been added some general formulas for tile record
of such proceedings as usually occur in a chartered Lodge during i.ts existence, and
as under our laws are necessary when it desires to cease labor and surrender its
charter to the Grand Lodge. It 'is, of course, not presenled as a form to whicil e.n
1Lb•olute and slavish adherence is expected, but simply as suggestive of those things
which should be recorded, and of the mannner in which, so far as they are stated, it
would be well to make such record. A copy of the printed form for record book is
herewith submitted.

The forty-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of this State was held
in the city of Montgomery, commencing on the third day of December, 1866,-the
M.·. W.-. WILSON W1Ltl.1.¥S, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.-. W.·. DANIEL
SAYRg b~ing Grand Secretary.

·
The Address of the Grand Master relates principally to matters of local interest.
Sundry petitions for dispensations to form new Lodges had been denied, the requirements of the Grand ~odge not being in any instance complied with; and petitions
for dispensations to confer the degrees within the period prescribed by law had been
Invariably refused. A perusal of the address conveys the impression that in Bro.
WJLLIAHB the Grand Lodge of Alabama possesses a consider11-te and efficient officer.
The Report on Correspondence-a review of the proceedings of thirty-two co temporaries, California for 1865 being one of the number-was presented by Past Grand
Master, WILLIAM C. PENIOK. Quite 11 fengtby quotation from the Address of Grand
Master BELCHER is given, and his opinion in regard to the position of a candidate,

1867.]

Grand Lodpe of O<ilif01·nia.

29

elected to receive the degrees, but to whom objection was afterwards made, is pro·
nounced to be correct. · Bro. PENICK also agrees with Grand Master BELCHER and
our Committee on Jurisprudence, that when a sentonce of suspension or expulsion
is reversed by the Grand Lodge, ~he accused is at once restored to all the rights and
privileges which he before enjoyed. The oration of Bro. Niles is highly commended,
and the Report on Correspondence by Bro. RnEES is pronounced to be an able pro·
duction. We regret to see that Bro. PENICK was misled in regard to the alleged
establishment ot' negro Lodges in North Carolina in the same manner as was the
Grand Lodge of that State; and wonder that be should have been thus deceived.
The allusion inade to the Grand Lodge of New York In his review of that proceeding, was uncalled for, and the language used in the paragraph relating to that sub·
ject should never have 1rppeared In a Masonic paper. We are inclined to think that
Bro. PENICK, with our brethren of North Carolina, now regret the haste in which
they arrived at their conclusions, and doubt not that the amende honorable will be
made at the first proper opportunity.
We observe that the duty assigned in our Grand Loilge to the Committee on Re·
turns ls divided, in that of Alabama, among ten committees, consisting of five each.
Experience llas taught us that this duty can not be performed during the sessio11s of
the Grand Lodge with any approach to accuracy. We have the.refore made the
Committee on Returns a standing committee, of which the Assistant Grand Secre·
tary has heretofore been chairman, and the reports of the Lodges, which are requirep to be transmitted to the Grand Secretary two months prior to our an11u11l
meeting, are ca1·efully examined in his office as received. If any of them contain
err<>rs of any kind, that officer immediately writes to the Secretary of the Lodge
sending the incorrect report, and the proper corrections are made without delay.
Thus, during the time that Bro. ABKLL has been Grand Secretary of this Urand
Lodge, now a period of moro than twelve years, not a subordinate has failed to make
ito annual report; a thorough aud correct record of the Masonic Bti.1tll.8 of every
member of every Lodge in the jurisdiction bas been preserved ; and, at the present
time, not one is indebted to tile Grand Lodge for dues-a showing which can not be
excelled by any other jurisdiction in the world.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported that the conviction of a Mason by a
criminal eoul't should not act as a conviction in a Lodge, but that be must be regu·
larly tried therein, as tl1e tlrst might pos~lbly be an unjust ve1·dlct; that notice of
charges must bd se1·ved upon a Mason sentenced to the penitentiary, and that, after
such service he may be tried ez parle; and th11.t when a brother is tried and found
guilty of unmasonic conduct, proper punishment mW!t be meted to him, and he can
not be shielded by the pal'tlality of the triers.
The Committee on Appeals justify High Log Lodge, No.193, (" Phoobus! what a
name!") in ref1uing to punish a member who retailed ardent 11plrits in violation of
an edict of the Gr11.nd Lodge, and very sensibly say :"Your committee see no more harm In selling a drink of ardent spirits than in the
sale of a barrel or more, Ol' i11 the manuf11.cture of spirits. 'l.'he State of Alabama
bas statutes regulating the traffic in ardent spirits, and your committee are ot' opln·
ion that the Gra.ud Lodge bas uo power to supercede the laws of the State."
A system of work was adopted, and a proposition to have It taught by Lecturers
was submitted to the subordinate Lodges; and a committee was appointed to compile
and codify the constitution, laws, edicts, ond decisions of the Grand Lodge now In
force, the work when completed to be styled the" Masonic Code of Alabama."
'fb.e flnancal reports show a balanoe In the treasury of $2,997 13 in lawful money,
and $6,410 64 In Confederate currency-the latter, of course, worthless.
Among tile pleasing incidents of the Communication was the presentation of a
jewel to Past Grand Master WILLIAM C. PKNICK; and, from the remarks made on the
occasion, we should judge that the testimonial could not have been more worthily
bestowed.

and confers the degrees upon a non-resident is not to blame, we do caot believe.

mav, when absent from home, Innocently apply for them to J,odges which are pro·

hibited from receiving their applications. Committees of investigation can, in the

The Grand Master recommends the establishment of new Lodges in the large

Quite a lengthy report was presented by Past Grand Master BENJAMIN Il. FRENCH,
from the Committee on Jurisprudence, in relation to a difficulty between La FayeUe
Lodge, No. 19, of the District, and Resurgarn Lodge, No.169, of Iowa, the real cause of
which is to be found in the usage that has obtained in the District of Columbia, sanc·
tioned by a provision of the Constitution of its Grand Lodge, which permits its sl)bor·
dinates to confer the degrees up.on a non-resident, u11less the Lodge nearest the place
of the applicant's residence gives, within reasonable time, some tangible reason why
he should not be made a Mason-a refusal to grant permission being no impediment.
La FayeUe Lodge 1·ecei\"ed and acted upon the petition of an Indiana soldier tempo·
rarily stationed at Washington, and conferred upon him the first degree. Before tak·
ing the remaining degrees he removed to Iowa, and petitioned Reirurgam Lodge for
advancement, which Lodge applied to La Fayette Lodge for permission to confer the
other degrees, If the candidate was found worthy, which proviso would seem to imply
that his petition should be referred to a committee and be acted upon in the usual
manner. Instead of giving the permission as desired, La Fa.yeUe Lodge authorized
Resurgam Lodge to confer the second degree upon the candidate, and promised that
when notice was received that that degree had been conferred, he would be elected
to receive the third degree, and permission would be given to confer it. Though
nothing had thus far been said about the fees, this action of La Fayette Lodge
seemed to imply that they should be paid to it, as no Lodge In the District is allowed
to ballot for any of the degrees until the fee is paid. Resu,.gam Lodge feeling
offended, a very Intemperate letter was written by its Master to La Fayette Lodge,
and the matter was also laid by him before the Grand Master of Iowa, who presented
it to his Grand Lodge, denouncing in strong terms the action of the Washington
Lodges in conferring degrees upon non-residents, and their Grand Lodge for permit·
ting them to do so. The report of Bro. FRENCH establishes that La Fayette Lodge
had no disposition to act otherwise than properly, but it does not in any manner
defend the power claimed by his Grand Lodge, which claim has given, and as long
as it is persi~ted in will continue to give just cause of offence to every other Grand
Lodge in the United States. We need not go beyond its own proceedings for unan·
swerable reasons why it should not be exercised. In a Report on Correspondence
presented to and approved by it some years ago, it is said in referedce to this sub·
ject, that" The right can not for a moment be seriously entertained by any Grand
Lodge, and its practice should be discountenanced in every possible manner, as dis·
creditable to individuals, subjecting them to the imputation of endeavoring to evade
a just scrutiny at home, and unmasonic on the part of Lodges, subjecting them to be
imposed upon by unworthy persons, and wearing the appearance of a desire more to
increase the number of the craft and realize the fees .thence arising, than to guard
with scrupulous care the approaches to the temple committed to their charge."
Again, in 1860, Bro. FRENCH, from a similar committee, in reporting upon the well
known difficulties existing at that time between the Grand Lodges of England and
Maine, which originated in the exercise of this alleged right by a Lodge subordinate
to the former, quotes the following language used by the Grand Master of Engla.nd :"Every Lodge possesses the inhe.rent right to initiate any person whom it may consider fit and proper, without considering where his residence may be. It is not desir·
able nor convenient that a Lodge should bind itself to confine its initiations to residents
in its own immediate iocality ;"and adds, "There is no question in the minds of your
committee that the position in relation to juri~diction asAumed by the Rt. Hon. the
M.·. W.·. EARL OF ZETLAND, Grand Master of England, is wrong. It can not be sus·
tained by any Masonic law or precedent known to your committee."
Another evidence of its evil effects is to ·be found in a report last year of one of
the District De~uty Grand Masters of Maine, which states that a person who had
been rejected in that State by a number of adverse ballots, returned from a visit to
Washington, a Master Mason, having been made such without permission from home .

A handsomely printed pamphlet of ninety-six pages contains the proceedingt of

In bis Address; the Grand Master reported that the increase in num hers and
means during the year had been unexampled-a statement borne out by the fact that
fifty-seve'!l dispensations for the formation of new Lodges bad been issued during
tb~t period-and congratulated the Grand Lodge upon the fact that, notwith~tandlnr
this great Increase, the peace and harmony of the jurisdiction had not been in the
least disturbed. He also r~ported the issue of one hundred and six dispensations to
confer degrees, a.nd said th~ fees from the latter source were lesseneii, not so many
having been granted as applied for, because good reasons for their Issue were re·
quired. The work of the Grand Lodge bad been taught with good effect in a.II portions of the State, and had been received by the Lodges in a fraternal Rp.irlt. The

The Grand Master having been absent from the jurisdiction during the ·grel\ter

Grand Orato.r, the R.·. W.·. MARTIN W. WILLIS, but, though a copy of it was requested
for publication, it does not appear in the proceedings. A resolution was adopted
permitting persons residing within the jurisdiction of a Lodge which had ceased to
work for six months, to apply, after that time, to the next nearest Lodge for the degrees, and amendments were proposed to the by-laws of the Grand Lodge, which, If
adopted, will permit rejected applicants for affiliation to renew their appiications at
pleasure, and prohibit the conferring of degrees upon more than one candidate at a
time. The first we conceive to be a very sensible resolution, and the two le.st have
been the law in this jurisdiction since the adoption of the present Constitution.
The Grand Lodge decided that a brother could not be elected Master of a Lodge
who had not previously served as Warden, unless by dispensation from the Grand
Master, and that a Lodge could not enforce from its memberB.the payment of special
assessments, thongh levied for Lodge purposes exclusively. For reasons. heretofore
set forth in our proceedings l:ly thoe.e who have. preceded ns, we do not agree with
the first decision, believing that merit alone should be considered in the selection of
a Master; and it appears to us that a Lodge should have the undoubted right to deal
with a member who, if able, refuses to pay .his just proportion of its legitimate ex·
penses.

Of the style of the Addresses delivered by Grand Master GUILBERT, so much bas

Aside from the vanity and'' hifalutin" which are exhibited in all papers emanating

member known to be opposed to his admission; that objections made at any time
prior to the initiation of a candidate are equivalent to a rejection ; that Master
Masons are not required to reside any specified time within ~be jurisdiction cf a
Lodge before they can petition for affil!ation; that "neceSBary proficiency" consists
lo the acquirement, by the candidate, of the whole of the first section of the lecture
of the degree in which he Is examined ; that fees accompanying petitionR belong to
the Lodge when the candidates are elected, and need not be returned If the petitioners decline to receive the degrees; that a Lodge has the right to levy a special

discipline ; that degrees should not be conferred npon more than one candidate at a
time ; and tbttt the vote of a Lodge granting a dimit severs the connection of the
member applying for it, the written certificate usually issued being simply an evidence
of the fact.

Bro. McConul!l does not believe in the policy of compe!Ung Masons to be mem.
bers of Lodges, Masonry being 11 voluntary association. We certainly do. A person
upon being made a Mason voluntarily pro!Oises to conform to all the requirements of
the Fraternity, one of which is," that 11 Mason must be 11 member of some Lodge;''
and we do not think that he who voluntarily breaks bis pledge, has .cause to com·
plain, or is deserving of any sympathy, because the benefits and privileges of the
Order are confined to those who faithfully observe it. Bro. McCoBK:LE also deems
the regulation of our Grand Lodge, requiring 11 member suspended for non-payment
of does, to pl\y dues for t.he period during which he was suspended, lu order to
restore himself, to be unjust, it placing him in 11 wor>1e category than If he had com·
mitted a greater offence. When a member of 11 Lodge is suspended for non-payment
of does, it is his own fault. He should pay his indebtedness, if able to do so; if
unable, he should represent his inability to his Lodge, and his dues would be remitted.
The punishment for failure to do either of these things is not, as our brother says, 11
greater one than i~ inflicted for a violation of the "grand principles of Masonry/'
restoration, under the mil'dest sentence for the last cause, requiring at least a two·
t~ird vote. of the Lodge inflicting it;· while, in the other case, 11 Mason can at any
time, by his own act, place himself in good standing. We beiieve, therefore, in the
enforcement of the requirement, unless inability to pay be shown. Otherwise, 11
peraon suspended during twenty years, or longer-there is no limit-might at any
moment, for 11 comparatively trifling sum, place himself in the enjoyment of the
rights and privileges to which those only who have zealously performed their duties
should justly be entitled.

Lodge of the District of Columbia- that that body has the right. to make Masons of

of life-membership adopted by our daughter of Nevada wiil prove abortive, and

Seven dispensations for the formation of now Lodges were isssued ; one charter
was surrendered, and one Lodge had suspended labor and forfeited its charter. A
number of Army Lodges were organized under dispensation during the war, some.
of which were afterwards chartered. With the close of the conflict their powers as
Lodges ceased. Many of them lost all their records and other papers, and the sur- ,
viving members dispersed to different sections of the S~ate, without having or being
able to procure any written statement showing that they were members of such
Lodges. In view of this condition of affairs, and in answer to the repeatedly asked
question-What is the proper course to pursue in such cases? the Grand Master is·
sued an ediot authorizing the subordinates, to rece!.ve the petitions of those "".ho had
belonged to these Army Lodges, and to confer upon them the remaining degree or
degrees, or allow them to affiliate, with the proviso that if any member of 11 Lodge
to which such application was presented was not fully satisfied as to \he good stand·
Ing of the applicant, all the regular tests should be administered.

NEW YORK.
The Grand Lodge of the Empire State held its Annual Communication for the

The Address of Bro. HOLMES is one of those papers which, for many years past,
have evidenced the wisdom exercised by the brethren of New York in their choice
of Grand Masters. It lays before the Gl'and Lotlge, in a terse and business-like manner, every official act performed during the year, and presents for consider11tion many
useful and valuable suggestions. From it we learn that Masonry in that jurisdiction
was never in a more prosperous and peacefal condition ; and the g1·atifying intelligence is conveyed that the Grand Lodges of Virginia and New York are once more
in perfect accord, the differences heretofore existing between them having been satisfuctol'ily adjusted. Bro. HOLMES recommends that, in c11ses wh~re it is clearly ap·
parent that a brother charged with a Masonic offtlnse can not have a fair trial before
a COl!Jmlssion of his own Lodge, he be permitted to nsk that the commissioners be
appointed by the Grand Mas\er, the Deputy Urand Master, or the District. Deputy
Grand Master of the district in' which the Lodge Is located. A recommendation
which we heartily approve, and which we would like to see adopted in this jurisdlo·
tion, with the addition, that the ace.user should also be entitled to the same privilege,
if it was palpable that either the sympathies or prejudices of the Lodge In favor of
the accused would prevent the selection of an Impartial tribunal. He also recommends an increase in the fee for dl3pens11tlons to form new J,odges, as such Increase
would benefit the treasury and tend to check applications therefor ; and an amendment to the Constitution embodying the recommendation by increasing the fee to
eighty dollars was proposed. He o.nnl\unces the passage of a law by the Legislature
of the State, enabling the subordinate Lodges to hold real estate through Trustees,
without requiring them to be incorporated, and recommends, for the following reasons,
that those Lodges already incorpornted take advantage of the law:"All Lodges in any given jurisdiction should stand on the perfect level of equality,
and no Lodge shonld. have any existence save that which Is derived from Its wnrrant.
If an inc?rporated. Lodge should offend against the law~ of the Fraternity, the Grand
Lo~g~ might ~ecla1m it• warrant and such a Lodge still exist as a Lodge unde1· its ac&
?f mco1·P.01·11.~1011, a_nd the general laws of the State would sustain it, no matter how
mdefens1ble its action towards the Grand Lodge, so long as it would refrain from any
act violative of its corporate existence."
This recommendation was also approved by the Grand Lodge, and the ac& of the
Legislature, with directions for the manner of procedure to enable Lodges to o.va!J
themselves of its privileges, is appended to the proceedings.

refuse meat to those who will not work, or to forbid the exercise of Masonic privileges to tlw>se who will not take upon themselveR correspondinir duties by keeping
up their affiliation. We all know that it is the duty ot every Mason to 'belong to
some Lodge and contribute to its funds; and we all know, too, that great numbers
refuse to discharge this plain duty. and It logically follows that what one may do
with impunity, others may imitate wit h like freed om, and thns the Fraternity might
be extinguished by the remissness of Its own memhers. This knowledire hu led to
Ii great deal of brain-badgerin11; during the past ten years, and has given birth to

Regulations were adopted prohibiting Lodges from striking officers from the roll

.
opinion is undoubtedly correct. I
A committee was appointed to Inquire "as to the propriety of making such

increasing representation, from the burdens of local legislation, and executive and
judicial action, by distributing those powers among local bodies, without detracting
from the authority or powers of the Grand Master, or lessening the dignity or impairing the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge, as now constituted."

NOV A SCOTIA.
We have before us the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia, which,
contain 11 history of its formation, and a record of the transactions at its first Annual
Communication held at Halifax on the twenty-fir~t day of June, 1866. The reasons
assigned warra~t the organization, and if it could be shown th •t a majori~y of the
Lodges in Nova Scotia participated in its formation, we would not feel at hberty to
question its legality, for we believe in the right of the maj<>r~ty to determine. But
there is no evidence that a majority took part in the proceedmgs; all those Lodges
holding under the Grand Lodge of England refusing to countenance tb~m ! a.nd. since
the fof mation of this body, the Provincial Gra~d Lodg~, .under the Jur1sd1ct1on of
which the Lodges forming it were held , at a special meetmg declared the new Grand
Lodge illegal, the Lodges clandestine, and their members suspended. H?w many
Lodges adhere to the Provincial Grand Lodge we have no ·means of ascertaming, nor
can we learn how many there are in the Province. It is very unpleasant not to be
able to act in accordance with our sympathies, and that ours are with the new
organization we will not pretend to deny; but a sense of justice req~ires that no
decision should be rendered until all the parties are heard from. The circumstances
which caused the formation of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia resemble, in a remarkable degree, those which occasioned the creation of the Grand Lodge of Canada, though the disalfection which resnlte i in the organization of th.e first named
seems to have been exclusively confined to the Scottish Lodges, while the Grand
Lodge of Canada was established by a union of Lodges holding under the jurisdiction of all the Briti•h Grand Lodges. The reasons which induced the Grand Lodge
pf California to hesitate in acknowledging the Grand Lodge of Canada, when the
request to do so was originally made, apply with equal force in the preseut instance,
and the conclusions arrived at by the distinguished committee, to whom the matter
was at that time referred, are so pertinent now that we reproduce them in preference
to anything we could say:" The statements before us being purely ex parte, are not reg~rded by your com·
mittee as a sufficient ground for definite action, at the present time, o!1 t'he part of
this Grand Lodge. Thus, :While. w& extend to our. agg~ieved b~etbren !n IJanada all
the sympathy which taxation without representat10n, mconvemence without recom·
pense, and petitions treated with coldness and neglect, ar~ calculated. to exc1tewhile we would extend to them the hand of fraternal alfec.t10n, an~ desire to be regarded as their true Masonic brethren and co-worker~-w~1le W~· w1!l be ev.er rc~dy
to come to their assistance in the great struggle of mmd with mmd m the d1scuss1on
of those important questions which can only be settled by sue)! a c.ourse-and wlule
we would fondlr, hope for the time speedily to arrive when their br1ghtes~ ~opes and
anticipations will be realized, we are compellr.d to defer a formal recogmt1on .of the
body thus created until fntnre developments shall make that duty more plam nnd
.
imperative."
Since the formation of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia, an event.,has transpired,
~hich, it seems to us, may be the mea.ns of adjusting the present · difficulti.e~ in a
manner satisfactory to all parties. We allude to the creation of the Dom1mon of
Canada, by the union of a.II the British Provinces in one common g~vern~e~t, ~nd as
the principle is conceded that there can be but one Grand Lodge. IIl a Jnr1sd1ctlon,
we presume that the authority of the Grand Lodge of Canada will extend over all
parti of the Dominion. That it will be gracefully acknowledged by the Gra.nd Lodges
of Eagland, Scotland, and Ireland, and joyfully accepted by the Lodges 10terested,
we. can not permit ourselves to doubt. Believing with tbe Grand Mast~r of Canada
that this is a consummation earnestly to be desired, we look forward with hope for
its early accomplishment, and with it the restoration of harmony a.nd good fellowship a.mong our brethren of Nova Scotia.

SOUTH CAROLINA.
For the first time since the commencement of the unhappy troubles which con·
vulsed our country,. we are enl\bled to acknowledge the receipt of the proceedings
of this Grand Lodge. Two pamphlets have been placed in our hands, the first con·
talnlng a record of its transactions for the five years from 1861 to 1865, inclusive ;
the second, the record of 1866. The Annual Communications of 1861, 1863, 1864.,
and 1866, were held in the city of Columbia; that of 1862 was held in the city of
Yorkville; and that of 1866 in the city of Charleston.
At the Commun'cation which was held on the nineteenth and twentieth days of
November, 1861, the M.·. W.·. B. Rusu CAJlPBEJ,L, Grand Ma~ter, presided; and at
shat, as at all the subsequent meetings, the R.·. W.·. ALBERT G. MACKEY was Grand
Secretary. No address was delivered by the Grand Master, and but very little busl·
nesa· was tran~acted. The Grand Secretary read his Report on Correspondence,
which was ordered to·be printed; but, much to our regret, the order was not c.om· .
plied with. The Grand Master elect, the M.·. W.·. DAVID RAllSAY, was requested to
address an Encyclical Letter of advice and admonition to the Freemasons of the
jurisdiction, which request was complied with, and we are surprised that o. ).)aper so
creditable to Its author and to Masonry is nowhere to be found in the proceedings of
the Grand Lodge. .At the Communication held in 1862, on the eighteenth and nine·
teenth days of November, the R.-. W.-. T. P. SLIDER, Deputy Grand Master, presided.
lio addrees or reports of any kind, except financial ones, were presented, and, as at
the preceding meeting, the bueinees transacted appertained entirely to domestic mat·

.At the Communication held on the seventeenth day of November, 1863, the
R.·. W.·. D. J. BARNETT, Deputy Grand Master, presided. In a brief address pre·
eented by that officer, the sad announcement was made of the death of the Grand
Haster, the M.-. W.-. DAVID RAMSAY, to whose memory a glowing tribute was paid
by tho Grand Secretary. The Deputy Grand Master stated, as one of the effects of
the war, that but few of the Lodges in the State continued to work. Dispensations.
had been issued for the formation of five Military Lodges, but of their condition
nothing was known, no returns or reports from them having been received. The
usual local businees was transacted, and the M.-. W.-. JOHN H. BOATWRIGHT was
elected Grand Master, and the Grand Secretary was reelected.
At the Communication which was held on the fifteenth day of November, 186,,
an address was presented by the Grand Master, the first paragraph of which we
quote, to show the epirit·whlch seems to have animated some of our brethren or ·
South Carolina during the war:-'"Brethren : I congratulate you on the opportunity that is once more affo~de~ to
us of communing together under the consecrated roof of our beloved Institution.
While without, the startled ear is struck on every side with the crash of conflicting
arms, and the sky is overcast with the lurid clouds of war, here, at least, for a brief
period, around this sacred altar, and within this holy temple, all is serenity and
peace. Whlle we mourn the lose of many of our brethren who have fallen on the
t'leld of battle, or sunk under the exposures Incident to a so'dier's life, we cnn not be
too thankful to the Supreme Architect of the Universe, that we have been spared to
rekindle the fires of our altars, and to preserve for better and for happier times the
ble~sings of our philanthropic Order. Impre•sed with those sentiments which such
a condition of things is well calculated to excite, I come, as I trust you all do, to the
performance of the duties which lie before us, with an humble reverence for, and an
abiding trust in Him whose shield has been over us, and with a solemn determina·
tiou to do a.II ihat our Masonic duties will demand, In the.t spirit of brotherly love
which alone can make us deserving of the continued protection of Him whose name
we are taught to inv(Jke, or entitle us to the appellation of Masone and Sons of
Light."

course to be pursued in these ;:ases. My answers have uniformly been to this effect:
l ba~e looked upon these Millitary Lodges as extinct Lodges, whose records have
been lost or destroyed, and of whose membership there is no documentary evidence
in the archives of the Grand £,odge. In such cases it is impossible to obtain dimits,
and as the law does not and can not require impossibilities, I have ad\'ised that the
Lodge to which application is made for affiliation or advancement, ma.y lawfully
rlispen•e with the production of the dimit, and, on the person applying proving his

The Grand Master's Address opens sadly. The death of the M:. W.·. ARCHIBALD
S. RUTHVEN, Past Grand Master, and for so many years Grand S,ecretary, at the home
of his childhood, in Scotla1nd, is announced, and of his own bereavements he says:
"Almost in sight of where we now are, lie the remains of what a few months ago
were the denrest objects of our affections. The heart that beat in unison with our
own, and the hand that delighted to administer to our wants, are forever stilled, as
well as the little feet that ran to meet. and the arms that were stretched forth to
greet us when returning to refresl1ment from the toils of the day. A common grave
holds them both, and nongl1t is left bnt !Jte momery of the faithful love of the one,
and the innocence and affection of the other."
.

Five dispensations for the formation of new Lodges were issued by him during

The Grand Master, in his Address, contrasts the auspices under whieh the present meeting of the Grand Lodge is held, with those under which it assembled the

recognition of that body receive a very patient and deliberate investigation, and

from the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia in regard to

of thirty-two Grand Lodges, including those of California, but for what years does

rhetoric."

ing upon that portion of it which refers to the communication received from the

of the District-all which were adopted.

of West Virginia, in Jone, 1863, as an independent State by the Federal Government,

Masonic usage. Thus advised, a convention of Lodges was held in Grafton, on the
twenty-eighth day of December, 1863, in response to a circular issued by Fairmount
Lodge, No. 9. Great exc!tement, consequent upon events of the war, existing at the

more than a constitutional number of Lodges were rep.resented, it was thought best

mBy he remedied. The work was exemplified, but nothing was done to secure the
object desired. He also recommends the grunting of dimit< to members withdraw·
ing from Lodges, which custom was not practiced in that jm·isdiction, as the omission to do so led to serious inconvenience to brethren removing to other States.
A Const itution was adopted which contains some provisions that we 11re not accustomed to, and which seem to us strange. By it the Grand Master is Buthorlzed,
when he must necessarily be absent from the meetings of the Grand Lodge , to depute some member of that Ilody to officidte in his stead, provided the Deputy Grand
Master Is not in attendance. Nominations of candidates t'o1· offices is made obligatory
in both the Grand Lodge and the subordinates ; and iu the latter the candidates
named arc obliged to 1·etire during the balloting. There are many other provlslone
which we would like to note, but we confine om·selves to the following, the first or
which seems to give the Grand Lodge jurisdiction over the Chapter degrees, nnd the
second implies that it has in common with its subordinates the right to receive ancJ
act upon pctitio,ns for degrees.
"The members of the Grand Lodge and of all warranted Lodges within their Ju·
rlsdlctlon, so far as they have abilities and members, have an undoubted right to exercise all degrees of the AncieIJt Craft, and consequently the Royal Arch.
" Ever.v perRon admitted to any degree of Masonry in this Grand Lodge, shall pay
for the benetlt of this Grand Lodge, sixteen dollars."
No business of importance other than the adoption of the Constitution was trans·
acted. The Grand Lodge continued in session two days, and the Grand Master and
Grand Secretary were both reelected.

The Grand Lodge of this Territory held its Annual Communication for 1866 in
the city of Olympia , commencing on the nineteentl1 day of Sept ember, the R.'.

The Grand Master, the M.-. W.-. ELWOOD EVANS, having been absent from t he
State during the greater ·portion of the year, t he government of the Cr aft devolved
upon the Deputy Grand Master, who , in a brief address, presented an account of his
official acts. The Lodges, with one exception, which he forbears to name, in the
hope that the forbearance may be properly appreciated Bnd be productive of good,
are reported to be in a prosperous condition. He had decided that R Lodge could
not be held in a, frame building occupied, also, by a private family, if the voices could
be heard throughout the bnllding, and that the Masters of t he Lodges would be held
responsible if legal tenders were accepted for fees or does, the Grand Lodge having

prescribed that gold coin only should be received therefor. He bad also decided,
and his decision was concurred in by the Grand Lodge, that upon a proper application he would grant a dispensation to form and open a new Lodge in British Columbia, and that if tb.e Lodges established in that Colony refused to recommend the
petitioners for it, he would be satisfied with the recommendation ot' the nearest Lodge
under bis own jurisdiction, balling his reasons upon the ground that there never having been a Grand Lodge either in Vancouver Island or British Columbia, both Colo·
nies are open to all Masouic Grand Bodies, and that he knew of no law or precedent
requiring Maso~s residing therein to apply to any particular Grand Lodge for a dispensation. We are of opinion that Masonic usage has · conceded to the British Grand
Lodges the right to establish subordinate bodies in all countries acknowledging alle·
glance to the Crown of England, and in which there is no Grand Lodge established,
they having co·equal authority outside of their own immediate jurisdictions. If the
decision of Bro. Woon is a correct one, the Gmod Lodges of England, Scotland, or
Ireland would have the right to establish Lodges in auy territory of the United States
in which there is no Grand Lodge; nod yet if either were to do so, what a storm oC
indignat·ion would be aroused! There is no question that in countries independentln
themselves, like China or the Hawaiianlslti.nds, and in which no Grand Lodge exist.a,
any Grund Lodge bas the right to establish su bordinntes; but we doubt very much
whether this rigilt extends to a country subordinate to a government in wWch a
Grand Lodge is established, being of opinion that the Grand Lodge would have tha
same jurisdiction Masonically that the government had politically.
'f he Grand Secretary in bis report says that "as compared with former years, 11
general dullness in' matters Masonic' seems to have pervaded the entire jorisdlotion, the increase in membership being only four since the year preceding."

Bro. Bm11. H . FREEHA.N presented the following* memorial from the
Masters of the Lodges in San Francisco, composing the Me.sonic Boe.rd of
Relief of the.t city:To the M•., W.-. Grand Lodge of California:The undersigned, Masters of the several Masonic Lodges of San Fraoclaoo,,
respectfully memorialize your Grand Body upon the subject of the present method
of dispensing Masonic charity to those brethren belonging to other Jurisdictions w-ho
are destitute in our midst, and desire to present for your consideration the follow.l.ng
statement of facts :.,
About twelve years since the Masonic Board of Relief of the Cltq of San Fran·
cisco was organlZIJd, and since that time It bas expeuded in Masonic c'haritles abonL
sixty thousand Willa.rs, which sum has been exolnsively drawn from the Fralernlt]' of
• Bubaequentl:r ordered to be printed.

[Oct. 9.,

this city, with the exception of the sum donated from the funds of the Grand Lodge
at its last Annual Communication, and sundry comparatively small amounts refunded
by L:idi.:es whose members have been relieved by the Board.
We would represent that our city, being the principal commercial seaport of this
coast, naturally receives a large majority of all the Masone from other jurisdictions
whJ arrive in our State requiriag M1nonic assistance, thus devolving upon the seven·
teen hundred members of Lodges of this city a burden which we think should be
shared by the entire jurisdiction. From our experience as members of the Board of
Relief, we b elieve that the whole matter of the dispensation of Masonic charity
should be under the control and direction of the Grand Lodge, that body raising the
requisite funds therefor by a tax upon each Mason in the jurisdiction, and the fund
so raised to be applied in such manner as that body, in its wisdom, may direct.
We would further represent that, under the present Grand Lodge regulations,
where a member of a Lodge in this jurisdiction has been assisted by a. Board of Relier
or from the funds of another Lodge, there is nothing requiring the Lodge, .w hose
member has been so relieved, to refund the money thus expended. We believe that
it is incumbent on each Lodge to p1·ovide for its own members, and would respectfully request from your Grand Body the passage of a law requiring each Lodge to
refund all moneys which may be expended by other Lodges, or a Board of Relief, for
the relief of any of its members.
Confidinit in the justice of our representations, we offer the following resolutions
for the con3ideration of your Grand Body, and respectfully request their adoption:Resolveii, That the sum of ten cents be and is hereby levied monthly npon each
Master Mason in this jurisdiction; and that the money so raised shall be collected by
the Secretaries of the several Lodges, and transmitted to the Grand Secretary on the
first Monday of each month.
.Resolved, That a standing committee of three on Charity shall be elected by the
Grand Lodge- at each Annual Communication, whose duty it shall be to receive from
the Grand Secretary the money raised as provided in the foregoing resolution, and
disbnrse it as hereinafter directed.
Resolved, That, in any place where two or more Lodges have concurrentjurisdic·
tlon, the M1i..ters of such Lodges may form a Board of Relief, with articles of agreement to be approved by the Gmud Master.
Resolved, That the standing committee on Charity shalt disburse the funds by
it received, upon orders drawn by the Chairman and countersigned by the Secreta.ry of any Board of Relief duly organized.
Resolved, That each Board of Relief shall, on the fifteenth day of September or
each year, transmit to the Grand Lodge a plain and comprehensive report of their
operations during the preceding year.
, Resolved, That the money raiRed; es provided by the first of these series of reso·
lutlons, shall only be expended for the relief of Master Mesons, in good standing,
hailing from other jurisdictions, their widows and orphans; but that the several
Boards of Relief which may be organized under these regulations shall have power
to 11llieve the temporary necessities of M11ster Masons of this jurisdiction, their wid·
ows and orphans-the emount so expended to be refunded to the said Board of Relier
by tho Lodge of which the brother relieved may be a member.
Resolved, That whenever a Lodge within this jurisdiction shalt receive written
notice from the Secretary of another Lodge, also in this jurisdiction, or from the
Secretary of any Board of Relief which may be organized under the provisions
of the90 resolutions, under the seal of such Lodge or Board of Relief, that they
have expended nny sum of money for the relief of any of its members, or their
widows or orph11ns, it shall ba the duty of the Lodge so notified to transmit the
amount stated, immediately, to the Lodge or Board of Relief from which the notifica·
tion shall be received, together with Instructions as to whnt further relief in the case

93

'

Your Committee on Finances respectfully report that they have examined the
books, papers, and vouchers of the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary, and find
them in all respects correot.
The gross receipts for the year ending thirty.first July laat, for account of the
General Fund, were $11,722 46, whlle the appropriations are in excess of this amount
in the sum of $1,334 56. Whether the extraordinary appropriations made at the last
Annual Communication, in'l'olving the sum of aibout $3,000, were In every particular
judicious, is not a question for your committee to determine. Yet they deem it
proper to allude to the subject, in order that the Grand Lodge may be warned
against a too lavish authorization of expenditure at the present session. While
liberality is commendable, a proper economy, which shall 1'estrict our appropriations
at least within our revennes, is absolutely necessary.
Your committee are of the opinion that, while the office of Grand Lecturer Is,
perhaps, still necessary, t!ie onerous duties devolving upon that officer have so far
decreased, by the diffusion of the work in the appointment of his numerous deputies,
that the salary attached to that office should be dispensed with, and that the expenses
of obtaining the lectures should be borne by those who desire them. The salaries of
the other officers of the Grand Lodge, as fixed yeau ago, are not, in the opinion of
your committee, more than oomruensurate with the increased labor devolving upon
them by reason of the·growth of the Order throughout the jnrlsdlctlon ; and for the
same reason we may look fw no decrease of the necessary contingent expenses.
The revenue is amply sufficient to meet the requirements of the Grand Lodge, and
leave a fair balance each year In the tre11sury; and your committee recommend that
in the matter of donations it be not anticipated.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. JAMES L.i.WRENCE Ei10LISB, from the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following report:To the M:. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifomia :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal in the matter of the acquittal
of Bro. THOMAS R. ANTHONY. by San Joaqutn Lodje, No. 19, of charges preferred
against him, have had the same under consideration, and respectflllly report that, as
the specification to the charge was clearly established, the aocused could only have
been acquitted upon the assumption by the majority of the commissioners that the
offense charged and proven was not ,one for which the brother could be punished
masonically. But in this they were mistaken. The offense charged and proven Is embezzlement of a large sum of money. The law of our .F raternity Is that when a
Mason commits an offense which is a violation of the moral law and of the law \)f
the land, he also commits a Masonic crime, because he thereby brings shame upon
the Craft. The majority of the comml1sloners in the case erred in their judgment,
and your committee therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
Reaolved, That the action of San Joaquin J,odge, No. 19, In the case of Bro.
THOHAS R. ANTHONY, be reversed and set aside, and that the case be remanded for
a new trial.
All which is respectfully submitted.

"We learn from Holy Writ that it was decreed in the wisdom and counsel or
Deity aroretime, that a house should be bnilded at Jerusalem, erected to God and dedicated to His holy name. We also learn from the same Yacred source that it was in

We also learn from history and tradition, that thiP building was the most spacious,

walls, its roof, its co.rridors, blazed with the lustre of precious gems; tllat in its inner
courts, the Deity had chosen his earthly abode, and that there, between the cherubim, the divine presence rested, whence issued the voice of God, and whence the subtle
perfume of deli~ate woods Rhed fragrance over the sacred place. That temple, in
its earthly form, Is gone. No longer does its roof of beaten gold reflect the glittering

and the splendor of its internal adornment hllve for centuries only existed, ns dreams

torice.lly, my brethren, we only date from the building of the Jewish Temple, and
yet we have outlived nations, and states, and empires. System after system of
religion has risen, has flourished, he.a decayed; and yet, a.mid the wreok of creeda,
of religions, and of nations," Freemasonry still survives I" Aye, still survive&, with
all the vigor of eternal youth, with the wealth of thirty centuries frosting her brow
with glory; and while all things else of human origin have succumbed to the gie.ni
Time, which has written on their tombs the inexorable word "decay," we yet exist
with as much certainty or Immortality as anything on which an earthly imprint Is
stamped can possibly hope for.
It were a thankless task to follow up the broken threads in the tapestry of
ancient mythology, to trace through the labyrinths of doubt the mythological
representation of the death and resurrection of Osiris, the orgies of Bacchus, the
rites to Ceres, or the mysteries of Dionysius, of Mitbre.s, or of Egypt, or of the Se.mo·
thrac!11n rites, even could we pick our steps with safety to the conclusion that the
base of their secret worship, their" great mystery,'' was belief in the "unity of God"
and the "immortality of the soul." For, while as speculative Masons, we may
we~ve beautiful theories to flatter our self-love, we need not the adventitious aid of
such a beginning to make us love aud venerate onr institution; since we know that
none can enter its sircred portals but those who believe in God and In the soul's im·
mortality, and that on those cardinal points we build our grand speculative structure.
Believing in God's unity and me.n's immortality, we a.re forced to the adoption of the
virtues which a.re traced on our" tl'estle board" with characters of living light"brotherly love-truth-charity." We know we shall be immortal, for truth can not
die. We she.II progress, and yet be unchangeable ; for from our initial point, year
after year, and through all the centuries, our teachings have been Impelling us onward in the faith of me.n's brotherhood; while the everyday necessities of man impel
us to relieve the distressed, to whisper good counsel, to wipe a.way the tear of the
widow, and to comfort the orphan. This work gives us a. higher and holier grasp of
charitable thought. It not only goes with us through life, but, as we stand around
the last rest!ng·ple.ce of mortality, it teaches us to give our brother, with prayers and
hope, into tho arms of the Great Father. Our faith looks beyond the vs.ii; and while
we do not dictate to any a religious system or creed, we yet recognize that Me.aonry
is the handmaid and a.id of religion in its highest and purest signification.
It is true that our first Grand Master gave us this admonition-" Forget not the
law and remove not the ancient landmarks which thy fa.tilers have set;" but it has
not been kept simply as a duty, for laws have been made which the framers decreed
should be unchangeable and perpetual, yet they have passed a.way. The light upon
our altar he.a not been kept bright simply by the discharge or the duties of benev·
olence or charity, nor because of the command to cherish that which is good; but
rather because our Order has seized hold of grand truths, and, without forcing them,
he.a, by its teaching~, led the wor.d from a low barbarism to a high civilization;
because we have bmlded on a sure foundation, not blown by adverse winds Into the
eddies ,.nd shoals of error ; because through all our mystery there runs the golden
thread of" brotherhood :" And, while we know that the source whence has flown all
of theology, all of philosophy, and all of science is to be found in the ancient my•
teries, and that we must go back of history to find the fountains of truth; yet, as those
societies were the fountains of moral life, so we have become heir to their virtuee,
and stand to-day by our record in the light of hfatory as the mother of c1vilize.tion.
l do not overdraw the picture, nor is it painted in a. spirit of pride or boa.sting. Yet
when we reflect that all ideas which look to the elevation or advancement of our
race are received at first as fanatical ; that vast cycles of time sometimes elapse
between the birth of the thougl1t in the brai11 of some true brother, and its actual
practical e.pplice.tlon in the world ot science, or politics, or theology; when we
remember this, we rejoice that the corner·stone of' our temple of Love was ever

all preferment depends on real worth and personal merit only;" and in that we onl;r
carried out in our practice the philosophy of the theory that "Masonry regards no
man for hia worldly wealth or honors." While we all vigorously repudiate the
doctrine of the levelers, we yet cherish the fact that "rank is bat the stamp on the
guinea.''
Masonry, while t~uly conservative, is a progressive science. In its ritual every one
of its symbols will lead the mind into delightful paths in scieooe or morals. From
the moral truths drawn from the impressive ceremonies of the several degrees, we
niay go out into nature and drink in a perpetual joy in thought. Every throb in
nature has its counterpart in our mysteries. So long as sickness, sorrow, and death
exist on earth, so long will our mission remain nnfnlfiiled; so long as morality, as
philanthropy, as charity, shall remain human virtues, so long wlll our destiny force '
us to exist as a power potent for good , the enemy of vice, the twin-brother of virtue.
We are hut instruments in the hands of the Omniscient, carrying out the problem of
human destiny; and, as generation succeeds generation and the bubble of individual
life breaks on the shore of the river dividing life and death, we shall realize that " it
is the dead who govern; we, living, but obey."
Our tendency is to destroy individualism and to aggregate the world into unity
and. brotherhood. Our most important truths are not taught by language, for that
is an imperfect mode of expression. By the quiet growth of symbolic teaching we
shadow forth the eternal and the Infinite. God reveals himself to man more power·
fully through the symbols of nature than through verbal machinery. No language
can speak so eloquently of God's magnificence and power as the sight of " the world
with its corollary of stars and drnpery of gold-fringed clouds." Symbols are the
speech of Deity. So Masonry speaks more clearly through the allegory of symbols. .
To the ear of the initiate there is a deeper meaning in all the sounds of nature ; to
his sense, the sun at morn, at noon, at eve, is more than suggestive; to him the world ie
a book, and nature a kindly teacher; the drops of rain, the river , the waterfall, the '
sprig of evergreen, the golden grain, the fragrant valleys, the everlasting hills, the
voice of the lion, the hum of the b ee, the light of day, the gloom of night , the din of ·
labor, or the quiet hour of rest, each b rings reflections symbolical of truths unknown
to the profane. To us each of our signs and symbols is fraught with meaning, and,
connected with nature, is clothed with magic beauty. The prodigality with which
the universe is decorated teaches us to avoid mate1'iallsm-skepticism. No one can
bring his soul face to face with nature and not be drawn by the subtle attraction of
spirit to a closer communion with the great, divine, invisible centre. Go out in nature's
solemn hour and cast your eyes upon the harmonious scene, and you will unconscl·
ously become divested of self, and, looking into the immeasurable depths of apace ,
will exclaim"How often we forget all time, when lone,

Your committee, to whom was referred the application of JERRY C. NOONAN,
expelled by Chico Lodge, No. 111, on the seventh day of January, 1865, to be restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration, and respectfully report that the .applicant was expelled for unmasonic

solicits the Grand Lodge to consider favorably his application for restoration, on

contrary, your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That JERRY C. NOONAN, who was expelled by Chico Lodge, No. 111, on
the seventh day of January, 1865, be and he is hereby restored to all the right.a and
privileges of Masonry.

From the above favorable exhibit, and it being shown by the Grand Secretary
that the expenses of the Grand Lodge for the ensuing year .will be materially lessened, unless the Grand Lodge should again order some extraordinary appropriations such as those of last year, your committee, at his suggestion, recommend
a reduction of the dues for account of the Representative Fund, to the sum of
twenty-five cents for each member borne upon the rolls of the subordinate Lodges.
Believing that such amount of dues, with the balance of funds now on hand, will be
amply sufficient to meet all the demands upon that Fund for the coming year, they
olfer for adoption the following resolution:Resolved, That there shall be levied upon the Lodges of this jurisdiction, for the
ensuing MasoniC year, in addition to the dues prescribed by the Constitution, the
sum of twenty-five cents for each member borne upon their respective rolls at the
date of their annual returns, fo1· account of the Representative Fund; which assessment shall be in lieu of the assessment heretofore levied for that purpose, and shall
be paid at the same time and in the same manner as is prescribed for the payment of
the regular annual dues.
Your committee also recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That hereafter no Lodge under this jurisdiction, located beyond the
limits of this State, ~hall receive an allowance for the expenses of a representative
to this Grand Lodge ; nor shall any such Lodge be chargeable hereafter witll dues
on account of the Representative Fund.
All which is respectfully submitted.

B1·0. J.&MES L. ENGLISH, from the Committee on Grievances, presented
the following reports:-

Bro. HARRISON JoNES 1 from the special committee to whom was referred
the memorial of the Masters composing the Board of Relief of the City of
San Francisco, presented the following report:-

To the M.'. w... Grand Lodge of California:The committee, to whom was referred the memorial and accompanying proposed
resolutions from the Board of Relief' of the City of San Francisco, have had the same
under consideration, and report as follows:Your committee believe that the Lodges of the interior owe it to themselves and
to justice, to aid in every manner in their power the brethren of San Fr•ncisco in
dispensing charity to the sick and destitute of other jurisdiction• who may there be
found. Your committee also think that it requires no argument to show how just it is
that they should, when able so to do, reimburse the Board of Relier when assistance'
has been given by that body to one of their own members, bis widow or orphans.
But they do not deem it advisable to enact any law upon that subject at the present
session of the Grand Lodge, and they therefore recommend that the memorial and
resolutions be published with the proceedings of this Communication1 in nrder that
the subordinate Lodges may have an opportunity to instruct their representatives
whether to vote for or against said resolutions at the next Annual Co1Dmunication.
All which is respectfully submitted.
N. GREENE CURTIS,
ADOLPHUS HOLLUB,
HARRISON JONES,
Committee.
JAMES ANDERSON,
WM. C. RANDOLPH,

[Oct. 12,

To the M." W .'. Grand :f,odge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal in the matter of the a cquittal
of Bro. WILLIAM M. LA ROCHE, by Occidental Lodge, No. 22, of charges preforred
against him, have had the same under consideration, a.nu respectfully report as
follows:·
The accused has unquestionably been guilty of a Masonic oftense. The specific&·
tions are, that he made s'ta.tements of a highly defamatory character against a
brother. Every Mason is under the obligation · not to injure a brother in his good
name. He must neither originate statements of a defamatory nature against a
brother, nor give circulation to any that he tnay have heard, because injury may
be done as well by the one as by the other ; in fa.ct, it is the circulation that gives
slander its effect. It is as much an offense to circulate such statements amongst
Masons as amongst others. If the offense is committed without malice, the offender
is deserving, at least, of a reprimand; if it is committed maliciously, the offender
deserves expulsion.
In the present case, in order to rebut the pre~umption of malice, the accused
introduced witnesses to prove that injurious r eports were in circ.ulation, and had
been communicated to him; but he introdur.etl no witness who testified that any
such report was in circulation a.s that set out in the first epecillcation, and which
was clearly proved as uttered by him.
'!'hat a. brother commits a:1 offense und~r the influence of liquor is no excuse
upon a Masonic trial, because his condition_ is itself a disregard of one of the car·
dinal virtues of a Mason-temperance.
When the commissioners, upon a trial; can not find the accused guilty of the.
charge or specification, as set out, they may negative any part of the charge. or
specllication which they do not fiud against the accused, and return a verdict, or
judgment, for that portion of the specification or charge of which they find the'
accused guilty. Inasmuch, therefore , as the accused was guilty of a Masonic
offense , the commissioners erred in thdr judgment, and your committee recom".
mend the adoption of the following re•olution :Resolved, That the actio11 of Occidental Lodge. No. 22, in the case o( Bro.
WILLIA::ll M. LA RocHE, be reversed autl set aoide, an 1 that the case be remanded
for a new trial.

'.lb the M. ·• W.·. Grand Lodge of California :Y onr committee, to whom was rP.ferred the question proposed by the Master .o f
Occidental Lodge, No. 22, Rs to whether 11 brother, a party to a. trial, is entitled or
not to a transcript of the record of the tri11l and evidence, where an appeal is ma.de
to the Grand Lodge, respectfully report that they have considered the question, and
are of opinion that the record and proceedings had upon a trial belong to the secret
archives of the Lodge , and ought not to be made public in any manner, except so far
as it may be necessary for the purpose of transmitting the same to the Grand Lodge
for review. They can re11dily see how a party, found guilty of a charge before a
Lodge, might make unworthy use of the evidence rendered before ~e J,odge, if furnished to him in authentic form, a.nd how he might desire to preserve it for purposes

to have complete accesA to the record, to enable him to make a full and perfect

Your committee, to whom were referred certain questions propounded by Bro.
JORN MABTIN, report that they have carefully considered the same, and are of the
opinion that the first qnestlon, which Involves the absolute right of visit by a Malter
Mason in good standing to any Lodge where he may present himself, ~fter dne
proof of his qualifications, has been and still ls a somewhat dispnted point in
Masonic jurispru4ence. But your committee consider the question as permanentl7
settled in this jurisdiction, the Grand Lodge of this Stat e, at its last annual Communication, having atllrmed a decision of the Committee on Jurisprndence laying down
the general rule that the right of visit is not, as IB sometimes supposed, absolute
and indefeasible, and that the Master of a Lodge is clothed with authority to aay
who of those hailfng from other Lodges shall visit his.
As to the second question, whether a Master of a Lodge can receive a mlnor1&7

7b the M. ·. W." Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the question submitted. by Bro. BENNET
PULVl!IBHAN, as to whether, under the circumstances detailed in his statement of
facts, the Master of a Lodge had a right to exclude one of its members therefrom,
respectfully report tha.t they have given his written statement (which is somewhat
voluminous) a careful consideration, and from it extract the following facts :-That
a member of a Lodge was supposed, improperly, and almost generally, to use the
black-ball on the application ot' candidates for admi~sion into the Order; and that,
tor that reason, and for some harsh expressions used by him relative to the election
of a caudidate, the Master refused, and still refuses, to allow him to enter the Lodge.
Your committee are of the opi.n ion that the Master was incorrect in his action. A
member of a J,odge is at all times entitled to be present and participate in its proceedings, while he conducts himself with due order and propriety; and nothing
1hort of a violation of such rules authorizes his being refused admission to his Lodge
whilst he remains a member of it in good standing.

1b the M:. W.•. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the question submitted by Bro. RICHARD
DALll, as to whether a Lodge can receive the petition of a brother from Rhode Island
for affiliation, without his producing a dlmit, report that under the regulations of the
Grand Lodge of Rhode Island a dimit is not granted to a brother until he has actually
joined another Lodge. As an applicant is, by that regulation, unable to obtain his
dimit, through no fault of his, your committee think that the existence of that fact i1
a sufficient explanation of his inability to furnish It, and satisfies the requirements of
Sec. 2, Art. 111, Part 111, of the Constitution of this Grand Lodge.
All which ls respectfully submitted.

'rhe Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows : BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF 0A.LIFORNIA :The Supreme Ruler of the Universe has permitted us to meet again in annual convocation; and, before engaging in the business of the session, it is our pleasnre to
acknowledge our dependence upon Him, to return thanks for the great bene.flte re·
ceived at His hands, and to implore His continued blessings upon our time-honored.
institution.
We have 1o-day opened the nineteenth .Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of California. Young llmong sister Grand Lodges, it occupies a high and honorable
position ; let it be our purpose so to legislate during the present session that, when
our recorded acts shall be added to its history, we need not to be ashamed of the
result of our labors as workmen of the temple. The history of the past year but repeats the prosperity of its predecessor. Harvests so abundant as to excite the admiration of the world have brought us increased wealth, and strengthened our c<infl·
dence in the resources and stability of our young State. The year has, in trpth, been
to us one of peace and abundant prosperity, yet amid its successes we have been
called upon to pause in our labors and exclaim, we deposited the sprig of acacia
in tbe grave of a beloved brother, this is indeed the end of all our building and of all
our labor. There is a vacant place in our temple to-day; a column has broken;
one of the principal supports of our conscious edifice has fallen; "the silver cord
is loosed, the golden bowl is broken, the pitcher is broken at the fountain, the wheel
is broken at the cistern; the dust has returned to the earth as it was, and the spirit
unto God who gave it." We mourn the loss to-day of brother HENRY HARE HARTLEY,
Deputy Grand Master, who departed this life at his home, in Sacramento, on the
twelfth day of March last. .A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge was called,
and on the seventeenth of March the last sad tribute of respect and affection was
paid to his remains. Brother HARTLEY had long been identified with us ; his name
is familiar to all who read our proceedings, as was his manly form and genial countenance to those of you who for the last twelve years have attended our annual
meetings. Exemplar of the faith he professed-zealous Mason-Christian gentleman-may the sweetness of the summer's last rose linger long over his resting place,
and green be his memory forever.
We also mourn the loss of another brother, gone from among us during the pa~t
year. Brother WILLIAM H. PETERSON, Past Senior Grand Warden, died at his home
in Los .Angele~, in the month of May last, in the prime of life. He has obeyed the
dread summons, and passed from his labors on earth to the rewards awaiting the
faithful craftsman. Let us who survive our departed brethren be admonished by
their untimely decease of the uncertainty of human life, and by our lives and actions
henceforth, in accordance with our professions, may we be designated as Free and
Accepted Masons.
The most friendly relations exist between our jurisdiction and other Masonic

as

1868.J

Grand Lodge of Ccdifornia.

273

bodies. A few cases have occurred of violation of our jurisdictional rights by tlte
subordinates of other Grand Lodges, but, when presented to their notice, the promptness with which such acts have been disavowed and censured, and the regard shown
for the principle of personal and territorial jurisdiction, so wisely adopted and urged
upon the attention of the Fraternity during a series of years past by this Grand
Lodge, has been so heartily indorsed and commended that we may reasonably hope
that this prolific source of discord is at no distant day to be controlled by uniform leg·
islation and an honest desire anio.ng Grand Lodges to respect each others' rights.
.At the last .Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of New York It was resolved that it shall be made an imperative duty on the part or subordinate Lodges
to present, in print or writing, the following questions to every candidate for initia·
tion, req~lring him to answer in writing each question, and to state that he does so
upon his honor as a man; the said questions and answers to be returned to and become the property of the Lodge before any ballot shllll be taken upon his petition:"Where were you born? What is your age? What is your occupation? How
long have ;vou lived in the State of New York? How long in the town, city, county,
or village m which you now reside? Have you ever to your knowledge been pro·
posed as a candidate and rejected in a Masonic Lodge, and if so, when and in what
Lodge? Do yon believe .in the existence of one ever-living and true God! Do yon
know of any physical, legal, or moral reason which should prevent you from becoming a Freemason?"
This, it seems to me, is a sure preventive of the evils it Is designed to cure;
and, at' the same time, furnishes an indisputable cause for discipline in cases of mis·
representation or false statement.
In .April last I addressed a communication to the M.-. W.-.Jurns M. ANDERSON,Grand
Master of Masons in Tennessee, calling his attention to a violation of the jurisdlc·
tional rights of this Grand Lodge by one Qf its subordinates; and In July I received
his answer, fully recognizing, in the most fraternal manner, the principle contended
for, expressing his regret at the occurrence, and promising to bring the matter be·
fore his Grand Lodge, at its first Communication thereafter, for Investigation. Com·
plaint has also been made to me of a similar violation by a subordinate of the Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts; but not being furnished with the details of the case, I have
not communicated with the Grand Master of that State in regard to the matter.
In May last I received from the Grand Secretary, to whose care it had b1!en
addressed, a communication from B. B. French Lodge, No. 15, Washington, D. C.,
addressed to - - Lodge, San Francisco, informing said body that a former real·
dent of this juristiiction had applied to B. B. lfrench Lodge for the degrees of
Masonry·, and demanding to know if any reason existed why he should not be re·
ceived into the Order, stating that the petition would be due for 'action on May
fourth. Inasmuch as the communication was under date of .April tenth, It will be
readily seen that the inquiry was in effect but a matter of form.
In January last I was informed that a Lodge in our jurisdiction had, about a year
since, received the petition, elected, and conferred the degrees upon one known by
them to be an E. A. Mason, owing allegiance to the jurisdiction of a sister Grand
Lodge. Upon investigation, the facts being admitted, I directed the offending Lodge
to communicate with the Lodge whose jurisdictional right had been Invaded, to
explain the error, m11ke such reparation as Is just, when the circumstances should
be understood, 11nd petition for their consent. This Grand Lodge having ever been
je11lous of its rights in this respect, and having declared in its q~l!fral Regulations
that it would not tolerate an invasion of them, has also taken equal care to avoid
Infringing upon the same rights of other Grand Lodges. Our system of jurispru-'
dence, settled by the able decisions of my predecessors, and confirmed by your
action at successive Cpmmunications, has rendered my duties comparatively light and
pleasant. In so large a jurisdiction as ours it is to be expected that inquiries will
arise, from time to time, both in regard to the construction of laws, and the duties of
