During the last year I have granted six dispensations for the creation of new
Lodges, seven to permit certain Lodges to hold elections at other than the time
prescribed by the Constitution, and five to permit the reception and action upon
petitions of rejected applicants within a less period than twelve months after their
rejection. The evidence justifying this action, with the various proposed amendments to by-laws, approved during the year, will be presented by the Grand Secretary for your consideration. In granting the dispensations for new Lodges, I have
required evidence in regard to the locality of the proposed new Lodge, with refer:
ence to its permanency, its business prospects, and the quality of the material
from which the future membership of the Lodge would probably be drawn. All
applications for dispensations where the petitioners could not present satisfactorf
evidence that the proposed Lodge would be a living association, competent to exeIIJplify our work with credit to itself and honor to the Fraternity, have been
refused. The Lodges applying for dispensations to elect officers at other than the
usual time, in one instance, were prevented from assembling by the storms of last
December; in another, to fill vacancy oocasioned by the death of the Master; lftld
in the others the necessity arose from the refusal of the officers elect to serve. In
granting dispensations to re-ballot, I have required conclusive proof that the application was not foimded npon, and had not grown out of, the illegal dis.11nssion
of the ballot, but was for the. correction of a mistake. In approving the various
amendments of by-laws, I have required said amendments to be in conformity with
the uniform code.
Application was made to me in April last, by one of the Lodge8, requesting permission to appear in Masonic clothing to participate in public procession with the Odd Fellows in celebrating their anniversary. Again, in May, application was made on behalf
of another Lodge, for permission to celebrate the annrversary of Saint John the Baptist, by a "public procession in full regalia , an oi:ation, and ball." Heartily concurring, as I do, in the opinion of Grand Master 'BsIJCHER, approved by the Grand Lodge,
that " on no occasion, except for the burial of a brother, is it permitted for any
J,odp:e or number of Masons to appear fo Masonic clothi11g without permission from
the Grand Master, and that permission ought very rarely to be asked or granted;"•
and. with the Grand Master of Maine, who says, in a decision on the same subject"we are constrained to say that it is contrary to the usages of the Order, and improper for the Fraternity to take part, in their conventitmal character, in any public demonstration, except to perform some Masonic labor;" and these opinions
having been reiterated by Grand Master CLAIBORNE, and again approved by the
Grand Lodge, I hold the same to be the law of the jurisdiction, and have refused
the desired permission, where no Masonic labor was to be performed, i;eporting lllY
action for yonr consideration.
The following question was presented to me, arising out of circumstances con·
nected with a trial in Natoma Lodge, No. 64. Article IV, Part VI, of the Constitution,
is silent as to the precise manner in which testimony can be obtained for the purposes of a Masonic trial, where the witnesses reside without the jurisdiction of the
Lodge trying the case, and will not attend voluntarily. Yet the spirit of the whole
8 .rticle seems to suppose that it can be had, as otherwise the right of trial would be
seriously impaired, and in some cases absolutely denieq. The fifth section directs
the Master to summon the witnesses, if residing within the jurisdiction of his
Lodge, and then provides generally that they, if Masons, shall testify on their honor
as such, and if not Masons, by deposition before a proper officer-the party reqllil'ing the depositions, to notify the other of the time and place where they will be taken.
Jt does not need a very forced construction of this article, and particularly to pre••
vent a failure of notice, that depositions can be taken at any place on due notice.to

I have received. nn~e.rons letters inquiring in regard to the physical qualifications
of appllcants, the IDqumes generally representing the particular case presented as
one not cover~d by G~neral Regulation No. 18. My ruling has uniformly been in
accordance with a strict construction of said regulation, t1l wit: that the applicant
must not only be able "to conform literally to what the several degrees require of
him," but t~at he must not be dismembered. The rule may appear rigid" but having
observed with regret the prevalent disposition to enroach upon our old established
custo~s, I deem_it safer to hold firmly to the rule as Interpreted here. J find that
alt~ough the ru!1Dgs of my predecessors have been uniformly In accordance with such
strict oonstruct1on of the law, yet there is so general a disposition to allow individual
cases, throug.h personal friendly considerations, or through sympathy, to be • empted from its requirements, that I submit the consideration of Regulation No. 18 to
~he Committ_ee on J~risprudence for reindorsement and approval, or for modifloation,
if so determmed, with t~e recommendation that the report thereon, when ratified by
the Grand Lodge, be pr1Dted and sent to every Lodge in the jurisdiction and that
the Master be directed to call the attention of committees of investlga;ion there.
after appointed, to such reg?latlon and report. Jn this conMctlou the question bu
b~en presented as to the right to confer the remaining degree or degrees upon a
dismembered Entered .Apprentice or Fellow Craft, such dismemberment having- 00 •
curred supsequently to his initiation or passing. In the case presented I decided
that as the applicant was physloally perfect at the time of his Initiation hi~ faith and
good intentions toward Masonry, together with the fact that he had re~eived partial
knowledge of o.ur mys~ries, wlfnld justify the Lodge In conferring the remaining
degrees upon him, provided he was able to conform literally to the requlremente of
the remaining degrees. I am aware that this decision may be considered by eminent
Mas.ons, learned in Masonic law, as Inconsistent with our General Regulation on this
snbJect, but I trust the question may be duly considered and definitely settled at the
present session.

During the past year I have visited many of the Lodges, and have been gratified to
notice the genera~ observance of the requirements of the Grand Lodge In regard to
work. While some excel In the degree of proficiency attained, all appear to be deal·
rons of conforming to the standard adopted. In these visitations I h11ove been deeply
Impressed with the necessity for the adoption of some system that would secure an
annual Inspection of all the Lodges, particularly of the smaller ones remotely situ·
ated. Many irregularities creep into their management from the change of Masters
and other causes. Errors, easily corrected if discovered in time, grow to be serious
elements of discord after the lapse of 11 few months. I can offer no stronger
argument in support of the necessity of some system that will secure to the Masters
of Lodgea advice and practical instruction in the business of governing 11 Lodge,
than the Grand Master's correspondence, on file in the Grand Secretary's office ;
but perhaps 11 single Instance, Illustrative of the fact alleged, will impress the
importance of the suggestion more deeply upon your minds. In one of our older
Lodges the following circumstance occurred during the past year. At a stated
meeting A Informed the Lodge that B was desirous of joining it, and had authorized him (A) to sign his petition ; whereupon the petition was signed, recom·
mended, received, and referred to the usual committee, who In due time reported
favorably, and B was elected, initiated, and made a Master Mason. After the lapse
of a few months B desired to visit a neighboring Lodge. He was examined and found
to be tolerably proficient In his knowledge of the ritual and the modes of recognition,
but, In answer to the r equest for his signature upon the Lodge Register, he Informed
the Tyler that he could not write. Upon an investigation, the Lodge pleaded entire
ignorance of amended General Regulation No. 18, and acknowledged gross carelessness in the transaction of its business. This case is mentioned to illustrate the Irregular
manner in which business is disposed of in many Lodges, and to direct the attention
of every Master in our jurisdiction to the necessity of studying the Constitution and
Regulations, causing them to be read in his Lodge, and conforming to the mode and
manner there laid down for the performance of all his duties-remembering that he is
responsible for the acts of his Lodge, that in the faithful performance of his duties
lies the security of our beloved Order, and that herein is its only danger, for if Freema·
sonry is ever destroyed, it can only be by the criminal Ignorance and neglect of its
f'riends. Brethren, let us carefully guard the entrance to our household. Keep out
every unworthy intruder, and our Fraternity will receive the continued approbation
of all good men, and its foundation remain unshaken.
At our last Annual Communication 11 memorial tras presented from the Masonic
Board of Relief, setting forth the expenditures and history of t~at organization, and
submitting for your consideration certain resolutions, to be found in the printed pro·
ceedlngs of last year at page 89, the object being the. adoption of some plan to equal·
lze the raising of funds to be dispensed for purposes of Masonic oh11rlty,' 11nd proposing to place the same under the control of the Grand Lodge. As it has now been
before the Lodges during the year past, it Is hoped that during this session It wl\l
receive the consideration which Its Importance demands.
Brethren, with the close of this Communication will cease my connection with the
high and honorable position which I have occupied, through your partiality, for the
year p118t. If, In the performance of my duties, errors have been committed and
offense given, I beg yon to believe that the only motive prompting me has been the
honor and welfare of the great trust committed to my•care. I submit this record of
my official acts for your oonsideration, and invoke upon your deliberations that
harmony which is the lltrength and support of all institutions, especially of Free·
masonry. •
WILLIA.V A. DAVIES,
Grand Master.

Th the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :In submitting this Report from the Committee on Correspondence, the writer is
fr~e to say that had he known the magnitude of the task imposed upon him, when
appointed by the Grand Master, he would have shrunk from undertaking it. Pressed
as he Is with a multiplicity of duties, growing out of his position In relation to Church
and sohools, he feels his Inadequacy to do justice to the mass of material which It has
been his duty to pass In review. He submits this report with diffidence, fearing that
in oomparison with those of his illustrious predecessors, It will appear lame and impotent Indeed. But such as It Is, It Is respectfully submitted to the Fraternity. The
writer has not aimed at a discussion of the many points of Masonic law that have
presented themselves, and henoe but little has been written thereon. He has sought.
rather to skim the cream of information from the proceedings of all the Grand Lodges,
and to give his brethren In this jurisdiction a fair account of what has been said and
done elsewhere. If he has suceeeded in this he is content, and without further apol·
ogy, submits the result of his labors to the Grand Lodge.

ALABAMA.
The proceedings of the forty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Alabama for 1867, fill a well printed pamphlet of nearly two hundred pages, and
give gratifying evidence that prosperity, as well as peace and harmony, again bleHes
the Fraternity In this jurisdiction, whereat, as scripture enjoins, we " rejoice with
them that do rejoloe."
The Communication was held In Montgomery, on December 2d, Sd, 4th, 6th, and
6th, 1867 -the M:. W.·. WILBON W1LLI.l.¥B, presiding as Grand Master, and the
R:. W.-. DANIBL SAY!IB being Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from
one hundred and forty-one Lodges.
The Grand Master's Address is a model of Its kind; brief, but pertinent and well
written. He commences with this brotherly acknowledgment of the well-timed

286

Pr<>CRRAlings of the

[Oct. 13,

contributions from Northern Masons to the sn1fering Fraternity in Alabama and other
Southern jnrisdiotions, which were indeed the best evide.noe that Masons, P.B they
say, do not know any geographical limits to their charity, but gitJe as well as talk:While the surrounding circumstances for the last two years have been such BB to
deprive us, in many instances, of the prompt and active discharge of our duty in
relieving the distressed widow and orphan, the aged and infirm, yet their wants have
not been entirely neglected. In many instances the subordinate Lodges have relieved that distress as far as they were able. From East to West, and between North
and So11th, Freemasonry extends, and in every. clime are Masons to be found. Ma·
sonry, in the extension of her charity, knows. no bounds; and like good and
tme Masons, our brethren in different parts of th.e United States have come to our
relief. Hearing of our distress, the7 have set to work and raised means to assist in
relieving that distress within our j ur1sdiction.
Since our last Commnuication, myself, Bro. SAYRE, Right Worshipful Grand
Secretary, and Bro. HASTINGS, Right Worshipful Grand Treasurer, have received
the amounts from the sources specified in onr joint report and account current, which
will be submitted to you.
On the reception of the specified amount by each one lof us, we returned our
acknowledgments and grateful thanks for the respective donations ; and I now rec·
ommend thls Grand Lodge to express her gratitude to them for their remembrance of
llll, and assistance in the honr of need.
May, In the future, all the strife between brothers of the North and the South
(why not, as Masons; cease the. use of these seml·invidious terms?) be, who shall
most excel in all such good works of loving kindness and brotherly love.
The Grand Master had one singular applieation made to him, which he very prop·
erly met with a prompt and decided negative. The Master and Senior Warden of
a Lodge having moved ont of its jurisdiction, the Lodge asked for an order to declare
the office of Junior Warden tJacarit, and for a dispensation to elect a Master and
Senior Warden. He gave the petitioners some information on Masonic law and
proprieties, by which, It is to be hoped, they will be benefited in the future. He
had also declined several requests for dispensations to confer the degrees upon
maimed candidates. He simply says, "the law against the admission of such per·
sons is too well established to need comment."
He preludes the account of the several decisions made by him dnring the year
upon Masonic law with these remarks, In which· we fully concur. The true "Tree·
tie-Board" of Masonry is the word of God, and not the opinions, acts, or decisions of
any body of men outside of the Order:It Is a well established law of Masonry, that everything that contravenes the moral
law Is a violation of Masonic law. And everything that affects the relation of man
to God, his neighbor, or hiIDBelf, Is the proper subject of Lodge jurisdiction and
Masonic investigation. The line of demarkat10n, whi<;h is moral rectitude, is sharply
drawn, and while a Mason keeps himself circumscribed within those precep~ .em·
bracing the moral law, it is impossible that he should materially err. But when he
transgresses those bounds, then it becomes necessary for the law to take hold, and
punish the offender in vindication of its honor. Hence the necessity of a power to
say what that law is, and how it shall be administered. This power is vested In the
Grand Lodge, while in session, and In the Grand Master, during vacation. The forum
for adjudication is the subordinate Lodge. Neither is it the dnty, nor shonld the
Lodge wait for the adjudication of such offense by any other tribunal, either Church
or State; but to investigate for itself, and punish or exonerate, as the case may require, regardless of what others may do or say.
He ruled that at the conclusion of a trial of a brother., the accused should retire
during the deliberation of the Lodge, but that the accuser might remain. We do
not say that this last would be the violation of any written law, but it certainly would
be of the unwritten code of good taste. We can conceive of no more fruitful source
of discord in a Lodge, than for either the accuser or the accused to hear the remarks
which might and should be made, upon the charges and evidence. We think that at
least one door, and that a tolerably thick one, should intervene between the Masonic
jury and the parties Interested.
We notice several other decisions, but none calling for special remark, as most
were regniated by the local provisions of the Alabama Constitution.

The finances of this Grand Lodge are in a healthy condition, there being of re·
ceipts $8,9n 13; and expenditures $2,891 55; showing a cash balance of $6,020 58.
The Grand Secretary reported, that from special returns made to him from one
hundred and forty Lodges, it appeared that seven hnndred and twenty brethren had
lost their lives while in service in the Confederate army. As to maimed Masons from
the same cause, sixty-one Lodges returned the loss of nine limbs only.
From a tabular statement in the appendix, we learn that there are or were three
hundred and thirty-nine Lodges is this jurisdiction, only two hundred and eighteen
however being" square upon the books." The charters of fifty-eight had been for·
feited, and nineteen were " Army Lodges." There were initiated during the year,
seven hundred and fifty.five; passed, seven hundred and sixty-three ; and raised,
seven hundred and thirty-eight; the present membership being nine thonsand seven
hundred and seven.
The Report or the Committee on Correspondence is from the able pen of Bro.
W. C. P111NI01C,'a Past Grand Master, and occupies about seventy-five pages. It
reviows the proceedings of thirty-eight Grand Lodges, our own for 1866 being of
the number. He quotes liberally and approvingly from the Address of Grand Master
CLAIBORNE. The Report of Bro. Rm1111s, he says, "is both lengthy and ably done.".
Bro. RHEES, In that year, had rapped an Alabama brother over the knuckles, rather
sharply, for his remarks about Northern outrages, during the civil war. Bro. P111NI01C
defends his brother of 1865, but says his allusions were to the Northern army, ans
not to the N drthern F'ratemity, and hence they were justified In the use or the termp
"vandals," "heartless enemies," etc. Well, well, good brethren, perhaps both
writers were a little too sharp. We prefer to bury the hatchet out of sight and
forever, rath~r than continue this unpleaMant controversy. One of these days we
hope the brethren of the North and South will fully appreciate each other, and dwell
together In unbroken unity and harmony. Let " by·gones be by·gones." We are
through with our accursed civil war, and may we never see another.
Bro. PRATT'S Oration is highly commended. "Those," says our brother, ' 1 who
delight to see Masonry presented before the world as the great moral, religions,
scieotiflc, and literary Institution of the world, should read it. If. ls a gem I" We have
elsewhere expressed our decided dissent from the second of the above positions
Masonry is not a religious Institution, and brethren only do wrong to it as well as to
themselves, by so representing and acting.
We had marked several passages in this very interesting and able report, but
time and space forbid our copying to the extent we could wish.
The M.·. W.·. GEOMB D. NORRIS was elected Grand Master, and the R.·.
DANIEL SAYRlll, reelected Grand Secretary. A proposition to change the time and
place for the meeting of the Annual Communications was voted down.

ARKANSAS,

We have before us, In a very neatly printed pamphlet, the proceedings of the
twenty-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge or Arkansas, held in Little
Bock, November 4th, 5th, and 6th, 1867-the M.-. W:·. E. H. ENGLISH presided as
Gt:and Master, and the R:. W.·. W. D. BLOOJIBR was Grand Secretary. Representatives
were present from eighty-one subordinate Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master ENGLISJI occupies nearly sixteen pages, and Is, as
usual, worthy of its source-Bro. ENGLISJI having acquired an enviable Masonic reputation for the ability that has uniformly marked all that has come from his pen.
The Address opens with· a series of philosophical suggestions, or axioms rather,
which would not be out of place in a treatise on Moral Philosophy. From these
general positions, the Grand Master passes gracefully, to apply the truths to Masonry an.d its work, and to give some excellent advice to the Fraternity. We copy the
subjoined paragraphs, which tell their own story, and need no comment. Such

practwal Masonry is always its best apology and defense against the miserable tra-

All along the track of time. blackened by crime and stained with blood, Masonry
has erected her temples of light, and taught men to be virtuous, charitable and good.
But her voice bas too often been as unavailing as the feeble wail of the child amidst
. the hoarse howlings of the storm. She has said to the waves, be still, and beedlell8
of b.e r voice they continued to rage. She bas said let there be light, and darkness yet
prevailed. But never discouraged, she has toiled a.way at her noble work, a.nd has,
at no period, however dark, been wholly destitute of Influence. It often happens
that daring the darkest night, the rays of some beautiful star strugf!le through the
rifted clouds, a.nd light up the pathway of the belated tr!'-veler. Bo 1t II.as been with
Masonry. But now her temples are springing up in every land, her sons of light are
becoming numerous, and her moral influence is surpassed by no social organization.
Illustrative of the influence of Masonry over the p888ions and prejudices of men,
may I be pe~mltte d, without intending to tread upon forbidden ground, to allude to
a striking comrast. Whilst extreme partizans among the profane, have been clamoring for the blood and extermination of the Southern people, the Ma.sons of the
North, rising above the p888ions and prejudices engendered by the late unhappy
war, have been sending bread into the Aouth to feed her impoverished and starving
families. Among other instances of the liberality of our Nortbern brethren, the
Grand Lodge of New York donated five thousand dollars for the relief of the desti·
tote of the Southern States, and the Grand Treasurer, our Ill. Bro. JOHN S IMO.NS, sent
me five hundred dol\ars of the contribution to be distrJbuted at my discretion. I
have been endeavoring to divide it among a hundred of the most destitute widows'
to be found in the different parts of the State. So that, sma.11 as the sum is to each,
a hundred hearts might feel emotions of gratitude to the Grand Lodge of New York.
We hope that some of the contributions of the California brethren reached the
same worthy hands of Bro. ENGLISH, and dried up some of the tears of sufferers in
that jurisdiction.
We are pleased to learn from this Address, that after a suspension for five years,

Mater." It Is situated in Little Rock, and has made arrangements for the free tuition
offorty-flve students, five from each of the districts of the Deputy Grand Masters.

The Committee on "Masonic Law and Usage," approve of these decisions of
Deputy Grand Masters: "Where the rules of a Church lead a Mason to renounce
Mlll!onry, asa matter of conscience, it is not a matter for Masonic discipline." (How
is his Lodge then to get rid of him 1) "A Mason may he a member of more than one
Lodge." (Why should he be 1) "A near sighted man may be made a Mason.''
They dissent from the opinion that "a Master Mason who takes the benefit of the
bankrupt law against a brother Mason, is subject to discipline therefor. • • • The
bankrupt law is just like any other law; and a man who obeys it is no more subject
to discipline, than if he obeyed any other law.'' We think both decisions are too
sweeping. The case is analogous to those which have given some trouble in California, viz.-where a brother pays a debt due to a brother in greenbacks. Sometimes
the animua of the act makes this a high Masonic crime, and sometimes it is justified
under our laws, human and divine. Ee.ch case should, in our opinion, be decided
upon its own merits or demerits, and these be determined by the accompanying circnmstances. An iron rule on either side will be sure to breed confusion among the
Craft.

CONNECTICUT.
The eightieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Connecticut was
held In Hartford, May 13th and 14th, 1868. The M.•. W.·. WILLIAM STORER presided as
Grand Master, and the R.·. W.'. JOSEPH K. WHEELER was Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from eighty-eight Lodges.
The Address of the Grand Master was quite long, but it is an able, well expressed,
and business-like document. Here is one of the opening sentences worthy of being
engraved on gold:Freemasonry is something more than a mere system of forms and ceremonies. It
is a living reality ; a tangible good ; and while it does not claim to be religion, or
oven a substitute for religion, it has , nevertheless, a direct tend.ency to make all men
better who will practice its teachings. It inculcates every virtue, and discounte·
nances every vice. It teaches its votaries to be temperate in all things; to he fear·
less, though not reckless , in maintaining the right; to be cautious and prudent in the
indulgence of thought, word and action; to praotloe the strictest and most infiexi·
ble Integrity In all his dealings. It Is 11 noble solence, and opens to the searcher for
truth an u(\fathomal>le depth of knowledge. He who most diligently pursues the
profound study of Masonry, is most thoroughly aware that there Is much more yet to
be learned.
, 1
He congratulates the Fraternity on the prosperity of the Craft during the year.
Uut the very popularity which Masonry had attained, called for caution and for speo·
ial guards at the outer door. In relation to this, the Grand Master well and truthfully
~ays:-

Let us guard against the notion that tho strength of 11 Lodge consists In the number of its members. This is a mistaken idea. Moral and intellectual qualiflcatlons
are the characteristics on which we should ever depend, in selecting ma.terials for
our spiritual building; and such alone can be depended on to give stability to the
edifice. In operative Masonry, the architect does not calculate tho strength of his
work by the number of stones laid in the wall; bub looks rather to their size and
solidity. So in speculative Masonry, the character of the members Is what consti·
tutes the value of the institution. A Lodge of thirty upright, honorable, intelligent
members, may be said to have achieved a success; whereas, one with 11 hundred
men of doubtful character ls an utter failure.
He had issued dispensations for the establishment of two new Lodges; and had
also granted dispensations in a few "cases of emergency," though personally dis·
1'pproving the practice. In one case, however, we think the Grand Master would
have done much better If he had adhered to his first decision. A Master having removed his residence, application was made for a dispensation to elect a new Master
in his place. It was denied on the very proper grounds that in all such cases the
Senior Warden succeeded to the east, and in his absence the Junior Warden. Subaequently the Lodge, by a unanimous vote, the two Wardens being included, renewed
the request for a special election. Distrusting himself, the Grand Master " consulted
some of the most experienced and best informed Masons In this jurisdiction, and in
accordance with their advice granted the dispensation asked for." Our own most
decided opinion la, that the aforesaid "most experienced" &c. Masous, gave very
bad and un-Masonic advice, and that the Grand Master should have returned as an·
swer the traditional dictum of the Pope of Rome, "Non Possum us."

IDAHO.

We have the pleasing duty of welcoming another fair sister to our already large
and constantly increasing family. The fanatics who recently bored our Pittsburg
triends with their semi-insane howlings about wicked Masonry and other secret soci·
eties, will please note this fact, and govern themselves accordingly.
Idaho, anothe'r of the Pacific coast commonwealths, asks for admittance into the
grand army of the Grand Lodges of the Union. We welcome the new-comer, and
recommend that our Grand Lodge extend to her full sisterly recognition and fellowship.
The proceedings of the formation of the Grand Lodge only fill a modest little pamphlet of fourteen pages. From it we learn tliat a Convention of Free and Accepted
Masons, delegated by the several Lodges in the Territory·of Idaho, assembled at the
Masonic Hall in Idaho City, Idaho Territory, December 16th, 1867. Bro. GEORGE H.
CoE, P. M., was called to the Chair, and Bro. P. E. EDM02''1lSON-both of Idaho Citywas appointed Secretary.
Upon due examination of credentials, it was found that four chartered Lodges were
represented, viz: Idaho, No. 35; BoiBe, No. 37, and Placer, No. 38, under the jurisdiction bf Oregon, and Pi.oneer, No. 12, under that of Washington Territory. A
delegate from Owyhee Lodge, under dispensation, was also admitted to a seat. A
Lodge of Master Masons was then opened for the purpose of organizing and opening
the Grand Lodge of Free and Acc11J!ted Masons of Idaho Territory. The following
were elected as Grand Officers: Grand Master, GEORGE H. COE; Deputy Grand Mas•
.t er, G. W. PAUL; Senior Grand Warden, A. HAAS; Junior Grand Warden, GEORGE T.
YOUNG; Grand Treasurer, S. B. CoNNELLYj Grand Secretary, P. E. EDMONDSON.·
A Constitution was adopted, being-with a few local alterations-that of the Grand
Lodge of Oregon. Idaho City was fixed upon as the place of meeting. A Charter
was granted to Owyhee Lodge, making five in the new jurisdiction.
The Grand Secretary was instructed to correspond with the Grand Lodges of Oregon and Washington Territory, in reference to matters growing out of this formation
of the Grand Lodge of Idaho.
A standing resolution was adopted, that there should be only one ballot for the
three degrees; also, the following in relation to non-affiliated Masons :Resolved, That any non-afllliated Mason living within the jurisdiction of this Grand

ILLINOIS.

This State has made such rapid strides in population, wealth, and importance that
it well deserves to be called the "Empire State" of the Mississippi Valley. And in
its Masonic position it loses nothing of that rank. We find, by the proceedings of the
thirty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of' Illinois, held at Spring·
field October 1st and 2d, 1867, that there are five hundred and sixty Lodges in the
State, with a membership of twenty-eight thousand one hundred and eighty-four. Of
these Lodges, four hundred were actually represented at this Communication-a
goodly host of the Fraternity, indeed, and as a body not given to overmuch debate, as
we assn.me, from the fact that all their business was transacted In two days. They
must be regulated by the motto which says that "the world [Masonry] is governed
t\ie best when it is governed the leaBt." We, in California, hardly get our harness on
before the close of the second day. Will our Illinois brethren send us the secret of'
their success " under due guards and signs!"

pamphlet of two hundred and forty pages. The M.·. W. ·. JEROME R. GORIN presided as

" in gratitude to the Grand Architect of the universe for the manifold blessings that
had been vouchsafed to the Fraternity during the past Masonic year."

As in California, so it appear• that in Illinois some brethren are so curious to ascertain how 11 brother votes by ballot, that they very unmasonically watch the ballot-box.
and the suspected brother too closely. The Grand Master 11dmi'1isters to these "Paul
Prys" of Masonry 11 deserved rebuke, and thus reasons, In which we fully concur:-. "
In Masonry, all brethren stand on a level in the duties, obligations, sacrifices, and
burdens; there is not in theory, and there should not be in· pr.wtice, any inequality.,
It is not supposable, among Master Masons, that there are any who would reject II·
candidate through malice, envy, ill-will, anger, jealousy, or spleen; if any Lodge has
ad~te<l to its fold any who can be guilty of such base conduct, 1t is her misfortuneperhaps her fllult-llnd,for which there is no Masonic remedy. The right to reject 11
candidate is 11 clear sequence of the right to vote, and is as clear and sacred a.s the
right to elect. The ballot is not spread to elect 11 candidate alone, but to determine
whether the candidate shall be rejected, and for the further protection of the weak,
of the timid, or the poor, the secret ballot is spread. The duty to reject is also as
clear as the dutl to vote; and that duty Is to be th~ result of conacientious convictions
in each brother s breast, and he votes upon those convictions in the presence of Deity
·
alone.
The rejection of 11 candidate, when declared, is to be shared in silence by every
brother, no matte.r how unpleasant; for if any one states how he voted, he violates
fue secrecy of the ballot, and thereby violates his obligation. The more shields there
are thrown around the ballot, which 1s the great safety-valve of Masonry, the better.

In his Address, covering twenty closely printed pages of the pamphlet, the Grand
Master speaks his mind very freely, and in a peculiar style, about many matters that
to him seemed of importance to Masonic affairs in his jurisdiction. Unlike his worthy
brother of Iowa, Grand Master HAZELRHHI dues not indulge In the high-flown Ian·
gnage of an ambitious sophomore, but is a Western man all over, much given to the
"calling of a spade, a ' spade,'" and leaving no doubt whatever on any reader as to
his meaning or intention. We were quite refreshed as well as slightly amused at some
of his half-quaint expressions and originality of figures employed in this very able
address. It being the Semi-centennial Anniversary of the Establishment of Masonry,
or rather of the Grand Lodge in Indiana, the Grand Master opens his Address with an
appropriate reference to that fact and to the associations it suggested. Four brothers
named by him--'some of whom were subsequently introduced to the Grand Lodge and
warmly welcomed by the brethren-yet survived of the representatives of the
six chartered Lodges who met in the town of Corydon in 1817, and resolved to organize a Grand Lodge. Prosperity attended the Order until the wild-fire era of AntiMasonry, of which we have these spicy words and somewhat commingling of metaphors, which we give as a fair specimen of our good brother's style of composition:Suffice it to say that all the venom and splee'!' that a vitiated press a'!'d f9:natical ·
clergy could iuven~ were p~ured out, as S? many vials ?f wrath, upon a. qmet, molfensive and unassummg assoc1at1on, that aimed at nothmg but the amelioration of the
condition and promotion of the happiness of their fellow-beings-who , when reviled,
reviled not again, but relying upon the purity of their motives and the rectitude of
their actions, calmly awaited with patience and resignation the unbiased judgment of
the future. The hail pf legislation did not remain an idle spectator to this tornado ar
persecution, but, lent itself as .a supplia~t tool to the _bidding of rec~less and
unprinciJ!led demagogues, who, hke the Witch of Endor with the manes of Samuel,
would rai•e the gho•t of Morgan from the vasty deep to aid them in their unholy projects of ambition, and sow the seeds from which a bountiful crop of discord and con·
fusion was not only to be produced in the Lodges, but also in Church and State.
The result of this crusade and panic. reduced the number of Lodges from thirty to
nine; and, indeed, as late as 1834 the Grand Lodge opened, having present the representatives of but three chartered Lodges, and one under dispensation. From this time,
however, Masonry began to live again in Indiana. In 184.4, wken the present Grand
Master was first a member, there were seventeen chartered Lodges, and ten under
dispensation. "Since then," sa:ys the Grand Master, "progress has been uninterrupt·
edly onward and upward, until every city, town and hamlet sees and feels the happy
influences of a well-directed organization, whose grand aim is to impress upon the
minds of its votaries the important principles of brotherly·love, relief and truth; temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice, obedience to the 111ws of God and man."
In 1867 there were three hundred and sixty-one chartered Lodges and one under
dispensation, with a membership ot' eighteen taousand two hundred and sixty-five,
being an increa~e of two thousand and eleven over the returns of the previous year.
In accordance with the recommendation of the Grand Master, this Semi-centennial
Anniversary was duly celebrated by the Grand Lodge, an able and interesting Add~ess,
published in the minutes, having been delivered by the Grand Orator, w... RICHARD
W. THOllPSON.

1md South, as to the impropriety of indulging in the hard feelings and harsh, reproac~­
ful language which the late civil wor called out, and which, being still nourished , shows

ages by all her best teachings. We second, cordially, his excellent advice, and hope
soon.to know that, among Masons, at least, all these "by-gones will be by-gones."

IOWA.
We have before us in a well but rather curiously printed pamphlet of three hundred and six pages, the proceedings of the twenty-fourth Annual Communication of
the Grand Lodge of Iowa, held at Davenport, June fourth and fifth, 1867. The curi·
ous part, to which we have alluded, is the substitution of a parallelogram for the word
"Lodge,'' and a double one with lines crossed for the plural number. We are aware
that tastes differ and are not to be disputed, but in our humble opinion, this intended
improvement is a sad disfigurement of this otherwise tastefully printed pamphlet.
We suppose the Masonic typos of Iowa will take our criticism for what it is worth,
and hereafter, as heretofore, please themselves, which will be all right of course.

Grand Master CAMPBELL R. PECK transmitted in print his Annual Address, which is
a well written business document of thirteen pages, touching on a variety of subjects,
Masonic and otherwise. It would not have disfigured this address, or detracted at all
from its ability, if all this " otherwise" had been omitted.
During the Masonic year he had granted dispensations to establish twenty-six new
Lodges. A goodly number, indeed, if the same were legitimately called for, and of
this the Grand Master had no doubt, after making diligent inquiry. It indicates, in his
opinion," unmistakably the unprecedented prosperity of oar honorable Order." Three
other applications were not granted, one being positively denied, and the other two re·
ferred to the Grand Lodge. The first was'denied because it grew out of disaffection in an
existing Lodge, which should not be countenanced. The second asked for a new
Lodge la Des Moines to be composed of "young men," it appearing that the "Old
Fogies" and " Young Americas " concluded that they could agree better apart than
together! A very funny reason, as it seems to us. The third presented the question
of geographical limits merely. Th~se applications were referred to the incoming Grand
Master •
.A.n application for a German Lodge, to work in that language, was referred to the
Grand Lodge, with a strong expression of disapproval from the Grand Master, because
he "believed the tendency would be to separate the German brethren from the Am&ri·
cans, whereas Masonry ought to unite them." We have found no difficulty from this
source in California, nor do we apprehend that oar Iowa brethren would.
Some of the" otherwise" portions of this address related to the status, p_resent

neither ready for conversion nor open to conviction. The committee, to whom the
subject was referred, reported against any action on the subject, for these reasong;
which were satisfactory to the Grand Lodge and adopted by it; a subsequent attempt
by a zealous brother to reopen the matter, being summarily laid on the table:We know the views of the M.·.

LOUISIANA.
The proceedings of the My-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of

The angel of death has been hovering over our State. Our cities, onr towns, and
villages, and country places, han felt its chilling presence, and many an aching heart
and lonely hearth-stone mourn the departure of loved ones during the year just closed.
Neither bright intellect, nor lovely form, nor high character, nor modest truth have
sufficed to turn aside the fatal shaft, but all alike have :yielded and now mingle in the
dust. But we thank God that in these times of sad visitations, of desolation and sorrow, the brightest features of our nature came forth, and charity and benevolence,
with constant vigils and tender hands, strove hard to equal the necessity. The Good
Samaritan still lives, and our noble institution is no laggard in her ministrations ro the
sick and sorrowful. n· I have learned Masonry aright, " to be good and to do good "
is an epitome of the lessons she teaches, of the moral standard she erects, and to
which she invites- and urges all her children to attain. The records, If not the report
of our Relief Lodge, and, I trust, the unwritten records of each brother's heart, will
show that we have not been deaf to the calls of brotherly love and relief. Then,
brethren, let us not tire in well doing, and while we may and ought to be earnest in
our searche~ and researches alter the truth, let us not forget the practical part ot' our
faith. Brotherly love and relief may .be felt and practiced by all, from the highest to
the lowest, while, pel"haps, a few glimpses of the true Masonic truth may be now and
then caQght by our brightest intellects, who have the time and ability to delve deep
and long into the hidden mysteries of nature.
.A.s the system of District Deputy Grand Masters adopted in that jurisdiction, in
common with many others, had not worked as well as the Grand Master had desired,
in securing uniformity and efficiency of work, he recommended the appointment and
liberal compensation of a Grand Lecturer, who should visit and instruct all the Lodges.
We believe that practice will determine this to be by far the best of the two systems.
We have the same, except the traveling idea. Our Grand Lectnrer instructs and ap·
points Ddputy Grand Lecturers, and then, at each Annual Communication, exempllfiH
the work in the three degrees, before the Grand Lodge. The plan has worked well
thus far, having been in full operation about four years.

busiest of workers.

MARYLAND.

We have received the proceedings of the Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of Maryland, held at Baltimore, November eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth,
1867. As usual, these are preceded by brief minutes of" the Grand Stewards' Lodge,"
held July fifth, August fourteenth, September nineteenth and twenty-eighth, and
October seventh and twenty-ninth. This seems to be a Maryland notion designed to
perform much of the routinp business of the Grand Lodge, such as approving amendments to the by-laws and considering appeals from the action of subordinate Lodges
-a further appeal from its decision being to the Grand Lodge-and acting as a general
Finance Committee. This Lodge is composed of twenty Master Masons, "good men
and true," who are elected as such, by the Grand Lodge at the same time as other
Grand Officers. The "Grand Stewards' Lodge " convenes, as we gather from its pro·
ceedings, whenever three members request a meeting. The most important business
transacted at its meetings this year, was the trial of two brothers for writing and pub·
lishing a tract, called" Walks and talks about the Temple, or the veil uplifted," which
the Building Committee of the new Tempie alleged was a gross libel upon them.

MASSACHUSETTS.
We have before us, according to the title page, the "Proceedings of the Grand
Lodge of the Most Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free and Accepted Mas<ms or
the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, in union with the Most Ancient and Honorable
Grand Lodges in Europe and America, according to the old Constitutions ; from March
thirteenth to December twenty-seventh, 1867.'' In this pamphlet of two hundred
pages we find the proceedings of a Quarterly Communication of March thirteenth,
1867; ditto, ditto, June twelfth; proceedings at the dedication of the new Masonic
·Temple, June twenty-fourth; Special Communication, same date; Quarterly ditto,
September eleventh; Annual ditto, December eleventh, and Stated ditto, December
twenty-seventh. Having such a profuse and diverse "Table of Contents" before us.
we hardly know where to begin, how to proceed, or where to leave off. We fear that
our hurried review, to which the late day of the reception of this pamphlet necessarily limits us, will be nearly as much "scattering" as the proceedings themselves.
At the March Quarterly Communication, the M.·. w. ·. CHARLES C. DAME presided
as Grand Master, and then.·. W.·. CHARLE8 w. MOORE was Grand Secretary.
We have no address from the Grand Master, but instead thereof the · report of a
eommittee on his Annual Address, delivered, as we sup'p ose-though not so stated-at
•the December Communication previous. This report alludes to a comment upon ~er­
tain recommendations relative to the Masonic Temple and the funds of the Grand
Lodge, as connected therewith. The beginning of this great work seems~so far as
we can gather from this report-to have been pretty much a matter of faith, there
having been in the treasury only $20,000 to commence a work the estimated cost of
which was to be $175,000-the actual, however, being $!50,000. The anticipated revenues from the temple are put at $30,00(); and, to provide for any deficiency and to
create a sinking fund , it was proposed to tax every Mason in the jurisdiction one dollar per annum for thirteen years, which would, if paid, yield at the end of that period
e320,240, and thus leave the temple free of debt, as the property of the Gr1md Lodge.
This report, we are told, was adopted without a dissenting voice. We give the closing
paragraphs of this able report, only adding that we sincerely hope 'the sanguine anticipations of our brethren will be realized:If the plan proposed by your committee can be carried out in ten years Crom now,
we shall see our Grand Lodge entirely free from debt, in possession of property worth
over half a million of dollars, and with a revenue ample enough to place our Masonic
charities upon a systematic foundation. The Lodges could then tie relieved from taxation for the support of the Grand Lodge. Every brother in the jilrisdiction,if needy,
could enjoy its benefits. The widows and orphans would not in vain apply for assistance. Greater and more extensive charities than we have conceived ol' in our day
could be inaugurated. It would be within the power of the Grand Lodge to establish
a system of benevolence which would be grand and Imposing.
The Temple of Masonry, itself, free fi·om every liability, will be the common prOI?·
erty of the Masons of Massachusetts, to which they can repair as their own Masomc
home, as did the .ancient Israelites to the Temple of' Jerusalem in the days of its
pride and glory, from all parts of Judea, to participate in the solemn ceremonies of
their festiva.ls.
We find nothing else done at this Communication calling for Special notice.

MICHIGAN.
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Michigan was held in DetJ·o!t,
commencing its session on the second Wednesday in January, 1868. The M.-. W: •.
s. c. COFFINBUlW presided as Grand Master, and the R.-. w. .. JAMES FENTON was
Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from two hundred and eighteen of
the two hundred and twenty-one Lodges in the State-a percentage almost unprece·
dented, attesting the interest felt by the brethren in the deliberations and acts of their
Supreme Masonic Legislature.
An" Emergent" or Special Communication had been held in Detroit, July third·.
and fourth, 1867, to participate in the ceremonies of laying the corner-stone of the
"Michigan Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument." The proceedings, with the opening
prayer and address, are given at length; and it must have been 11 refreshing time. A
" sumptuous banquet." was a feature of the occasion.
The Address of Grand Master CoFFINBURY, at the Annual Communication, is 11
somewhat long, but interesting document. It is mainly taken up with the record of
his official acts during the year, though containing besides many valuable suggestions
and eloquent passages. With heartfelt satisfaction he welcomes back to brotherly
union the brethren of the Southern States, and speaks justly of the power and
efficiency of Masonry In again restoring peace after such Jong and sad estrangements.
He speaks at length of the Interesting services at the Special Communication.
During the year he had issued eighteen dispensations for opening new Lodges, and
had denied the petitions for three more. He had decided many questions of Masonic
Jaw. We note some of them:1. That an unaffiliated Mason " has no rights in connection with our Lodges. He
has not the right of visitation of 11 Lodge, except three times by special permission;
therefore he can have no right to prefer charges against a member of 11 Lodge, nor
has he 11 right to appear as counsel or attorney for 11 brother nnder charges. The
position of 11 voluntary unaffiliated Mason, in relation to our Order, is such as himself
has sought, and therefore he must submit to its consequences and embarrassments."
The Committee on Masonic law were divided in opinion opon this ruling. A majority took issue with the Grand Master, and reported that 11 non-affiliated Mason had
the right to prefer charges against a brother to the Grand Lodge, etc. The minorit,y
went further even than the Grand Master, and insisted that" a voluntary non-af!!liated
Mason has no Masonic redress for grievances other than is awarded to profanes!' The
Grand Lodg~ adopted this substitute for both conclusions: "Resotoed, That accusations or charges against members of Lodges, or against subordinate Lodges, oan not
be received from non-affiliated Masons, except in case of charges against 11 member of
a Lodge by leave granted by a vote of such Lodge, and in case of charges against a
subordinate Lodge, by leave of the Grand Lodge."

by good words and works, that they are brothers, and that bitterness and strife can
end only in universal disaster and ruin; to assuage suttering, by the well-directed
hand -0f unobtrusive charity, and to preach peace and good will to men by all those
great acts of brotherhood and benevolence which are more eloquent than words, are
among the chief ends and aims of Masonry, and they come into play with emineni
appropriateness in troublesome times like these.
The Grand Master recommends that something effectual be done to prevent the
alarming increase of "non-affiliated Masons." Try our law, good brethren. It is
quite effectual, though we sometimes think 11 little too harsh. and rigid.
A stone is hurled at that imaginary sin of New York against North Carolina, In the
matter of the " W.·. PAUL DRAYTON," etc., etc., and the negro Lodge. This has
already been sufficiently ventilated, and we fancy we can see the wry faces of our
Southern friends, as the truth bursts upon them, that the object of their wrath had not
even the ideal substance or magnitude of an ignis fatuus I Northern Masons are nei·
ther fools nor knaves, and it would be well to take that f;ict for granted hereafter,
before starting out on 11 Quixotic expedition against all the windmills in the land. Let
the " W.·. PAUL DRAYTON 11 rest in peace.

ANTHONY O'SULLIVAN, for many years Grand Secretary of the jurisdiction. He died on
the eleventh of August, 1866. The well deserved reputation which the departed brother
had not only at home, but everywhere, among all Masons," good men and true," will
be our only excuse for extracting somewhat at length from the interesting proceedings of the Grand Master and Grand Lodge in relation to his death and valuable services. The Grand Master says of him :~THONY O'SULLIVAN, the accomplished ·scholar, perfect gentl~man, true . patrio~

as that of a brother true and a father beloved. To see him was to admire him; to hear
him wlls to reverence him ; to know him was to love him.
The deceased was the highest type of a polished lrish gentleman, possessing rare
attainments in Masonic lore, as well as great acquirements in the fields of general
knowledge. As a historian, he was familiar with all the authors whose names are
entitled to a place in the temple of the unrecorded past. As a Mason, whether in
knowledge orthe unwritten ritual, the jurisprudence o(the Order, the practical duties
of the Fraternity, or in large-hearted benevolence, we know he stood unsurpassed, if
ever equalled, in our Grand jurisdiction. We may well 11Sk,
"'Shall "l'l~ ever behold his like again?"
As Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, his yearly reports will
stand and speak, monumental, of his labors, his ability, and his knowledge. Who that
has read the annual productions of his mind, the creations of elevated thought and
noble genius, as they flowed from his facile pen; who that has followed his laborious
researches, telt his scathing irony, while with trenchant blade he hewed the errors he
met, or listened to his lofty commendations of the right and earnest tributes to truth,
will ever regret that A. O'SULLIVAN lived and labored for Masonry, or ever forget his
works of faith and love I
He was· bnried by the Grand Lodge, assembled in Special Communication. A
committee, raised for that purpose, submitted an able report, in itself almost a full
and elaborate memoir of the deceased. From it we can only cull these eloquent
sentences : In Important positions, whether Grand or subordinate, the great Masonic qualities
of the man shone forth with a brilliancy and intensity that cast no uncertain light.
He ever exhibited those qualities of indefatigable labor, research and administration
which characterize a man of high purpose and steady resolve to accompli~h the
greatest good in his day and generation. Being a man of strong will, he WllB not
easily batlled in the course he marked out for his official duties; and having the
highest good of the Fraternity at heart, he determined to leave the spirit of the Order
bett<r than he found it, however exalted that might be.
Having entered behind the sacred veils that enshrined the mysteries of Freemasonry, he sat at once to the work of becoming a master of its rituals. He was not
satisl!ed with the mere drapery of words that surrounded it, but penetrated into the
deep reasoning of the great heart of MllBonry ; he studied its past-back to the
farthest memory and 1·ecords of man; he compared the work of localities with the
great framework of the Continent and of Europe ; he analyzed word by word, sentence by sentence through every degree, from the petition of the Initiate up to the
last step ol the finished Mason. He was one of those men who could be satisfied
with nothing less than perfection as far as the human mind could carry him. His
great and grandest pride was the Grand Lodge of Missouri; his ambition was to see
her second to no other jurisdiction in the universe in the perfection of her work. He
. traveled from the Lakes to the Gulf, and from the Mississippi to the Atlantic in search
of every ray of light that had not yet penetrated his own .Masonic home, and with a
most remarkable memory, he lost nothing he acquired; but by the force of analogy
and his own strong mind he brought order out of chaos, and at the sacrifice of health
and comfort, ease and profit, he visited every corner of our Commonwealth, and
there relit the pure fires of rational Masonry upon the altar o! every Lodge.
He grappled prejudice and ignorance with a giant aand, and broke down the barriers of false doctrines as though they were cobwebs. When once satisfied his work
was right, he allowed no tampering with it by- itinerant peddlers and lecturers from
abroad, but covered the proud monument of his labors by the broad mantle of Grand
Lodge authority. There was, perhaps, no man of his times who had such great
Masonic difficulties to overcome, and none perhaps that ever so successfully conquered
them. He has left the impress of his signet upon the works and lectures of this jurisdiction that can never be effaced; there is a system, a harmony and a force of character in his work that will not e11Sily pass away. His mission as Grand Lecturer he
always recognized as the greatest mission of his life, because he appreciated the
great soul of Masonry and struggled to see it embodied ln the perfect similitude of
its own harmonious character.
Discord in work, next to discord In the Lodge, caused him inexpressible mortifi·
cation; and it is no wonder, then, that having gone out into the broad field of his
.labor-" having led the blind by a way they knew not-made darkness light before
them and crooked things straight," that he should be known the country over as the
great ''Masonic Lycurgus of Missouri." He had mingled with the best and greatest
of the Order, and was at home wherever he went, for bis genial nature, his exuberant love for his fellows and the warm heart that he ever carried in his hand, secured
him a life invitation to every Masonic fireside of the land. Loved thU.8 by strangers,

The Report of the Committee on Correspondence Is from the able pen of the
R:. W.-. Grand Secretary, Bro. GOOLEY. It occupies nearly one hundred pages of
the pamphlet before us, and Is a review of the proceedings of twenty-fl.ve Grand
Lodges, fifteen of which are in foreign countries. Kindly notice is taken of those
of our own Grand Lodge for 1866. He char11cterizes the address of Grand Ma.ater
CLAIBORNE as an" able paper," and makes liberal extracts therefrom. In common
with another brothAr, whose mistake we have already corrected, Bro. GouLEY comes
to the strange conclusion that in some Lodges in thiii jurisdiction members vote for
applicants in some viva voce way, and not by ballot. He quotes this paragraph from
the address and adds the following comments :' The Constitution provides that it shall be " by an unanimous vote," without
directing how that vote shall be discovered. It will be readily perceived that un)flB8
the ballot is used, the conscientious opponent is compelled either to disclose how he
originally voted, or· to absent himself from his Lodge on such occasions to avoid
invidious prominence, if such things be. Feeling that I had no authority under our
law to require the, use of the ballot on such occasions, and that the language is not
imperative in its direction, I chose to intimate an opinion that the use of the bl!.llot
would appeal stronger to the discretionary executive authority than the vote viva
voce or by uplifted hands.'
It has always been our understanding that all votes for degrees should be s~cret,
and how it can be so without a ballot is incomprehensible to us. We did not suppose that any other custom prevailed in the world. We rather admire the nerve of
the negative voter by " show of hands ; " but as many good men lack courage under
certain circumstances, we must disapprove of the custom which tends to override
the independence of the ballot.
"Wondering much," as good old JOHN BUNYAN says, how our brother could possibly suppose that we were so green and unmasonlc in California, we turned to the
address of Grand Master CLAIBORNE for an explanation. Standing by itself, we
admit that a stranger might get an impression akin to that of Bro. GouLEY. But If
our worthy brother will examine the addreBB a little more closely, he will perceive
that the subject matter was not voting for degreeJJ, (which, of course, is always by
ballot with us as it is elsewhere), but the vote by which a Lodge asks for a ai8pen8ation in the. cases referred to by the Grand Master, where great feeling and some ani'
mosity existed, and were likely to Increase unles11 secrecy of action could be secured.
For that purpose the Grand Master recommends a vote by ballot on all such applications. We hope Bro. GOOLEY will, after this explanation, do our late Grand Master
and the Fraternity here full justice in the premises.
Bro. RHEES, of course, is complimented as usual, but due regard for his feelings
bids us refrain from copying too much of the praises of his brethren. A long extract
Is also given from the oration of Bro. PRATT, which is characterized" as a most
beautiful and able address."
Approving of the action of the Grand Lodge of Delaware in its prohibition of the
initiation, eto., of negroes, mulattoes, or colored persons as Masons, or uniting with

We have received a somewhat bulky but well printed pamphlet, of five hundred
pages, containing a reprint of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Nebraska, for
the ten years from 1857 to 1867. As the proceedings of the previous years have al·
ready been reviewed by our predecessors, we shall only notice at this time those
for 1867.
The Tenth Annual Communication was held at Omaha, commencing Jnne 19, 1867,
the M.·. W.·. R. W. Fu&NAS presiding as Grand Master, and the R.'. w. .. J. N. WisB
being Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from fourteen J..odges. ,
The system of proxies seems to have been carried in this jurisdiction to a mnch
greater, or, as we should say, looser extent, than seems to be agreeable to some;
for we notice a resolution oflered, prohibiting, in future, the transfer of a proxy of
the Worshipful Master or Warden to a third brother. Such a practice has never been
allowed here, and we think that the soo.u er our Nebraska brethren close that aveque
to abuse e.nd intrigue, the better for the pee.ce and harmony of their Grand Lodge,
and the Fraternity generally.
The Address of Grand Master Fr;aNAS is a business-like, well written production.
He congratulates the Fraternity on the continued prosperity and advancement of
Freemasonry In Nebraska. He urges stronglyt'lpon his brethren tu remember'.in•
deeds of substantial kindness, their sutfering friends at the South. The Grand
Lodge voted $150 to that purpose. He had granted two dispensations for the establishment of new Lodges, and for good reasons had refused a third. He had also
Issued a special dispensation to revive a Lodge that had beoome extinot,or so nearly
so, as to amount to about the same thing.
The Grand Master stated, that in one or two Instances, upon the representation of
urgent emergency, he had granted dispensations to hurry particular candidates
through the degrees. But he did not like it, and recommended that the Grand Lodge
should have prohibitory enactments against such in future. The Grand Master truth·
fully says : "I have been a Mason for twenty-three years, and have never known a
•case of emergency' attended with good results. The great majority, too, of such
cases, arc those who have resided within the reach of some Lodge for years, without
thinking of making application for membership into the Order, until suddenly some
business or enterprise calls them to a distanoe, and then they must be made a Mason
before they go-have not time to wait, and can't think of going without the degrees.
It is an imposition upon both the candidate and the Order." These are strong words,
perhaps, but we think the Grand MllBter has "hit the nail on the head." Such
"high-pressure," railroad-speed made Masons seldom amount to mnch. We think,
with Grand Master FURNAS, that a man who has voluntaril:f/ waited a dozen years or
'more, can involuntal'ily hold on for ninety days longer, without harm coming either
to him or the Lodge that may be in such a hurry to reoeive him.
The Grand ltfaster also gives a word of friendly advice and admonition to the
over-zealous brethren who would modernize our venerable institution, by substituti'ng new-fangled devices and expressions for the " old patha " and time-honored
teachings; and also gives a caution against the disposition to nrge "all clever men"

NEVADA.

Our daughter, of the "Silver State," sends us greeting from her home in the land
of mines and sage-brush. We have the proceedings of the Third Annual Convocation, held in Virginia City, September 17th, 18th and 19th, 1867-the .M.·. w,., Jo~!f C.
CuRRIE, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.o, w,., ROBERT H. TAYLOR Grand Secretary,
Representatives were present from nine chartered Lodges and one under dispensation. In the form of printed Journal and Report of Committee on Correspondence,
the daughter copies closely the example of her now almost venerated mother-for,
have we not attained the age of majority? We are quite sure that no better
form could be adopted ; and although our juvenile offspring, in some things, puts on
the airs of age and experience, as if she were 11 Mother in Israel, as well as a little
sister well-beloved, we excuse all-for in this, too, she imitates the example of California, and proves herself truly a" chip of the old block." May she live long and
happily, even to gray-haired old age, and to be herself the mother of many sturdy
sons and fair daughters. Fair sister-" We greet thee.''
The Address of Grand Master CURRIE is a brief, but well-written and businesslike Address. It opens thus, and most appropriately:It is fitting that, before entering upon the duties of the session, we should bow in
humbl<i thankfulness before the Throne of the Supreme Architect and Ruler of the
Universe in reverential thanks for the blessings which he has vouchsafed to us
during the 11ast year; for those of peace, plenty, and individual health and prosperity, and harmony in our Fraternity.
Masons, like other men, need oft remembrance of their duties towards the GoD
in whom they trust, and of the great" Trestle Board," on which is marked out their
rules of daily life. If they would live and act as Masonry enjoins, we should hear
but little of the silly and puerile attacks which some religious and political associations consider themselves in duty bound to make.
He speaks approvingly of the acts of Mount Moriah Lodge, Salt Lake City, during
the year past, and recommends 11 favorable consideration of its application for 11
charter. Before granting 11 dispensation to this Lodge last yMr, he exacted "from
the petitioners 11 pledge that they would carefully exclude all who were of the Mormon faith-knowing full well that, should 11 person bearing the character that is universally given to that sect gain admission within 11 Lodge, its peace and harmony,
and consequently its usefulness, would be forever gone." His reasons for so deciding are given in the report of our predecessor, Bro. OWEN:-" That the Mormons, as
11 people, are polygamists ; that they live In direct violation of the laws of GOD and
the laws of the land, and consequently-011nnot be good Masons." It appears, however, from the subsequent proceedings of the Grand Lodge, that both its Committee
on Charters and itself, differed in opinion from the Grand Master, and a charter was
refused. On account of the Importance of the issue here decided, and believing,
from our proximity to this same disturbing ;ilement, the question may in the futnre
be presented for our practical solution, we copy here at length the report of the
Committee on Charters which was adopted by the Grand Lodge :~
The Committee have carefully examined the records and papers of the Lodge,
and 11.nd them satisfactory, and neatly kept; and would have taken pleasure In recommending that a charter be granted, had it not been for the spirit of insubordi~a­
tion manifested in the lengthy communication from the officers of the Lodge, which
accompanies the petition, in which, after a great amount of special pleading, th~y
attempt to dictate terms to this Grand Lodge, by declining a charter, unless the edict
of the last Grand Communicatfon concerning Mormon Masons be repealed, and the
Lodge allowed to be its own judge as to who shall or shall not be q.dmitted.
Bro. Jos. DE BELL, P.-. G. -.M.·., in his letter of inRtruction which accompanied
the dispensation, in view of the facts that the laws of the land have declared polygamy a crime, and that the Mormons of Utah Territory have openly and defiantly declared their iQ.tention to resist the enforcement of the law whenever the Government
shall make the attempt, and that polygamy is a moral !Ind social sore which it is the

1868.]

duty of Masonry to discountenance, forbid the admission of Mormons to the Lodge.
The Grand Lodge, at its last Annual Grand Communication, approved of the instruc.tions.
The Grand Lodge considered at that time, and the opportunity which an entire
year has afforded for reflection has only strengthened the conviction, that as the representative of a Fraternity which has ever claimed to be the faithful supporter of the gov·
ernment under which it exists, and to discountenance all disloyalty and·rebellion,
and the promoters of good morals and true reli~ion without regard to sects or creeds·,

were not olfenses of which Masonry ehould take any notice.
The committee, therefore, report the following resolution, and recommend its
adoption:Resofved, That this Grand Lodge, in view of the unsatisfactory state of society in
Great Salt Lake City, and the improper spirit manifested in the communication from
the officers of Mount Moriah Lodge, U.D., does not deem it expedient or for the
good of Masonry, to grant a charter to the brethren of Mount Moriah. Lodge, U.D.,
as prayed for.
Subsequent' to this action, it was ordered that the Grand Secretary prepare and
forward to the Worshi~ful Master of .Mount .Moriah Lodge, without fee, proper certificates of the good standing of each member of that Lodge, and the furniture and
jewels of the Lodge were donated to the brethren thereof. And so " Banquo's
ghost" was laid for the time being.
One declsiori of the Grand Master is worthy of notice, and as far as we can see,
correct, according to evmmon sense at least:Charges had been preferred against a brother for unmasonic conduct, and a com·
mission of seven members was appointed to try him. In the meantime he had fled
from justice. Notice was seat to him by private hand, which notice had failed to
reach him. He was subsequently caught, tried by a civil tribunal, and found guilty
of the offense which constituted the charge o• unmasonio conduct. Pending these
proceedings, three of the commissioners had left the jurisdiction, and thP. Secretarl,
of the Lodge was absent from the State. The question was ••how are we to proceed?'
My reply was as follows:.
1. The summons may be served upon him personally, though in prison; and
though he may not be able to appear in person, he can, if he sees flt, appear before
the commission by attorney.
2. A majority of the commissioners can act.
3. You can appoint a Secretary pro tem.
4. All the evidence needed is the record of his conviction in the civil court.
The action of a subordinate Lodge in relation to non-affiliated Masons Is commended. The charge for affiliation had been reduced to one dollar, the Grand Lodge
dues for one year. "This step," says the Grand Master, "has been attended with
most beneficial resnlts. Masons who have been for years non-affiliated, are now In
full fellowship. I would even prefer not to have this merely nominal fee remain;
do away with all charges for affiliation, and then you can, with 11 clear conscience,
threaten those non-affiliates who may still lag behind, with the consequences provided in our General Regulations-ffiliate, contrib11te,or be denied all Masonic privileges, rites and charities.'' There is much good sense In all this, and it is certainly
desirable that the " vast army " of non-affiliates on this Pacific coast should be
diminished, but we hardly think it would do, to take so radical a step as Grand Master
CURRIE recommends; we would permit the one dollar rule to work awhile. It would
be a very poor Mason who would not, or could not, comply with its requisition,
The subject of Masons made in army Lodges is brought forward, and was referred
to 11 committee, which recommended a postponement of action to the next annual
Communication, and it was so ordered.
The Grand Master thinks well of the plan of life-membership, adopted at the last
Communication, and recommends all brethren, who have the pecuniary ability, to
avail themselves of its advantages.

own among the number. We have not found this document one ·page too long, and
congratulate our worthy brother on having made so decided a mark on this his first
appearance. The freedom and ability with which he speaks out his own opinions,
as well as combats those of other Masons, attest that he is an old and well informed
brother, however young in years may be our little daughter, for whom he speaks so
intelligently and authoritatively. In allusion to the grand agency of Masonry in
healing the wounds inflicted by our late civil war, and re-cementing the bonds of our
National Union, these well conceived words of Grand Master ENGLISH, of Ark11ns1111,
in 1865, arc copied and endorsed, and in reference to which, we too would cordi11ll1
extend the right hand of fellowship :·
There stretches from the stormy co8Rt of the Atlantic, to the calm and peacefll
shores of the Pacific Ocean, a fraternal chain of strong links. which, though nnseet
by the world, will do more than aught else to re-unite and strengthen the bonds of
union between the Northern and Southern people, who during the last four yean
were unhappily at war upon sectional questions.
Bro. TAYLOR speaks approvingly of the Address of Grand M~ster CLAIBOBNJI, and
of the Oration of Bro. PBATT-Bays "it Is lengthy, able and eloquent." Of our predecessor, Bro. RHEES, and his report for 1866, Bro. TAYLOR says that Bro. RHEES" has
exhibited 11 commendable Industry, and his own views are, in the main, jost anll discriminaiing ; while all of them seem to be founded upon a true devotion to the best
interests of our noble Craft." He then devotes some four pages to a lively, half
cominendatory and half critical review of Bro. Re:EEs' arguments and opinlon1.
Were our worthy brother intrusted with the pen which is this year assigned to
another and less experienced writer, we are not sure but his bump of combativeness would have been excited, and our other good brother (TAYLOR) have
received a Roland for his Oliver. We trust to escape the fate of ProKWIOK, when
that worthy peace-maker interposed as a third party between the two warring edi·
tors of the Eatonswill" Gazette" and "Independent!" With Bro. RHEES' reasoning
upon an Alabama case, Bro. TAYLOR agrees, but not so in relation to Virginia, Iowa,
and Kansas. But the heaviest blows come when our California brother is taken to
task for " rushing to the defense of Grand Master BsLOHSR," from the criticisms of
Bro. HOPKINS, the predecessor of Bro. TAYLOR. We have carefully read these later
criticisms, and are still of the opinion that both of our California brethren were
right in saying, that "mere verbiage" was not so much of an" ancient landmark"
but what it might in an emergency be cht\nged, provided the essence of the WORK
itself be unchanged. For, as Bro. RHEES had said, " the clothes do not make the
man." We think that ere Nevada is as old as her mother, California, an9 has had as
much to do with the same kind of material that for twenty years we have been try·
ing to get as near homogeneity as is possible, there will be the same course adopted
as with us. We had representatives from every State in the Union·, and of all the
kinds of MBBonic work ever heard of. Some of the advocates of this or that work
were "wiser in their own conceit than seven men who can render a reason." The
time had come for Bro. BELOHER, or some Grand Master, to say as he did : "It is
not so Important to inquire what. particular system should be used, as that we use
one uniform one-the same work, the same lectures, in all the Lodges of this jurisdiction." And with all due regard for Bro. TAYLOR'S arguments and criticisms upon
this remark and Bro. RHEES' defense thereof, we believe and say it was not only a
