In noticing the death of some prominent Mason in this jurisdiction, we have a
scrap of information about the first introduction of Masonry into California, which
was news to ns, though others that preceded may remember somewhat ~f the circnmstances. Bro. JoHN R. CROCKETT, of one of the Newark Lodges, with several
other Masons, in 1849, started on the overland journey to California. No Grand
Lodge at that time existed in California, and it was consequently open territory to
all the Grand Lodges of the world. Before leaving, a dispensation was obtained
from Bro. Enw.um STEWART, then Deputy Grand Master, to open a Lodge in Cali·
fornia by the name of New Jersey Lodge. By virtue of this dispensation, Bro.
CROo~ opened a Lodge at Sacramento on the fourth day of December, 184.9, and it
was hls boast that he had opened the first, or one of the first, Me.sonic Lodges in
California..
The :Masonic lite of this" New JerieyLodge" must have been short indeed. In a
bill of mortality it would be set down as "stillborn." Our first Lodge in Sacramento, that" moved and had a being," was our venerable'l:llother," '.lehama,No. 3,"
still living in a virtnous and green old age of eighteen years-herself one of the con·
stituent elements of the Grand Lodge of California, and furnishing the second Grand
Master. And may she live and fiouriilh until the eighteen is multiplied by ten, and
her posterity be as numerous i>s the sands of the sea!
The Grand Master devotes some five pages of his Address to this consideration of
the qnestion, "What Masonry is, and what it is not." We wish our space permitted
the transfer of all of his eminently wise suggestions and remarks. But we cannot
withhold this paragraph:I remark, in the first place, that the Masonic Lodge is not the Chnrch, or a substitute for it.
.
The Mason who subordinates the Church to the Lodge errs, and errs grievously.
Each has its proper mission and its appropriate s~here. But the mission of the
Church is higher and more sacred than that of our haternity. Masonry is of human
origin· it olaims no divine commission. It does not profess to be able to reconcile
Uod a~d man; it is powerless .t o change the_human heart; it cannot save a soul from
death. These are the prerogatives of Ommpotence.
" From David's lips this word did roll,
· 'Tis true aud living yet,
No man can save his brother's soul
Or pay hie brother' a debt."
The mission of Masonry is rather with the present than with the hereafter i. rather
with things temporal than with things eternal. Its labors and influence~ are mrected
to ameliorate the conditions of human life. It seeks to _open the fountains o~ ~enevo·
lence to make the selfish man less selfish, the avar1c1ous man less avar1c1ous, to
softe~ the hard heart, and tc. bring the erring back Into the path_ of d~ty. It Atretches
out its hands to succor the needy and the orphan, to dry the widows tears, to cause
the sun to shine where shadow had rested, to make life a joy and not a burden, and
to smooth the pillow of suffering and death. It concedes to the Church the more
honored influential, and sacred position, but strives, in its own peculiar way, and by
its own peculiar !nfiuences, as a handmaid of the lJhurch, to assist her In every good
and perfect work.
We indorse every word of this as sound morality and pertinent good sense.
If some o!" the Grand Master; and Grand Orators that we wot of could only real·
ize how illogical, untruthful-not to say absurd-their high-sounding eulogies of Masonry, as a substitute for Church, Bible, morality, and everything else, appear to.
many of the Fraternity, they would save very much ink and breath, and produce ad·
dresses and orations far more aatisfactory to the brethren, and creditable to their
own head, heart, and common sense. "Verbum sap. I"

We have before us, in a volume of two hundred and seventy pages, the proceed·
ingi ofthe Annual Communication of the mammoth Grand Lodge of the Empire State,
held in New York City, from Tuesday, June fourth, to Saturday, Jnne eighth, 1867.
The M.·. W.·. ROBERT D. HOLMES presided as Grand· Master, and the R.·. w.·. JAMES
M. AUSTIN was Grand Secretary, It will give the reader some idea of the magnitnde
of this assemblage and of what this Grand Lodge Is, to state that representatives
were present from five hundred and forty-seven chartered Lodges. There are six
hundred and six Lodges under this jurisdiction, quite a number of which had failed
to send in their returns to the Grand Lodge, and yet, without these, we find the footing to give a membership of flfty-aeven thousand four hundred and forty-four Master
Masons. .Truly a goodly array, and to be Grand Master ofsnch a host is scarcely second
in honor to the Chief Magistracy of the Empire State. The jurisdiction is divided
into twenty-five districts, five of which, including the r,odges which work in foreign
languages, are In the City of New York. Over each of these is placed a District
Deputy Grand Master, whose reports form a large part of this volume , and are exoellent business papers, attesting the fidelity and Masonic zeal of the respected authors.
Besides these there is a Grand Lecturer, whose office is by no means a sinecure. It
has been filled for years by Bro. JOSEPH B. CHA.FFEE, of Blnghamion. He reports
during three years that he had worked eight hundred days, and traveled twenty-six
thousand mlles. There were also present at this Communication, representatives
from twenty-eight Grand Lodges and Grand Orients, among which we find mentioned
the following: Zur Eintracht, GrandfOrient of France, Grand Lodge of Three Globes,
and Grand Lodges of Cuba and Dominican Republic, New Grenada, Venezuela, and
Chill.
The Address of Grand Master HoLMRS was, as usual, worthy of Its author and ita
predeoessor.s. It is a conClee, business-like document of only t welve page~, thn1
attesting the ability of the· writer to compress very much of infol'mation and sugges·
tlons into a small compass. The opening sentences are well worth copying, for they
breathe the true Masonic spirit. Would that we could say this of all the addresses
and reports which have passed under our notice :Once again, under the benign providence of the Supreme Architect of the Uni
verse, we are permitted to assemble together under auspices, much happier than
could have been supposed when we last had the pleasure of exchanging brotherly
greetings, upon an occasion similar to this. At that time our intercourse with our
brethren of the South had only recently commenced its renewal; but since then, the
bond which once held us together has grown stronger day by day, and the Masonry
of these States is now a nnit. We have been enabled, under the great cardinal virtue
of our Fraternity, to extend to those of them who have suffiired , and now suffer, in
the South, aid, comfort, and cheering words. It is proper now, in the very foreground of my addre~s to you, that I should urgently call your attention to the fact,
that although much has been done to relieve the fearful distresses of our brethren
and those who are dependent upon them in that section of our country, yet much

true Masonic work still remains ready for our hands. I earnestly hope that this

·
It has happily been said of these States, as I may now say of their various Masonic
jurisdictions, that they are like the ocean ; that though each wave is a billow by itself,
each still rolls upon the bosom of a single sea. We are separate in our governments,
but united under the dictates of the cardinal principles of our Craft, we still form one
great and inseparable brotherhood.

Bro. Raus' argument on the disputed boundary question "up North," is pro·
nounced correct; but Bro. LEWIS dissents from the argument against the Iowa brother, as to the power of a Worshipful Master to resign. Bro. L. thinks such a doctrine,
if carried out in practice, would throw the Craft into confusion. Here is his argu·
ment, which we pass over to Bro. RHEES for dissection, answer, or approval, as may
to him seem best:We are taught early in Masonry how soon the Craft are in confusion for WRnt of a responsible head, who can lay out the proper designs upon the trestle-board. The Master
is not only the overseer of the work, but is the connecting link between the workmen and the Grand Master builder, whose warrant he holds, and of which he Is the
sole custodian, and acts as their agent and representative. If he may resign, then
the Wardens who succeed him In office may resign also, and the Craft be at once In
confusion. If it Is answered that this is not likely to occur, our reply Is, that the
rule is safest which provides that it aha!! never take place.
· While he approves of Bro. R.'~ position that the Grand Lodge, for the purpose of
exemplifying the work, may confer the degrees on candidates elected by subordina~
Lodges, he thinks it Is going too far, and too fast, to maintain that a Grand Lodge
may, of its own motion, confer the degrees, without such preliminary, or any action,
on the part of a subordinate Lodge. Bro. L. says: "We believe that the world
moves, and that it should move; but our ideas of progress are, that in Masonic mat.
ten, the world had better be left to the operation of its own laws, than to hitch on a
locomotive to expedite its onward course."

favor of Masonry than the most eloquent of addreBBes, or even a mathematical demonstration that our Order has descended in an unbroken line from King Solomon
and the Builders of the Temple. If .Masonry be not the " handmaid of religion,"
she certainly does some of the work of the older institution. We copy from the
Report of the District Deputy Grand Master of the Third Masonic District, and the
narrative is so well given, and the lesson so apparent, that we will not attempt to
" gild refined gold or paint the lily." If Masons everywhere would "go and do
likewise," as opportunity otrers, we should hear but little of the base charges against
our Institution, which some small minds still like to indulge in:I will now close my report with a sad story, one of the saddest that ever fell to
my lot to narrate ; and 7et one that I cannot omit, without leaving quite incomplete
the history of Masonry m the Third District during the past year.
On the 26th of October last there came into the office of the R.-. W.·. Grand Sec·
retary a widow under twenty years of age, who stated that her husband (JAl!ES
WINSTON, a brother Mason, duly vouched for,) "had died in the hospital for the poor
at Ward's Islaud, and had been J?laced in a pine boz, and buried in a trench." They
had left their home in Europe with the brightest prospects, and in circumstances that,
with good health, would have been comparative opulence. On their way here, her
husband had· been attacked by a disease from which he never recovered. After
arriving here, they had lived many months upon the means they had brought with
them; and when those were exhausted, had taken a single room, and sold everything except necessary clothing, to procure the means of subsistence. When no
other resource was left them, they went to Ward's Island.
Our worthy brother had gone there, as he stated, in preference to asking assistance from his brethren, fearing that after his death his widow might need tlie aid of
the Fraternity, and he not wishing to be a burden to them also. With these views he
had sntfered in silence, and had not allowed his wants to be known until death came
to his relief. His widow now desired that he might receive proper Masonic burial.
By your consent, I called out Amwicus Lodge, and others of the Craft, and on
Sunday, October 28th, we buried the remains of our noble-hearted brother in Green·
wood Cemetery. His young widow was left helpless and alone, without a relative
in this country, and in a situation that would prevent her for some months to come
from following any occupation to obtain a livelihood. But Providence sent her kind
friends and a good home, until she was called away to one far beUer. She died on
the twentieth anniversary of her birthday (Saturday, May 12th,) leaving to the ten·
der care of the Masonic Fraternity an infant daughter but 8B'llen day3 old I Many
hours before her death, she was conscious that she was dying, and was willing to go.
She sent messages of love to her distant home, and uttered expressions of the deepest
gratiJ:ude to those who had befriended her. Among the last words she uttered was
the assurance that, " if permitted to pray after her departure, her constant
prayers would be otfered for blessings upon tlie Masonic Fraternity."
Standing by her bedside the last night of her life, while the shadows of death were
closing around her, and naught in the way of her perfect peace but the thought of
her orphaned babe• two Masters of Lodges In this city (one of them your represen·
tative), pledged the word of the F'l"aternity that the ahil<I of our departed brother,
thus leJt a 'helpless orphan in a strange land, should always be watched over, sup·
ported and protected I
Peacefully she went to her last sleep, trusting In GOD, and resting securely upon
the promise of a Fraternity that her husband had taught her was" as sacred a• liohl
writ," and in whose mystic ladder extended from earth to heaven the "principal
roumi is 0 harity."
Who can doubt for a moment that every brother who reads the sad story, and
who 'Yas ever " prepared to be made a Mason in his heart," will feel bound by that

ceeded his venerable father in the office on the occasion of hie decease, in February

Dispensations had been granted for the establishment of fifteen new Lodges. We
noticed, last year, the passage of some very pithy and somewhat violent resolutiona.
denouncing the Grand Lodge of England, for the very unmasonic course of the
Lodges in Halifax, Nova Scotia, which, as was alleged, were working under charter•
derived from that source. We find in this report of the Grand Secretary a very per·
tinent answer from that Lodge, disposing of' the whole complaint, by the quiet infor·
matlon that those Lodges had never had, directly or indirectly, any connection with
the Grand Lodge of England, and it was therefore difficult to see how the latter
could be held responsible for any of their actions, good, bad, or indifferent. It seems
that here, as in the somewhat celebrated" negro" arraignment in New York for high
crimes and misdemeanors, our North Carolina brethren assumed certain fictions to
be facts, and went off at "half-cock," as a sportsman would say. Such Hudibrastio
artillery generally damages the holder more than the game aimed at.
The Grand Lecturer and his five Deputies submitted written reports of their action
during the year. They generally report satisfactory progress on the part of the
Lodges; but one reports this rather queer proceeding on the part of one Lodge, for
which very unmasonic conduct, it seems to us, the least that should have been done,
would have been the revocation of its charter. It was worse than child's play, and
should not have been tolerated:St. John's Lodge, No. l, rejected the petition of Mr. B., who continued to reside
in Wilmington, for some time afterward. He then removed within the jurisdiction:!
Black Rock Lodge, and petitioned that Lodge for the do.grees before he had bee
one year in the neighborhood. This petition was entertained, and he was ·elec
and Initiated. My attention having been called to these facts, J sent a message to
the Lodge, informing them, that they had proceeded illegally, and advised them to
withold the remainiilg degrees; they delayed action and sent a message to St. John' a
Lodge, asking their consent to have the remaining degrees conferred, which they
were compelled to decline, on the ground that they could not consent to an illegal
act, and furthermore, that the candidate was repugnant to the members of St. John_'~
Lodge, and that they were unwilling to affiliate with him. After all this they called
an emergent meeting, and passed and raised him the same day. 1 have received a
message from the officers of Black Rock Lodge, regretting the course thns pursueil
in this matter, and promising never to do so again. There are a great many Lodglll
working up rejected material. Might I suggest to the Committee on .lurisprudencd;
the propriety of framing a law prohibiting them from doing so, without the unanlir
mous consent of the Lodge who rejected it, and of reporting a resolution, whereby
the Lodges may know when such material offers, either by having it expressed Iii thl!
petition, or adding one more question to the three now asked the candidate before
his initiation.
A very appropriate eulogy of the deceased Grand Secretary, Bro. DoNALD BAIN,
appears in the minutes. He was a bright and shining light in Masonry,,having been
a member of the Craft for half a century, and for more than twenty years Grand Sec·
retary of the jurisdiction.
The Committee on Masonic Jnrlsprudence submitted the following report on
" overtures," or, as we should say, " questions" referred to them:No. 1. A man worthy and well qualified was elected to receive the degrees of'
Masonry, and was initiated as an Entered Apprentice. He then, in the discharge of
his duty, received a wound that deprived him of his right arm. Is it proper and
right to pass and raise him to the sublime degree of Master Mason 1 Yonr committee
report they are of the opinion that it is not. Such a candidate is not, in the language
of the ancient Constitutions, "a perfect youth, having no maim or defect in his boltl
that may render him incapable of learning the art, of serving his Master's Lord, anif
of being made a brother, and then a Fellow-Craft in due time, etc." No. 2. A man
applies to be initiated into the mysteries of Masonry, by petition in the usual form,
except that being unable to write his name, it is appended with his mark, and ttie
Worshipful Master rejects the petition because the petitioner cannot write his name.
Is the reason for the rejection of the petition 11 proper one?
The committee report their opinion to be that this question should be answered
in the affirmative.

The Second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia was held

First, at .lfalifax, September fourteenth, 1866; second, December fourteenth, 1866at which proceedings were had intended to counteract the alleged illegal action of
the so-called "Provincial Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia," acting by authority of the

warned against holding Masonic intercourse therewith; third, March eighth, 1867-'at which the proclamation of the above action was ordered to be made ; fourth, June
fourteenth, 1867-at which no business of importance was transacted.
At the Annual Communication, Grand Master DA VIES delivered an address. He
congratulates the Fraternity on the prosperity of the year; complains of the " great
and crying evil" of non-affiliation; recommends stricter scrutiny into the character
of applicants; complains of the irregularity of attendance and consequent lnetll·
ciency of otllcers of Lodges, and makes sundry suggestions for the good of the Craft.
During the year, the Grand Secretary reports that charters had been granted to
five Lodges, and dispensations to open two new Lodges. The Grand Secretary snb·
mitted an able and conclusive document in defense of the proper organization of the
Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia, and com batting the objections by the supporters of •
the Scottish Lodges and members. He states that this Grand Lodge had received
the "fraternal recognition of thirty-eight Grand Lodges on this Continent, besides
several In Europe."

Grand Master SPABRow's Address occupies some fifteen pages of the pamphlet,
and is' an able and business-like document. By himself, or proxy, he had constituted
seventeen Lodges, to which charters had been voted at the previous session. Hav·
ing learned, however, that one Lodge, while under dispensation, had conferred de·
greee on an Entered Apprentice and Master Mason, he revoked the charter until satisfactory explanations, apologies, and promises for the future had been made. The
Grand Me.eter e.vaile himself of this occurrence to state at some length hie view& of
the powers of a Lodge under dispensation. As to the letter. of Masonic Law, espe·
cially as expounded, or limited rather, by a local regulation of Ohio, he is undoubtedly correct, as he very nearly quotes the words of standard authors. But, we think,
so far as the spirit and intent a~e concerned, our brother is somewhat too rigid.
Such Lodges in this jurisdiction are allowed to confer degrees, while as to the other
limitations we are as strict as our Ohio brethren. Grand Master SPARROW argues that
he must bP. right because, as he says, the Ancient Landmarks do not allow a Mason
to be member of two Lodges atthe same time. But another Grand Master, whose
address was recently under review, maintains precisely the opposite view. Both
cannot be right; or else the " Landmarks " are not so plain as our brother supposes.
We will not discuss this question, however; for unquestionably, under the Ohio Law,
which the Grand Master quotes as special authority, he could not have done lees.
But about those " Landmarks," we simply say-" Query?"
Dispensations had been issued for the opening of sixteen new Lodges. The peti·
tione of six others, on account of some informality, or the late period of presentr..
tlon, were referred to the Grand Lodge for its action.
The Grand Master strongly and, in our opinion, rightly opposes the " growing
disposition among subordinates" to become Incorporate under the State law. He
quotes from the Grand Master of New Jersey, where this practice had become too
common, and where its evils were beginning to develop themselves. We believe no
such policy he.s ever .been suggested In this jurisdiction, e.nd are quite sure it would
meet with but little favor should it be attempted. Masonry is celebrated for its
injunction of obedience to the laws ; but that is no reason why Masone should go
outside of the Order to secure spe cial favors, which will do no substantial good, and
may be produotive of great harm.

OREGON.

We have the printed proceedings of the seventeenth Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Oregon, held at Portland, on the 24th, 25th, aud 26th days of
June, 1867. They make a goodly sized pamphlet of one hundred and flfty·fonr
pages. The M.-. W.-. Grand Master being necessarily absent, the Grand Lodge was

were present from twenty-five chartered Lodges.
The Grand Master, the M.·. W:. A. W. FERGUSON, transmitted his Address, stating his
acts and decisions during the Masonic year. It had been 11 year of prosperity with
the Craft, and yet the scrutiny of applicants had been rigid, as it always should b~.
Rotten timber and shaly stones make as poor material in our edifice, as in the hand1·
wo;k of operative Masons and builders. The Grand Master bri_n~~ forward as. a
grievance, the want of uniformity in the work, and suggests the d'.v1S1on of the ju~IS·
diction into several Distriets, with a District Deputy for each, specially charged with
the duty of exemplification of and instruction in the work. The Grand Lodge adopted
the suggestion, and mapped out three districts, for each of which the Grand Master
is to appoint annually a District Grand Lecturer. The three, with the Grand Master,
are to eonstitnte a Board of Instruction, first agreeing on" somebody's" work, and
then authoritatively enjoining the same on the several Lodges. This plan may work
well in our sister jurisdiction, but we in California have never been favorably im·

In common with sister jnrisdfotions on the Pacific coast, the Grand Master of
Oregon complains of an unwarrantable interference with their rights, on the part of
New York Lodges, in making Masons of visitors to that State, who were, and in the
future intended to be, residents in Oregon. The attention of the Grand Lodge of
New York is called to this infringement, and its interposition invoked to apply the
proper remedy.
'
Beveral dispensations for the establishment of new Lodges had been issued, but
some applications denied, one, because there were two other Lodges in the same
county, within eight or ten miles of the locality petitioning. For Lodges in country
districts, the Grand Master is of the opinion, that such distance is no bar to a zealous
brother, and to form new Lodges. for mere convenience sake, would be to weaken
all, and thus work an injury to the Fraternity generally. As an abstract proposition,
we think the Grand Master correct, but all rules will have their exceptions.
Upon the question "what vote was requisite to restore a Mason to membership in
his Lodge, whose name had been stricken from the roll for non-payment of dues?"
the Grand Master ·decided that none was necessary, the offending brother himself re·
moving the disability and being at once reinstated. We allude to this decision to say
that another Grand Master, whose opinions have fallen under our eye, decides that
like an original application, an unanimous vote of the Lodge is requisite. We feel
enough of the spirit of mischief in our composition to ask our worthy Bro. TAYLOR
of Nevada, which of° these is in accordance with the" ancient landmarks?"
The Grand Master makes a feeling allusion to the decease, during the year, of Past

8or. The Grand Lodge took suitable action, and having at the last session ordered

memory.
1 he Deputy Grand Master read a short address, and made mention of tlle sudden
death of Bro. THOMAS J. HeLMES, a Pl\st Senior Grand Warden.
The Grand Lodge has an "Educational Fund," the income of which during the
year had amounted to $3,177 06, most of which was expended in the tuition of four

" go and do likewise." We are old-fashioned enough to believe that such would be

justify a commencement of this good Masonic work?

PENNSYLVANIA.
We have before us an abstract of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, at its Quarterly and Annual Communications, held In Philadelphia, in 1867.
The Quarterly Communication was held December fourth, the M.·. W.·. RICHARD
VAUX presiding, as acting Grand Master, the R.·. W.·. JoHN THOMPSON being Grand
Secretary, with representatives from one hundred and fifty-two Lodges. This Communication, preceding the annual meeting by !eS!I than a month, seems to have been
mainly called for the election of Grand Officers, although much other business of
local importance we.s transacted. The officers above named were reelected for 1868.
• rhe Report of the Finance Committee contains detailed statements relative to the
'Girard Bequest 11 and the "Grand Lodge Charity Fund," as well as the General
Finances. A Jot for a new M11-sonic Temple had been purchased at a cost of $153,000.
Upon this lot it is proposed to erect a granite strncture of Norman Architecture, at
an estimated cost of $750,000. The committee think the world may be challenged to
produce its superior when completed and finished. The building will be three stories
in hight. On the lower floor will be rooms for the "Grand Officers and Committees,
Library and Banqueting Room, Kitchen, and all the necessary accommodations and
appliances for which these rooms may be used." It Is quite evident that our breth·
ren mean to make something more than a mere form of the " call from labor to re·
freshment. 11 We hope there will be nothing stronger than coffee Included among
those" other appliances." The Grand Lodge Room will be one hundred and five by
fifty·three feet. There will be three rooms for Dine Lodges, each thirty-nine by fortythree feet; a Grand Chapter Room, eighty-one by fifty-three feet; while the third
story is to be devoted to the Encampments. 1'he corner-stone was io be laid on St.
John's Day last, (June twenty-fourth), and it is expected that five years will be consumed in the erection of the Temple. If our Pennsylvania brethren live to see the
realization of their hopes, and steer clear of the usual curse of heavy mortgages,

SOUTH CAROLINA.
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Sonth Carolina, was held in the
City of Charleston, November 19th and 20th, 1867. The M:. W.'. Juras L. ORR presided as Grand Master, and the .R:. W:. R. S. BRUNS was Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from eighty-two Lodges.
The Address of the Grand Master was very brief, but so good in it.A tone and spirit
that we copy nearly one half of it, permitting it to tell its own story:The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of South Carolina is an occasion
of the liveliest interest to the entire brotherhood of Masons within Its limits, and
I find it 11most11~ree11ble duty to congratulate you npon the recurrence of the event
with such 11uspic10us surroundings. No heartburnings, jealousies, or other disagree•
able Incidents have occurred during the last year to mar the fraternal relations o1 our.
Craft; and at no time previously has the institution enjoyed more deservedly the
sympat.hy of the public In general, and the zealous and cordial co-operation of its
members.
The ravages of war, and the disasters to the crops of the last ye11or, brought more
or less suffering to the doors of many who had just claims UJ;>On the Order for assistance. In this emergency, the Lodges of the State have provided 11s liberally as their
scant means would allow for the reflef of the sufferers, while private charity has accomplished much in the alleviation of the prevailing distress. From abroad we have bad
the most tangible evidences of the generosity of our brethren in the large donations
made through the Grand Masters or their associ11ote oftl.cers. From New York, we
have received two donations; one of $.500, another of $150. Illinois and Missouri
have likewise remembered us and rendered aid. Minnesota, far up in the Northwest,
with a comparatively young organization, has contributed the hansome sum of $500;
while, from the MoNTEZilllA Lodge of New Mexico, the hardy, generous pioneers of ,
the plains have sent to their brethren of South Co.rolina $300, thus beautit'nlly exemplifying the length and breadth of that noble charity which underlies and sustain~
ourThe
Order.
, amount thus received by me from various Lodges is $1,780. Of this
entire
sum, I placed $1,730 in the hands of the Grand Secretary, the deputy Grand Master,
and Bro. WILLIAM GILMORE Barns, requesting them to take charge of the distribution
of the funds, and after making proper enquiry of the various Lodges in the State, as
to the extent of t.he suffering in each, to carry out the instructions and intentions of
the generous donors. A circular was addreRsed to all of the Lodges, and their
report will show that the fUnd has been faithfully and fo.irly dispensed.
A donation of $50 from brethren in Ohio :was disbursed by me principally to the
widows and orphans of deceased M&Bons.
Our brethren in Kentucky likewise vlaced in the hands of this committee the munificent sum of $3,450, a portion of which has been distributed, and the remainder
retained for a similar purpose during the coming year.
In every insto.nce I have made suitable acknowledgment to the donors, but avail
myself of the iiresent occasion to reiterate the sense of profound gratitude felt by
!De and the entire fraternity of the State for the generous and timely aid furnished to
us by our noble hearted brethren abroad. May these acts Impress npon us still
more deeply the necessity of cultivating and practicing that charity and Masonic
affection which enters so largely Into the duties and obligations of our ancient
brotherhood. Let the example teach us that whatever may be the changes of time
or oircumstanees, the true Mason never departs from that line of frate1·nal duty which
for ages has been the guide and rule of our Order.
The Grand Master had issned dispensations to open nine new Lodges, and had given
a refnsal for a tenth. He speaks favorably of the work of the Grand Lecturer, Bro. B. R.
CAKPBELL, and of the good results of his labors. The finances of the Grand Lodge were

the sister Grand J,odges. A worshipful brother, JoBEPH RASEY, had dece11Sed, leav·

another year.

TENNESSEE.

The fifty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee was
held in Nashville, October 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th, 1867-the M:. W.·. JOSEPH M. ANDER·
SON presiding as Grand Master, and the R:. W:. CHAllLES A. FULLER being Grand
Secretary. Representatives were present from two hundred and twenty-three char·
tered Lodges, and twenty-eight under dispensation.
The Grand Master delivered his Address. He alludes in feeling and appropriate
terms to the death of Bro. AMA.SA S. UNDERWOOD, an aged brother," so loyal to the
cause, so charitable, so benevolent, so universally beloved.'' He also offers his condolence to the brethren of Pennsylvania, on the death of their Grand Master, JORN
L. GODDARD. Alluding to the mass of correspondence with subordinate Lodges,
thrown npon the Grand Master, he quietly and truthfully suggests, that if the officers

1868.]

Grand Lodge <f Ocdif01-nia.

363

and members would only acquaint themselves with the "Edicts and Resolves of the
Grand Lodge," they would save him and themselves much trouble. The Grand
Master, having been called upon to decide officially, how far maiming or subsequent
defect should prevent the advancement of an Entered Apprentice, he having been
all right at the initiation, argues that the local edict" forty-nine," only applies in its
rigidity to men entirely outside of the pale of Masonry. The edict reads as follows :
49. That subordinate Lodges within this jurisdiction, be and are hereby instructed
not to confer any degree in Masonry upon any individual who is physically or mentally incapable of earning a livelihood, or of recelviog and imparting the ritual of
Masonry.
He refers also to the " Landmarks," and "Ancient Charges," and urges, with con·
siderable force, that if the edict in question goei the length that some claim, it ii
an innovation thereon and should be modified. We quote the most of the addreBS ,
as it sets the whole question clearly before the reader:The facts of the case which called for this discussion, will serve perhaps to illustrate the soundness of, and more effectually enforce, the view I have taken. I am
asked to decide whether a Lodge sllllll confer the second degree upon an Entered
Apprentice who, since his initiation as such, had lost an arm. He is highly recom·
mended. He is a gentleman of unimpeachable character aod fine attainments. He
has exhibited a commendable zeal In the canse, and a hifth appreciation of the objects and purposes of Masonry. I have decided that he 1a not entitled to receive
the degree ; but I have done so because I thought it was eafer to err in excluding a
candidate than in admitting one. This was the only reason for my decision. Upon
the question itself, and the principle involved, my judgment was In his favor. And
indeed, upon what sufficient ground can he be rejected? It is admitted, that he la
physically incapable of receiving and imparting all the ritual of Masonry. But this is a
misfortune which has fallen upon him since he was made a Mason. And does the
loss of this physical. capacity make him any the less a Mason? Is there any record
that an Entered Apprentice, or Fellow Craft, or Master of this Work, was ever turned
out of the Temple because he became physically incapable of performing all the
duties of a workman? Such action now would be an innovation upon the ancient
spirit of Masonry. Who knows how long the Apprentice has been toiling in the
mountains round about the city of our Lord? Wbn knows that It was not the falling
marble which his own toiling hands had chiseled for the Temple of our King, that
crushed the limbs from his body and made him the helpless beggar at our door?
And must he be left to die, whilst another with leBB virtue but stronger limbs walks
over his body and Into the midst of the Temple? Snch should not certainly be the meaning of the Edict referred to, and if it is, Is it not unfortunate, and should It not be re·
vised by the action of this Grand Lodge! Believing that some action should be had,
and that the law referred to should be so modified as to meet unequivocally the view
I have taken, I respectfully submit the following for the adoption of the Grand Lodge
in lieu of the forty-ninth Edict:Candidates for the first degree in Masonry, who for physicul causes are incapable
of earning a livelihood, or of performing the ritual of Masonry, shall be rejected ; and
persons who are incapable mentally of receiving and comprehending the ritual of
Masonry, and imparting the same to others, shall be deemed unfit to receive any
degree of Masonry.
.
This has the virtue of being unequivocal in its meaning, and In exact harmony
with the Ancient Landmarks, the General Regulation•. and Masonic obligations.
The very large number of valuable citizens wlio have lost a limb, or are otherwise
maimed, make that a live question of the day. It must be met. I believe it will be
done with a proper spirit, and with the firm purpose of doing justice to all, and per·
petuating the ancient glory of Masonry.
It may be that, as some Grand Masters have urged, the writer of the above goes
too far, and allQJVs his sympathy for a" patriot," to run away with hie judgment as a
Mason. But having already given our views on this vexed question, we leave the
present case with the reader and the Fraternity.
It is proper to add that the Grand Lodge differed in toto from the Grand Master ,
and held that Edict forty·nine applied to advancement as well as application.
He decided, and as we think, wrongly, that a "Mason cannnot be charged and
proscribed by a Lodge for offenses committed by him before he became a Mason.''
This would never do, except with such limitations as would themselves practically
reverse the rule. We agree with all the Grand Master says about the neglect or

no objection exists, but positively that he is worthy of becoming a member of the

shaky stone gets into the moral edifice of Masonry. But if essential rottenness afterwards appears, the fact that it commenced while a "profane," should not, in our estimation, prevent the Fraternity from ridding themselves of this unsound member.

VIRGINIA.
The Grand Lodge of this ancient and venerable Commonwealth held its Annual
Communication, for 1867, in Richmond, commencing December ninth. The M.·. W.·.
EDWARD H. LANE presided as Grand Master, and the R:. w;., JOHN DovE was Grand
Secretary. Representatives were present from one hundred and seven Lodges, and a
large number of Past Masters. The pamphlet before us is marked by oar Grand Secretary with the ominous words: "No dnplicate." The use of the scissors is therefore prohibited, and our notice, in consequence, must be correspondingly abridged.
The Address of the Grand Master is brief. He commences with a tribute of thanksgiving to the Author of all good, for his bounteous blessings vouchsafed to the Fraternity and 'people, and then gives the brethren some excellent. suggestions as to Ma·
sonry being bQth "Conservative" and" Progressive," in the right understanding of
those words, and yet neither, as they are usually Interpreted by those without and
by some restless or fossil spirits within.
The brethren, notwithstanding their sufferings and poverty, caused by the devastations of war, had not forgotten their first great duty of charity. The Grand Master
mentions a visit made by him to a school established in Richmond for the education
of the orpba:ns (male and female) of Masons. Sixty.five pupils were in attendance.
He says he" never saw a school of that number of pupils conducted with more order
and system." He urges the establishment of like schools in other parts of the jnriB·
diction, and enthusiastically remarks that he "had rather be engaged in the great
and glorious work of relieving the .destitute, sympathizing with the unfortunate, ad·
ministering to the wants and necessities of the needy, and training up the rising generation for usefulness, than to be called either a Roman or American citizen."
The Grand Master pongratnlates the Fraternity on the fact that their relations are
of the most friendly character with all the other Grand Lodges, except that of West
Virginie.. He trusts that all difficulty with this last may soon be amicably settled,
and so do we. We fear, from a glance at the proceedings, that the other members
of the Grand Lodge are not so hopeful or peaceably inclined. There seems to be In
the horizon a" speck .of war," larger tb.a n "a man's hand." We hope, however,
that it will not increase in size, bnt that the rainbow of peace in the cloud may give
token that the brunt of the storm is past, and all is well. Mother and daughter
should not be jealous of each other's prosperity, but rejoice rather In the common
welfare of both.
The previous Grand Lodge had granted to the Grand Master the dispensatory power
to determine what, if any, maimed persons might be made Masons. This he thought
wrong in principle, and well nigh impracticable in action. He had refused to exercise the power, and recommended a repeal of the act, as inconsistent with ancient
landmarks. The Grand Lodge concurred.

things we find therein. We can only quote what he says of the Report of Bro. RHEES
of that year :•

The Grand Master speaks somewhat at length upon one of his decisions. A party
claiming to have been made 11 Mason In Pennsylvania, wished to visit 11 Lodge in
Washington, with an ultimate intention of affiliation therewith ; but he could not
pass even an "A, B, C" examination in Masons' work. Whereupon he wrote to

should be admitted and have the benefit of all needful instruct10n in those points
wherein he may have proved deficient.
This course may be all right, but our opinion Is that if any Master Mason ~
entirely forgets the use of all his working tools, It would be as well for him to begin
again as an Entered Apprentice, and work his way up legitimately. This business of
polishing materials by Lodges, that have been so entirely covered and almost ruined

in protesting against the invasion by Oregon of our territorial jurisdiction, and that
the course of the Grand Lodge has been marked by a strict adherence to correct
Masonic principle, and actuated by a desire to cultivate 'harmony with Oregon; and
that It Is a source of unfeigned regret that that Grand Lodge has rejected every
attempt of ours to secure a peaceable and satisfactory solution of our differences.
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary be instructed to forward a copy of this report
and resolutions to the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge or Oregon, from and after
which all correspondence shall cease between the two Grand Lodges.
We can only express our regret that such a result has been reached. We will not
dlscW!B the original question, our predecessors having already done that for us. But
when brethren are thus becoming estranged, we would utter a word of peac.e and
harmony. We would remind both sides or those excellent words of good King David,
which the Entered Apprentice hears when he first enters a Lodge. Cannot older
brethren make these their rule or action T We hope each side will waive some of Its
feelinga, if not of its rights, and that the door may be opened for permanent recon·
ciliation.
It Is but a suggestion of our own, and commits no one. It Is to refer the whole
subject to the Grand Masters of California and Nevada, the nearest nelghors. We
are sure they would do justice In the premises, and that their decision would be
acceptable to all good Masons in both jurisdictions.
The Grand M&1ter had prohibited the Port 1bumsend Lodge from proceeding to
the trial of a member, because" It was a matter of a domestic nature, to which one
of the members of the Lodge was a party.'' In this we think he erred, and such was'
the opinion of the Grand Lodge, which passed the following resolution on the subject:
.Resowed, That subordinate Lodges are reaponslble for the conduct.of all membera
of the Order within their jurisdiction, and it Is their duty to take oogmzance of all In·
fringements of the rules of the Order, and they may proceed to try all oll'enders, and
are responsible for their aotion only to this Grand Loage.
From the Report of the Grand Treasurer, we find that the receipts of the Grand
Lodge were $793 25, and the expenditures $769 85.
The number of Lodges In the jurisdiction Is ten, with a'membership of three hund·
red and f!fty·three. There had been twenty·nlne initiations during the year.

WEST VIRGINIA.

We have the proceedings of the third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of West Virginia, held at Wheeling, December eleventh, 1867-the M.-. W.-. WILLU.11:
J. B,lTES presiding as Grand Master, and the R.·. W.-. Ta0111A.S H. LOGAN being Grand
Secretary. Representatives were present from nineteen Lodges.
We have also the minutes of four special Communications, one of February
thirteenth, 1867, called to constitute" Nelson Lodge" No. 30; of June ,twenty-eighth,
1867, to lay the corner·stone of the "Soldier's Monumental .Association," of Monongahela county ; of August fifteenth, 1867, to lay the corner-stbne ef the " Regency of
West Virginia Normal School Building;" and of Angnst twenty-second, to lay the
corner·stone of" St. John's Episcopal Church," of Wheeling.
The Address of the Grand Master alludes to the prosperity of the Fraternity and
State, and calls for suitable acknowledgment to Aijnighty God therefor. He also
makes appropriate allu1ion to the death of an eminent brother; GEORGE W. SIGHTS,
Past Master of a Lodge in Wheeling.
He had issued dispensations to form five new Lodges. There are also given thirteen decisions on varloW! points of Masonic law Bild usage, but we find nothing calling
for special comment.
A regulation of the Grand Lodge permits the resignation of the principal officers
of a Lodge. The Grand Master thinks this is not correct Masonic law, and recommends an essential alteration.
He has some excellent remarks upon tha.duty of Masons to "exemplify" their
work by consistent and honorable lives, and particularly condemns profane swearing
and Intemperance, to which many of the brethren are unfortunately addicted.
The Grand '.l'.reasurer reports the receipts of the Grand Lodge to be $1,089 51, and
expenditures 8914 SS.
The proceedings of the Grand Lodge were almost entirely local in their character,
and present few points demanding outside notice.
The number of Lodges in the jurisdiction is thirty, and of members one thousand
three hundred and sixteen. There had been initiated two hundred and twenty·one,
passed one hundred and ninety·aeven, and raised one hundred and ninety-five.
The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were reelected.
WISCONSIN.

The proceedings of the Twenty.fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Wisconsin make a goodly sized pamphlet of two hundred and forty pages. The
Communication was held at Milwaukee on June 11th, 12th, and 18th, 1867. The
M.-. W.·. Grand Master being absent on account of sickness, the Grand Lodge was
presided over by the R.·. W.-. HARLOW P.1usE, Deputy Grand Master, the R." W.'. w.
T. PALMER being Grand Secretary. Ther~ were present representatives from one
hundred and forty-six of the one hundred and seventy Lodges in the jurisdiction.
The Address of the Grand Master, MELVIN L. YOUNGS, was transmitted and read.
It Is brief, occupying less than six pages, and Is mainly taken up with the record of
the work performed by the Grand Master. He compares the present condition of
the Fraternity In Wisconsin with what it was In 1843, when a "little· band solemnly
resolved that it is expedient to form a Grand Lodge In the Territory of Wisconsin."
That" little band" was .composed of seven members, representing the only three
Lodges In the Territory. The entire membership was less than seventy·flve. In
1867 It was his privilege to see about three hundred representatives from the one
hundred and seventy Lodges in the jurisdiction assembled In Grand Lodge. There
were now over seven thousand Master Masons, being an increase in one year of
two thousand and eighty-four.
Dispensations had been granted during the year for the establishment of twelve
new Lodges, to all of which charterl!'were issued by the Grand Lodge. No applica·
tions had been refused.

A Committee appointed at the previous Communication to " prescribe and pro·
mulgate such general rules, regulations and conditions as they may think proper,
in regard to the snbject of healing Army·made Masons," agreed upon these items:1. There should be 11 petition in due form, a committee of investigation, and the
lapse of at least twenty days before the ballot. 2. An unanimous ballot. S. Obll·
gation of each degree to be administered. 4.. Twenty days to elapse between the
healing in each degree. 5. A fee of not less than $1 O.
We should think this was very nearly like beginning de n01lO. But it was all right.
That was a questionable policy, at the best, which authorized work by Army
Lodges, so called, and we should think such mushroom Masons would need to review
their lessons in Masonry, beginning at the alphabet. If" all Grand Lodges had stood
firm amid the excitement and frenzy of our civil war, and had adhered striotly to the
" Ancient Landmarks," this " trouble in Israel" would not have molested the Fra·
ternity. Will men and Masons' ever learn true wisdom and 11 sound policy by e:x:·
perlence?
The Grand Lecturer, the w... Bro. A. B. ALDBN, reported a goodly amount of work
durmg the year, having visited and instructed some seventy Lodges.
The Report of the Committee on CorreHpondence is from the pen of the W.'.Brc. W.
H. NORRIS, Jr., and is a well written document of sixty pages. The proceedings of
thirty-six Grand Lodges are reviewed , and we are quite sure our friend had no good

A proposed amendment to the Constitution, changing the place of meeting from

The Committee on .Appeals, answering to our own on Grievances, made one report
covering the nine cases which had been referred to them. One approved of the ex·
pulsion of a brother for being 11 habitual drunkard. Another reversed a suspension
because the Lodge had acted on hearsay tefttlmony almost exclusively. The Com·
mittee very properly censures such action in these pointed words: " There ls a prac·
tice ln vogue among many Lodges, which cannot be too strongly censured, of entertaining the most frivolous charges against brethren, and Introducing 1111 kinds of
irrelevant and improper testimony to sustain the charges; such as "Dick BllYS that
Tom says that Prudence says as how it might be if It had not been otherwise." The
Committee insist that every brother shall have a fair trial, governed by the rnles of
evidence. The Grand Lodge concurred.
The sum of $1,000, from the funds of the Grand Lodge, was voted as a donation to
suffering Masons and their families in the Southern jurisdiction. ,

BTATIBTIOS OF THE FRATERNITY,
To inform brethren, here and elsewhere, as well as the Convention of" old ladies"
in pantaloons, who recently assembled In Pittsburg , and resolved that the world
should not turn around any longer, except as. they pleased, we have compiled from
the reports before us, a st atement of the goodly number of the Fraternity upon this
North American continent. Where we had not received the reports of 1861, we have
substituted the numbers as returned In 1866, and In one or two Instances were compelled to estimate merely. It will be seen that the number approximates 400 ,000,
"good men and true" ; and if our enemies will but take a moral and intellectual
census of the same Fraternity, they will find that, as a whole, no class of citizen•
can take a higher rank for Intelligence, patriotism, liberality, and all the virtues thai
make a good citizen and a faithful, upright man. When the sour visaged "Mawworms," who are Inaugurating another crusade against Masonry and all secret societies,
suooeed in annihilating: this ancient and venerable Institution, we hope they will send
us word:·

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, from the special committee to whom was referred the Address of the Grand Master and the Report of the Grand Secretary, presented the following reports:-

To the M." W.·. Grana Lodge of California:Your committee, having bad under consideration the Address of the M.'. W.•. Grand
Master, respectfully report that th~y have read with much pleasure the gratifying intel·
ligence which it contains of the continued prosperity of our Fraternity, and the har·
monions relations which exist between our own and other Grand Lodges in communication ' with ours. Although instances are mentioned in it where the rights of our
jurisdiction seemed to have been disregarded abroad, yet when our just claims have
been demonstrated, it has tended only to develop more clearly the strong and active
sentiment of fraternity by which we are united. We find much in it to confirm the
confidence which trustfully placed the gavel in his band, and are fully assured that the
welfare of our jurisdiction during the past year has been carefully and zealously
guarded.
Having considered the various matters contained therein, we recommend that they
be referred as follows:
To a speolal committee of three, so much as relates to the death of our late Deputy
Grand Master. Bro. HENRY HAR& HARTLEY, and of our late Past Senior Grand W4rden,
Bro. WILLIAM. H. PETERSON:
To the Committee on Cb.arters, so much as relates to dispensations granted for the
creation of new Loda:es :
To the Committee on By-Laws, so mu~h as has reference to the amendments to by·
laws of Lodges :
To the Committee on Jurisprudence, so much as rofers to the question arising out
of circumstances connected with a trial in Natoma Lodge, No. 64, together with the
suggestions in regard to procuring testimony in trials where witnes11es reside without
the jurisdiction of a Lodge so engaged ; so much as refers to the subject of physical
disabilities.of persons, in their relations to our Fraternity; so much as refers to brethren
reinstated who were formerly laboring under legal disability, owing to the extinction
of the Lodges to which they severally belonged ; and so much as refers to the granting
of specie.I dispensations for t.he election of officers and re·ballottiug for candidates.
Your committee recommend that the action of the Grand Master in refusing to
grant permission to Lodges to appear in public, where no labor was to be performed,
be emphatically approved; and they recognize, in the suggestions of the Gn.nd Ma1ter
on the subject of the growing necessity for the adoption of some plan or system that
will secure an annual inspection of all the Lodges in the jurisdiction, and particularly of
the smaller and more remotely situated ones, a matter which annually increases In Its
importance. Th11y believe that the Grand Lodge has nearly exhausted every persuasive measnre by which the members, and e•pecially the officers, of Lodges could be
prevailed up en to read the published proceeding~, or at least the Constitution and Regn·
le.tions of the Grand Lodge; and they think it apparent that the fruit or such ell'orts has
not been of such quality as the Grand Lodge be.s a right to expect. The subject is
worthy of serious deliberation by the Graud Lodge, anll they recommend its reference
t.o the Committee on Jurisprudence.
All which is respectfnlly submitted.

GILBEBT B. CLAIBORNE,

To the M. •• W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. E. P. MEILY from the
action of Forest Lodge, No. 66, in expelling him from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, have had the same under consideration and respectfully report that, whilst
the charges and specifications are sufficient to justify the sentence, the brother was
convicted solely upon hearsay testimony as to the material facts of the case. It
would seem from the transcript that abundant competent testimony might have been
obtained. Mrs. EASLY and Mr. BROWN ought to have been called upon to testify in
person, instead of their statements being detailed by witnesses. It seems s.trange to
your committee that hearsay testimony should continue to be received, when the
Grand Lodge reports are full of reversals because of the reception of such testimony.
Your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the action of Forest Lodge, No. 66, in the case of Bro. E. P. MEILY,
be reversed and set aside, and that the case "Be remanded for a new trial. ·
All which Is respectfully submitted.
JA.S. LA.WRENCE ENGLISH,)
GILBERT B. CLA.JBORNI!,
CHARLES L. WIGGIN,

To the M. •• W.·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. JA.oos FL&rSHHAN from
the action of GeorgetoUYn Lodge, No. 25, in the acquittal of Bro. FRLIOB RIOOI of
charges preferred against him, have had the same under consideration and respect·
fully report·that two of the specifications are unquestionably proven by the evidence,
and that the acquittal must have resulted from a misconception of the law upon the
subject. If Bro. Rrcc1 conceived that Bro. FLEISHll!AN had done him a wrong, he
should have preferred charges against the latter, instead of resorting. to abuse. In
using abusive language to 11 brother, he was guilty of a M1111onic offense. He is also
guilty of a Masonic offense in Indulging in the habitual use of profane language,
which is one of the specifications. " Profanity in a Mason, while it Is an insult to the
majesty of our Maker, is also an Irreverence for the religious design of the Masonic
science, and as such is a Masonic crime."
This case having been fully heard, your committee deem it a proper one for the
exercise of the undoubted prerogative of the Grand Lodge to render such a jndg·
ment as should have been rendered by the subordinate ; and they therefore recommend the adoption of ·the following resolution : Resolved, That the action of GeorgetoUJn Lodge, No. 25, in tLe acquittal of Bro.
FELibE Rrno1 of the charges preferred against him, be reversed and set aside; that
the brother be adjudged to be guilty of unmasonio conduct, and that he 'be sentenced therefor to be reprimanded; and that the Master of Georgetown Lodge, No. 26,
be and he is hereby required to execute the sentence of this Grand Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted.

1867, have had the same under consideration and respectfnlly report that, although the
petition was sent to this Grand Lodge through the Lodge which expelled him, no action

stands alone, without anything to support it or to show that it Is a proper case for the

petitioner, acknowledging that he "was rightly punished-that he feels his punish·
ment to be very severe-that he Is sincerely attached to the principles of Masonryand that he is truly sorry for his fault and asks to be forgiven," is not sufficient. If it
were, every unworthy Mason who has been expelled could be restored, and Masonic
punishments would be a by-word and a reproach. Your committ6e therefore recommend that tlte prayer of the petitioner be denied.

Bro. JAMES L. ENGLISH, from the Committee on Grievances, pre~ented
the following reports:To the .M." W." Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. GERGE G. WEBSTER
from the action had in the matter of charges preferred by him against Bro. WM.
McCLURE, before Rising Stai· Lodge, No. 83, have had the same under consideration
and respectfully report that, when the commissioners assembled for the trial, the ac·
cused moved to strike from the charges as presented certain portions thereof, which
motion being sustained by the Master, the accuser declined to proceed wit.h the trial
until the action of the Graud Lodge could be had upon his appeal from the decision.
The decision of the Master was correct. The portions stricken out contain no clear
and oertain specifications of an offense, but are rambling, uncertain, unsatisfactory,
and insufficient. If a specific charge could be found therein, it would be by sifting
them as one would sift chaff to obtain a grain of wheat. Charges must be specific,
and stated with conciseness, clearness, and certainty.
The Master would have been justified in dismissing the charges on account of the
language in which they are couched. Such expressions as " malignant heart," ''systematic coiner of slander and lies," "cowardly and lying assault upon his standing as
an officer,"" known to the accused to be a lie at the time he made it," and "having
with malice wilfully, from a corrupt heart, hatched a lie," etc., when applied to a
brother, are not to be tolerated, even in one preferring charges. Your committee
therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resolved, That the appeal of Bro. GEORGE G. WEBSTER, from the action had in
the matter of charges preferred by him against Bro. WM. McCLURE, before Rising
81,ar Lodge, No. 83, be and the same is hereby dismissed.
All which is respectfully submitted.
JAB. LAWRENCE ENGLISH,
GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE,
CllARLES L. WIGGIN,
Committee.
WILLIAM C. RANDOLPH, J

action of Los Angeles Lodge, No. 42, in sentencing Bro. F. A. OERTEL only to be reprimanded, have had the same under consideration and respectfully report that, upon the
case as presented, the punishment is sufficiont. Had the testimony convitited Bro.
OllRTEL of striking Bro. HOLLER, it would not have been sufficient. The statementB
of Bros. GOLLER and OERTEL being at variance, that of the profane who witnessed the
difficulty must control the verdict, and he says the " movement was not a strike."
According to the testimony, even his own, Bro. GOLLER is not entirely guiltless, bu'
is as deserving of a reprimand as Bro. OERTEL, having used equally as improper Ian·
guage.
The transcript in this case does not show the precise offenses of which the com mis·
•ioners found the accused guilty, but as the verdict and sentence are in accordance
with the facts proven, we do not feel disposed to reverse the case on that ground,
The Commissioners should have found the accused guilty of so much of the facts set
out in the specification as were proven. There is less excuse for their neglect in this
particular than for similar neglect in any other Lodge in the jurisdiction, as the law
on this subject was laid down at the last Communication of the Grand Lodge, upon an
appeal from Los Angeles Lodge.

JonN B. FELTON, Grand Orator, then delivered the Annual Oration, as follows : MosT WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE:We meet to-day as Masons. At the door of this Temple we leave behind us all prejudices, all distinctions, all differences of family and nation, of race, religion, and opinion.
We meet simply as men. The tie which binds us together is one which all humanity
can recognize, and if we insist, as a condition of entering our brotherhood, on the belief
in a God, it is not because we exact of any one to have a particular religion, or any
religion at all. It is because this belief is an irresistible part of our human nature ;
it is because this belief is born with us; it is because we cannot be brothers without
having a common father; it is because it is a universal belief; and however much a man
may persuade hlmself that he believes there is no God, when he is confronted with
his own soul, he knows and feels that God exists. It is not an exception excluding a
portion of mankind that we make when we exclude the atheist from our Temple ; i'
is only a condition that we impose that every man who comes here shall recognize
what his nature teaches him-what he cannot escape from-what is essential to the
obligations he assumes when he becomes a Mason. It' tbere is no God to whom we
owe our common origin, what relation can exist among men?
It-is one of the regrets of my life that I did not in my youth join the Masonic
Fraternity ; that I have not had time and leisure to study profoundly its beautiful
legends, to make myself master of its antiquities, to follow historically this noble
institution to its origin, and to comprehend fully Its scientific teachings : but fortunately the fundamental tenets of Masonry are simple to the comprehension of a child.
It is not necessary for me to understand fully the science of music in order to be
thrilled and swayed by the inHuence of harmony, nor is it necessary for me to give

388

Proceedings of the

LOct. 15,

myself up to a long study of Masonry to comprehend fully that exqnlslte but simple
harmony which addresses itself to every morfal ear. It is not because Masonry goes
back to the earliest antiquity; It is not because the great, the good, and the learned
men of every e.ge he.ve been proud to listen to its teachings ; it ls not because of its
badges, its regalia, its long processions, its ceremonies, and its pomps the.t I regard
. it as one of the great privileges of my life to be a Mason. It is because, by entering
our order, I felt and kne'I'!' that human sympathy, made more intense by this common
tie, would go with me through life. I knew and felt that the relation which exists
between men, because they have.a common nature, we.s made closer and more inti·
mate by admission to an Order whose prinoiples admit all mankind, provided they
are worthy of sympathy. .And yet I have had occasion to feel that, too often, in attending to the outward forms of Masonry, in the strict observance of its rights and cere·
monies, in the rigid performance of its external duties, the true spirit of Masonry is lost sight of; that frequently, while the body wears the outward emblems
of Masonry and is disciplined to all the signs aud tokens by which the fact of membership Is communicated from one to the other, the mind and soul are not trained and disciplined to a corresponding interchange of mutual good feeling, love, and sympathy.
It has been my misfortune often to hear Masons question the motives of their
brethren, and place unjust, uucharlte.ble constructions on their acts. I have se~n
brothers, whom I knew to be in all respects worthy, stopped in their e.dve.nces towards
Masonic light by the sectional spirit-the partisan prejudice-the opposition whlcH
competition In business and diversity of interests create. .A.ud I have found that the
Lodge, sworn to love, charity, and sympathy, has been often times convulsed by
cabals, Intrigues, and bitter personal enmities.
The mutual dependence of man on his brother man is the fundamental principle of
our order. But in what does this dependence consist? You and I may never have
need of material aid. It may be our good fortune to go through life independe11t, in
the ordinary sense of the term; to be in a position where we can dispense favors , and
have no need to receive them. Dut are we really Independent of our fellow-men, in
the deeper sense of the word? Whatever riches or position a man may acquire, what
Is he lfhe stands a.lone in the world! Selkirk, on his desolate island, in hi~ years of solitude, forgot the language which his mother taught him. But there is a moral isolation
which makes a me.n forget the very language of the heart, of the soul-the language
which he was born to speak ; and that isolation comes whenever there is a barrier
between him and his fellow men.
The experience of the man of the world brings him at last to the same conclusion
which our beautiful fundamental law adopts as a rule, and It Is this : " Rely on yonr
brother man; believe in him." Often we a.re deceived ; the lying tongue, the treacherous heart, the insincere protestations of friendship delude and beguile us; but the in·
stinctive reliance on human faith, which nature has planted in the mind of the child
for its pr9tection, abandons us as we enter on the threshold of active lifo only to return to us as a reasoned principle when we grow older.
I have seen witnesses swear in platoons to falsehood. I have found that the sweetest
smiles, the l!IOst honeyed accents, were put on with preconoeived purpose to injure and
defraud. Often I have said to myself, if man is like this, my great wisdom wlll be in
watching him closely, in never believing, in universe.I distrust; and then when I turned
to myself and se.w my own weakness, I comprehended that God he.d made me suoh
and that if man wished to destroy, I was destroyed-If he wished to deceive, I musi
be deceived-if I could not place reliance on him r had better die, for the world was no
place for me. For r was placed in such a relation with my fellow man, tb11t my sleep
by night was in danger e.nd my walk in the evening was beset by perils which, in the
broad light of day, only, my eyes would serve me to point out, if there did not exist
some In we.rd original bond of kindness, goodne 3s, and love between man and man, ~n
which each could rely. .A.nd when I saw the necessity for this reliance, and that life

was Impossible without it, I have turned to examine and see whether such a bond could
exist, and to what extent it could be relied on. I ae.w that the most intimate friends
· were sundered by death, and that iu a short time the mourner consoled himself and
l'Orgot. I ae.w that it would be unsafe to demand the greatest sacrifices, even from
friendship or family. I knew that if I said to myself-because there is this bond of
love and sympathy between me and my fellow·man, I can therefore lean my whole
weight upon it-that it would inevitably give we.y. I se.w that it had its limits, and I
saw too why it should have its limits. The world would be in perpetual mourning were
even love made so strong that there could be no consolation for its Joss. The sympathy between me.n and me.n, as such, must be bounded by necessity, by closer affec·
tlons, by patriotism, by one's duties to others.
But, make all the deductions which yon will, and see how much there is left in the
nature of man to sympathize with and to love. There is truth. Lying and deceit a.re
but the exceptions, and the basest man yields to a temptation and swerves from his
own lnna~e d_esire when he lies. The great.protection which the law gives to property aad hfe 18 based on the general deyotion to truth in men. In the oath administered to a witness, when on the story that he tells hangs a human life, the Jaw, with
e.~ experience taught it by ages of reflection on human nature, appeals, and appeals
with safety, to two great attributes common to all men-to reverence-to truth. Re.'
lying on man's love to God and his devotion to truth, the juryman renders his verdict
and the judge pronounces sentence. Every commercial principle, every rule of business, takes for grt\nted and as•umes the existence of original, high moral qualities in
man. The credit system, the promissory note, the trust In a man's word, the relation
of servant to master and of principal to agent, all have this lying at their baae. They
are all founded on the principle that when no eye is on him, when temptation to do
wrong holds out impunity, when Interest conflicts with duty, me.n's nature is worthy
of trust.
·
Analyze any custom of soolety, and you wlll find that-1t Implies and assumes the.t
human nature Is good, true, kind, benevolent, full of reverence e.nd love. The desire
to please, benevolenoe, love of our kind.• charity, all lie at the base of the evening
party, the social dinner, the elaborate toilet, the courteous salutation, the curtsy and
the bow. We grasp ea.ch other by the hand, for we wish to express, by e.n outward
union of the body, the union in feeling and affection. Scattered through the le.nd
the s~ire of the church, the frequent school house, the university, the commodiou;
hospital, the refuge of the deformed, the blind and the deaf, the temple of jostioe all
are the expressions of the love, the good will, the sympathy, the Ideas of the Just
and good with which the hearts of the generality of men abound. Crime shocks
and startles the natural moral feeling, just as discord falls harsh and clashing on the
ear, however untutored. God has tuned the mind to the good, as he has tuned the
ear to harmony.
There is not In the world a being more unfitted to live In it, to perform the ordinary business of life, to be successful in his undertakings, than the man who he.a become suspicious and distrustful, who attributes bad motives to acts, and who he.s lo t
• c.onftdence in his kind. He may have arrived at his conclusions from a bitter exp:.
r1ence; he may have been often cheated and deceived; where he had a right to lo k
for gratitude, he may have encountered the cold look or averted eye • but he ho
made the mistake of taking the exceptions for the rule. He he.a reason~d to himse~
beoause I have been deceived, man is deceitful; because I have had kindness met
with ingratitude, man Is ungrateful. What is there for such a man to do but to ha
himself, like Timon? He is but one ; he cannot be ubiquitous; he ca~not e.lwa~
wake and ~atch. How can such a me.n perform large enterprises, where trust in
manr. men 18 necessary ? How can he he a General, when he relies not on the highest
qualities in thousands? How can he be a statesman, when he has no faith that the
laws he frames liave any goodness in human nature to address themselves to? How

can he perform the slightest task, when he stands on the outside of the great army
of mankind, ready to run at the first sign of approach? Man Is so constituted that
even the intellect of a Napoleon could only work through the brains and arms of oth·
era. What a feeble creature Napoleon would have been had he not had implicit re·
liance on man. Instead of drawing strength and Inspiration from others, their
strength would have been to him a constant menl\ce; their enthusiasm would have
been hypocrisy ; their faces, lighted into radiance at his approach, would have been.
but the mask to hide the malicious, envious, and deceitful heart. And what is the
condition of him who has failed to gain the sympathy of his fellow men? How his
own sympathies wither and fade, deprived of the sunlight that beams from other
human hearts. What fruit or flower grows on the barren waste of his intellect?
The voice of the heart becomes mute when it speaks to ears that are deaf. It hM
often seemed to me that, for such a man, even the laws were less powerful to protect.
He goes before a jury, and there he finds men who are but human aft.er all-whose
prejudices alfect their reason. Even with the right aud the law on his side, there
Is a grapple, a struggle, and a fierce contest when It is a question of doing him simple
justice.
I wear my badge of Masonry with pride and exultation. I know, as I pass along
the streets, that men unknown to me look kindly upon me because I am one of them.
I know that I have no need of a long acquaintance before my brother trusts in meconfides his dearest interests and his most intimate secrets to me. I know that the
sunlight, as it is reflected from my M11Sonic symbol, carries back with it a ,ray of
sympathy and mutual understanding to the hearts of thousands ; and it is for that I
value and love it. But if' this badge stands merely by itself-a piece of lettered ii old;
if there is no great meaning symbolized by it; if the fundamental law of Masonry
ceases to exist, whereby the doctrine of love to man and confidence in the goodnen
of his character is inculcated as a precept; or if that law becomes a dead letter and
is not carried out in our lives and In the habits of our milids-what care I for the
bauble? I wear it now, and feel myself stronger and better because I am permitted
to do so. Strip it of Its idea, and I can only wear it from mere vanity.
It seems to me that the Mason who introduces disorder into our circle ; who
intrigues and plots for selfish ends ; who is suspicious and jealous of his brethren ;
who allows unworthy motives to act upon him.when it ls a question of their admission
or advancement-is guilty of a greater crime against Masonry than he who is dishonest
or dissolute, or who commits an olfense against society at large; for he is guilty Qf
treason against its organic law. Just assoolety cannot exist without government, Masonry cannot exist unless the law of good will is voluntarily and strictly observed.
This law is its fundamental Idea, and without this law Masonry itself has no value.

Bro. WM.. C. BBLOHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented
the following reports:7b the M.•• W. ·. Grand Lodge of Oaliforrtia:Yonr committee have considered the question proposed by Bro. WILLIAM H. HILL,
and respectfully report 118 follows :If a candidate h118 been elected to receive the three degrees of Masonry by a Lod~,
and, after having received the first degree, or fl.rat and second degrees, removes tem·
por11rily or permanently within the jurisdiction of another Lodge, the latter Lodge
may, at the request of the former, confer the remaining degree or degrees upon
him. In such case, the conferring of the degree or degrees is only an act of courtesy, and the Initiate becomes 11 member of the Lodge in which his petition was
received, and not of the Lodge conferring the last degree. But It, having received
one or two deg~ees in the Lodge in which he was elected to r eceive the three,
he removes to another jurisdiction and desires to become a member of the Lodge
within whose jorisdiction he hll8 removed, he most present his petition, stating the
facts of his case and asking ·to receive the remaining degree or degrees in that
Lodge. But his petition can not there be received until the permission of the Lodge
which had acquired jurisdiction over him by electing him and conferring upon him the
ftrst, or ftrst and second degrees, has been obtained; and when such permission is
obtained, his petition must take the usual course of petitions for degrees or for membership. In snch a case, if he is elected and the remaining degree or degrees is or
are conferred, he becomes a member of the Lodge conferring the last degree.
A degree conferred by one Lodge at the request of another is the act of the
Lodge preferring the request. Permission to receive the petition of an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft is a relinquishment of the rights of the Lodge granting
the permission.
Io the uase presented by Bro. HILL, your committee think the Lodge conferrlJlg
the degree by permission must have construe"d the permission as a request, and that
the recipient is a member of the Lodge In which he was elected .to receive the de·
