Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred a question proposed by Bro. JOHNS. WABn
In the following form-" A Mason, who is the only.witness to prove charges which
have been preferred against a brother, Is employed as counsel for such brother. Can
he refuse to testify before the oommission upon the ground that his knowledge of the
facts of the case was communicated to him by the accused brother, In his capacity as
counsel?" -have considered the same, and respectfully report as_follows :-

1868.]

Grand Lodge of OaJ,ifornia.

395

The rules adopted in our civil courts, with reference to communications between
attorney and client, we think should apply in Masonic courts as well. Those rules are
well-established. If one employs an attorney and discloses to him, as so.ch, the facts of
his case , the courts not only will not compel, but will not permit tbe attorney to disclose them upon the witness' stand. If one, charged with a Masoniu oft'ense, employs
counsel and discloses to him, as such, the facts of his oe.se, we think the same rule
should apply, and that the counsel should not be compelled or allowed to dfsclose the
facts so communicated, when palled as 11 w!tneBB. If, however, the brother employed
as counsel bas become acquainted with any facts pertinent to the case, otherwise than
through the confidential disclosures of his client, he should be compelled to give
them in evidence when called as 11 witness. The relation of attorney and client
should protect confidential disclosures of the client to the attorney, as such, and
nothing more.
All which le respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM C. BELCHER, )
HENRY F. WILLIA¥8,

The V.'. R:. W1LLIAH H. HILL, Grand Che.plain, addressed the Grand

MOST WORSHIPFUL GRA.ND MA.STER: I rise to move the adoption of the report and
resolutions which have jnst been read. From the position which I have so long had
the honor to occupy in this Grand Lodge, through the kind partiality or yourself
and your predecessors, as well as from the peculiar relations It was my good fortune
to sustain to our deceased and lamented Bro. liA.RTLllY, it seems proper, and per·
haps called for, that I should not allow these resolutions to pass in silence. A?d
yet, Most Worshipful Sir, there is, probably, no member of this Grand Lodge who is;
or can be, more averse to the delivery of mere eulogies upon the dead than myself.
Neither as a matter of taste nor of principle do they ever commend themselves to
my judgment. I have often expressed the opinion, and so feel and say now, that it
is a custom "more honored in the breach than in the observance." But there are
cases In which, ~bile this question of mere eulogy may be set aside, it is eminently
proper that a word of sympathy and of affectionate ad vice should be spoken, ere
our brother passes finally from our sight and our thoughts. These resolutions,. and
the well chosen words embodied In the report of the committee, commend themselves most heartily to my judgment and vote. In simple, concise, but most truthfnl
terms, they describe the life, the character, and the worth of our deceased brother. He
was indeed a good man; an emiuent and worthy Mason, in acts as well as in theor! ;
a courtly and polished gentleman; a sound jurist and counselor; an nnobtrus1ve
but practical Christian. In all these relations, as well as those more sacred ones of
husband and father, Bro. HARTLEY had but few snperiors or eqnals. When the
tears of so many hundreds watered his lowly grave, they were but the just tribute to
his worth-the evidence of their love for the truest friend of many a brother, his
widow and orphans.
I speak thus warmly and .decidedly, because it was my privilege to sustain, noi
merely cordial, but peculiar relations to our friend. I knew him, not only as a
brother Mason, faithful In all the trusts committed to his care, and a fellow-citizen es·
teemed by men of all parties and sects, but also in the highest and holiest relation
. which can exist between men-that of pastor and parishioner. As such, I have
known and loved him for years. I knew his open-handed liberality, his eminent
services as a brother and counselor of those who had no other earthly friend to
whom to look for advice and assistance, s~ve this friend and brother of the depa1·ted
Mason or Christian. I know well, therefore, why he was so much beloved and hon.
ored by his brethren of the Mystic Tie. In his own city, he held again and again the
highest positions the Fraternity could confer ; and I need not tell the older mem·
bers of this Grand Lodge, who, with myself, have met with him annually for more
than a half score of years, who and what Bro. HARTLEY was. Sound in judgment,
ripe In Masonic lore, ever courteous In speech and advice, he was, as a consequence,
ever popular, and deservedly so, with his fellow members. One year since, by an
almost unanimous vote, you honored him by electing him Deputy Grand Master, the
second highest office in your gift; and I know, Most Worshipful Sir, that I bui
speak the sentiments of all who hear me when I say that, had his llfe been spared,
and were he here, and should you have expressed no wish for a reelection to the
eminent place you now so successfully fill , Bro. HARTLEY, by the almost unani·
mous vote of the Grand Lodge, would have been chosen to fill your chair-the
highest demonstration of our regard which we could give. And it would have been
no more than he would have deserved. We should have honored ourselves, as well

as our brother, by such a choice. But while men thus plan and resolve, the .A.II-wise
God above, who does all things well, often disappoints and brings our plans to

Death claimed his own. That chair, that Holy Bible, the clothing and ornaments of
this Grand Lodge, all draped In mourning, tell us of a loss that will not soon be
repaired. A loss here, a loss to the Fraternity in his own city, a loss that words can·
not describe to his own family, a loss to the poor and destitute, a loss to his Church,
a loss to myself! fet God's will be done. We committed his body to the grave, in

my bro~her, be this earthy bed; bright and glorious be thy rising from it. "' "' • . Until
then, dear brother, until then, farewell."
Most Wotshipl'ul (}rand Master and Brethren: The death of our brother has a
word of warning to ns who survive. Often had Bro. HARTLEY, as the Master of his
Lodge, admonished the Entered Apprentice of the moral significance of the "twenty·
four Jnoh guage "-that Its division into three parts was emblematic of the proper
division of the day-an equal part being devoted to work, to the service of God and
our brethren; and to refreshment and repose. And legislation, as well as the growing
sentiment of the community, seems to be tending to the same point, which at no
distant day, In my opinion, will be a conceded truth, that eight hours Is all that the
laborer, whether In the field or in the workshop, or in the office, where the brain Is taxed
more than the muscle and often fearfully at its expense, should devote to his usual
avocations. There Is 11 limit, whether this be it or not, which the Maker of our frame
~eems to have fixed, beyond which we may not long or often pass, without sooner or
later paying the penalty for the violation of the law of God, written In our members.
But Bro. HARTLEY knew of no eight-hour, nor even sixteen-hour law In the pursuii
of his chosen and honored avocation. Often has the midnight hour found him por·
ing over the business committed to him by his clients, when his burdened brain and
exhausted body demanded repose and sleep. And it is no abuse of words, nor over·
statement of the truth, when I say here, that our brother Is this day in his grave
because he would not, for he could not, spare himself In the work which he felt him·
self bonnd to undertake and accomplish. Not even his robust frame could endure the
overtasking, and it Is now, in consequence, in its lowly grave. I said he could not
throw olf this additional work; and let me add, as a humble tribute to his memory
and his Masonic worth, the.t muoh, very much, of this hard work was undertaken for
his poor brethren, or for the widows and orphans they had left behind. For It Is but
the simple truth to say, that more than any other man, or half dozen men in our city,
was Bro. HA.RTLEY entrusted with the management and settlement of the estates of
his deceased brethren. He was faithful to all these most saored trusts, and hence his
business Increased. He would be the friend and helper of all, regardless of his own
strength, and often, too, of the cold, hard judgment of the ill informed about him.
That moved him not from the path of duty, but he went right onward, sustained b7 the
honest and manly conviction that he was but meeting his responsibilities as a Man,
e. Mason, and a Christian. .A.nd to this conviction he fell a prematnre victim. While
we honor our brother for the motive , let us take warning to ourselves in time. We
may not te.x either body or brain beyond its lea:itimate strength, or we shall pay
the sure penalty at some time and in some way. If, as the wise man said, there is a
" time for all things," let us ·remember, and act 11.Ccordingly, that there is and must
be a time in which to rest from our labors. Good would it have been for our brother,
as well as for those who mourn his loss, if he could have follow:ed this rule ere it had
been too late.
His death teaches us all a lesson, which I pray God we may never forget. I see some
brethren before me, whose whitened locks betoken that they are near or beyond the

Pro~dings of the

398

[Oct. 15,

three score and ten years allotted to man on earth. Others, like yourself and myself,
have passed the era of early manhood, even of middle life, and are looking forward
to the no distant day when, with ns, the almond tree will blossom for tbe grave. I
see many others, and perhaps the majority of this Grand Lodge, whose bright eyes,
youthful countenances, and well-knit, robust frames attest that they are the young
men whom our great Patron Saint exhorted so earnestly to be "skong in the Lord,"
for on them have come, or will soon rest, the interests and destinies, not only of our
beloved Order, but of the State and nation. But, Most Worshipful Sir, I see no man
before me who ct1n say with truth that he has made an agreemeflt with death, or a
covenant with the grave. That we all must die, we know full well, for that is the unchangeable decree oftbe Great Jehovah. But when, and how? Who can tell? Onr
brother was stricken down, as in the noon-day, inthe full Tigor of manhood, and when
all thonght he could least be spared. God above only knows who of us will receive the
summons next. History and experience attest the truth of th~ declaration of Scripture, that there is no order in the grave. It may be the oldest, it may be the youngest of the brethren who are now so kindly listening to my voice. And does not that
very uncertainty speak to us of the necessity of immediate and constan't preparation
for our great change? When we stand over the grave of a brother, we are always
reminded that the apron, the coffin, and the spade speak to us of our own mortality.
But the sprig of acacia-the undying evergreen, most beautiful and striking emblem
of immortality-tells of a son! within that will not, can not die-that no corruption
nor worm can fasten upon-no clods of the valley cover-no power annihilate. It
came from God, its maker, and to God it must return. Believing thus in the immortality of the soul, does not true wisdom bid us ask, where will it live, and how?
Preparation for death, merely, is of minor importance, compared with a preparation
for eternal life in the coming hereafter. The Author of the soul can alone answer
our questions, or satisfy these craving desires that all may then be well with us. And
He has answered them in that Holy Book which ever lies open upon our altars-our
true and only moral and spiritual trestle-board. Go to it, then, my brethren, and
learn the work you are to do, and how it is to be done. It will tell you that duty to
your neighbor, though well done, is but half your work, and that the least important. It tells you that love. to God and devotion to his service is the "first and great
commandment." And while it also reminds you of your shortcomings, imperfec.
tions and sins, it points you to the all-sufficient merits of a Redeemer, who died for
you, and yet rose again and liveth forevermore. Iil that Saviour our departed brother
trusted, and, because of this, we believe that death to him was no loss, but an nn.
speakable gain. So believe and do ye, my brethren. So love, not this Brotherhood
only, but Rim who" maketh men to be of one mind in an house"; so let all your
work be square, bearing every test, human and divine; and then, when this world
shall fade and disappear, and you shall appear before God in judgment, that work will
pass the inspection of the All-Seeing Eye ; and, as saved through the merits of the
Redeemer, you raise your songs of unending praise to God and the Lamb, you shall
feel and know, world without end, that with yon ALL 1s WELL.

to what,.if any, action of a Lodge Is necessary in the case of a member notified by the

Lodge has never taken any action on the subject. In the judgment of your committee the decision was right, and should be affirmed by the Grand Lodge.
This decision and the latter clause of Section 6, above quoted, seem to answer
11ll the questions proposed; but something more may, perhaps, be added.
Fin;t. If the Lodge in which the party was initiated refuses its consent or permission, no other Lodge can receive his petition for the remaining degrees. That
Lodge has acquired and has the right to retain jurisdiction of him. He can apply
again to the same Lodge by petition, and it is only fair to presume that, if worthy,
he will be elected and will receive the degl\Ces. The fact that a majority of the
members of any Lodge refuses to another T.odge, asking it, permiBBion to receive the
petition of such an applicant, Is very good evidence that the applicant ought not to
be advanced. One man might perbps be found mean enough to reject the petition
of an applicant, who. was in all respects wortv, to gratify some feeling of personal
spite or idle caprice, but that the majority of the members of any Lodge would do
so is more than we are wllling to believe; and the granting of such a request requires
only a bare majority-not a unanimous vote. Our faith in the manly character or
Masons and the sense of justice by which their action ought to be governed, makes
us exceedingly Ruspicious when one complains that he has been denied his j11st
rights by the many-that he is pure and that they are governed by caprice. Such
a oase might occur, but we think the occurrence would be so rare that It would be
better to abide by the rule as it now stands, and le.t that one bear his wrongs unredressed and without hope of redress, than to amend the law by opening the door for
f.hose who onght not to be allowed to enter.
Second. If the Lodge which initiated a party fortmer refuses to advance lllm, and
also forrroer refuses to give any other Lodge, within whose jurlsdlotlon he may
happen to sojourn, permission to receive his petition, he must be forever debarred
from receiving any further light in the mysteries of Mesonry; but he ls not debarred
from receiving all the benefits and enjoying all the privileges of Masons of his degree.
To those he is entitled, and he cannot be deprived of them, except upon trial and
conviction for some offense against our laws.
Third. One whom his Lodge refuses to advance, or permit another Lodge to ad·
vance, is placed In quite a different po~ltlon from one whose original petition was
rejected, and very reasonably so. In the case of an original petition, one vote may
reject; while in his case more than one-third of the members of his Lodge must con·
cur that the grounds of objection to his advancement are sufficient to stay his further
progress there, and a majority must concnr in the opinion that he Is unworthy to be advanced elsewhere, or else, in the one event, he is entitled to and will receive advance·
mentin his own Lodge, and in the other, wlllreceive permission to present his petition
elsewhere. One who has been suspended or expelled, after having received all the
degrees of Masonry, might complain that his position was worse with respect to the
Fraternity than if his petition had been rejected, with the same justice as one whose
advancement has been stayed by objection and subsequent action of th~ Lodge.
Fourth. Such a person can not disregard his initiation and petition another Lodge
for the three degrees. He is an Entered Apprentice, and the prohibition of Section
6, Article III, Part III, is absolute.
Your committee have answered the questions proposed at greater length than
was perhaps necessary, because such questions are frequently asked, and frequently
too in a tone of injured innocence, as though the party had been unjustly denied his
lawful rights. In conclusion they otfer the following resolution and recommend its
a.doptlon :Resol1led, That when an objection made to the advancement of a candidate, under
Rection 5, Article III, Part III, of. the Constitution, has been decided to be a valid
and Masonic objection, such decision shall have the etfect of a rejection for the remaining degrees; but the party so rejected may, after the lapse of one year, again

To the M:. W. ·• Grand Lodge of Californja :Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Address of the Grand
Master relating to the physi9al qualifications of candidates, have examined the general regulation upon that subject, adopted by the Grand Lodge in 186,, with the re·
port of the committee by whom that regul11tlon was proposed, and are of opinion
that the rule then adopted-that the candidate must be able 'to ooriform literally to
what the several degrees require of him-is o'orreot. They do not desire to relax or
modify the rule, and do not think that any words of theirs could make it more ex·
plloit. The language is clear and concise. The Grand Lodge has adopted the rule
as It stands, and it is the law of this jurisdiction. Reaftlrmance oould not add to its
binding force. If the Grand Master thinks it for the interest of the Craft to call the
attention of Masters of Lodges to it, it is hls right to do so in such form as he shall
judge most likely to cause his admonition to be observed. Your committee do not
find that any further action upon the subject is necessary.
All which is respectfully submitted.

the jurisdiction of Sotoyome Lodge, was sick and died during the latter part of the
year 1867, and was in need of assistance to provide for the necessary support and
care of himself and family during his sickneBB, and for his funeral expenses. Sotoyome Lodge contributed the sum of $132- 185 for support of the family, $30 for
watchers, and $17 for funeral llxpenses. OurtiB Lodge refunded the amount paid

plain duty of Curtis Lodge to provide that one of !ts members should not, during his

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee have given careful consideration to the resolution offered by Bro.
.• RrOHA&D Du111, in regard to the burial of Masons who, at the time of their death, were
in good standing.
The resolution evidently looks to a larger permission than is now given for the
burial of those who shall by violent means destroy their own lives, as the only restriction now in regard to burials relates to suicides and duelists, and the resolution
specially excepts duelists. ,
.
This subject was brought to the at.t ention of the Grand Lodge in 1864., in the Grand
Master's Address and in the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, which was
concurred in by the Grand Lodge ; and your committee are of the opinion that the
rule therein adopted is fully as liberal as any one ought to ask. That report says:- ·
It is difficult to conceive that any man in his right mind could be guilty of destroying his own life. It is probably true that one who commits suicide has prevlonsiy
become, by some means, demented. Self·preservatlon is the first law of nature. A.
very high authority declares that " no man ever yet hated his own fiesh. " This being
true, a man must in some way have lost the right use of his mental powers before he can
lift a hand against his own life. Reason may be dethroned, eith~r by the visitations
of God, or by indulgence in licentious and vicious habits. If the hand of God has
been laid upon a brother, recalling the reason which He had given , and, while thna
demented, he shall take his life; we think he may properly receive the honors paid
by our Order to the dead. But if, forgetting the first perfect point of his entrance
and the virtue by which lt is exemplified, and which it is designed to enforce-if, ne-

1868.]

Grand, Lodge of Odlifornia.

413

glectiug his solemn obligations and that prudence which should characterize every
!>rother in his condnct in the Lodge and when abroad In the world, he, by indulgence
m drink or other habits which are calculated to enervate the mind, loses his reason,
and, while thus out of his mind, destroys his own llfe, we tbiuk he is not entitled to
and should not receive the burial rites of the Order. We therefore recommend that
the sentiments of the Grand Master's Address on his subject be approved.
In our judgment no Masonic Lodge or body of Masons should ask a more liberal
role than this, leaving to the parties Interested to determine whether, in the particular case, the Lodge would bury the dead brother with Masonic honors or not, as the
circumstances of the case might show his act to have been the visitation of God or
the result of his own vicious habits or perverse will.
We agree with the committee by whom that report was made, that it is difficult
to conceive that any man In hls right mind could be guilty of destroying his own
life ; bot it is equally difficult to conceive that any one in his right mind should be
guilty of taking the life of another. Yet men, from time to time, with great deliber·
ation, do take the lives of others, and with equal deliberation do take their own lives.
It Is not very uncommon to hear men say that they would destroy their own lives
rather than be subje cted to such and such sutrerings, or anxieties, or disgrace, or
'Wl'Ongs; and they do it with the same sang froid that others talk of avenging an
insult by otrerlpg themselves as the target for the insulter's pistol or sword.
Of all the murders committed, nine tenths are probably committed in the heat of
paeslon, reason being for the time dethroned. But shall we therefore say that It was
the visitation of God, and hold him excused? And, If the law, disregarding bis excuse, shall cause him to be Ignominiously executed, shall we, charging the fault, If
fault It were, upon our Maker, piously follow his remains to the grave, saying to the
the world-This man was our brother ; we excuse him; God caused him to do the
act for which the law has unjustly punished him ; and we can pronounce over him
the beautiful words 'Of our burial service, and In conclusion say " The will of God
is accomplished ?"
The guilt of one who takes his own life Is as great as that of one who takes the
life of another. By all law, human and divine , it is the same, and the circumstances
of each case must determine the enormity of the offense. We would not hold ourselves out to the world as in any way excusing such crime.
A man may be a ravinit maniac, or suffering under some milder form of lneanity, and
in that condition may do an act for which he ls not morally or legally responsible ,
whether it be against himself or another ; bot It ls idle to say that any considerable proportion of the persons who commit suicide are ln that condition. More frequently than
otherwise they have met with reverses in business, and think they cannot endure the disgrace of failure ; poverty stares them In the face, and they have not the manliness to
meet It and do their duty In the world like true men; they have lived in atliuence,and
think they can not submit to the inconveniences and hardships of penury; and they
prefer rather to take the matter In their own hands, and, like the veriest cowards, slink
away from the cares, responsibll!ties, and duties devolving upon them, and which
have been caused sometimes through simple aooldent , sometimes through errors in
judgment, and sometimes through criminal disregard of their duties to others and of
the trusts rAposed in them. Ordinarily those who take their own llves prepare very
deliberately for It. They write their letters of farewell to their friends as carefully
and with as full apparent possession of intellect and reason as in their best estate.
They have considered the matter, and have chosen death rather than life.
We would say to all Masons, be men, and do your duty like true men, whether
that duty be pleasant or the contrary; whether your path has been strewn with
flowers or with thorns. It is not all of life to live to eat and drink and be clad. And
we would say to the world that Masons are men and true men, and, as a society, will
give no countenance to nor in any way excuse any deliberate otrense against the laws
of God or man; that the crime of self murder is one of the most odions and least

414

Prbce,edings of the

[Oct. 17,

excusable in the catalogue of crimes ; and that one who is guilty of such a crime is
not worthy to receive at the hands of the Fraternity the honors of a Masonic burial.
As men, we will decently and quietly bury him; but not as one who has run his race
and accomplished the work appointed for him to do.
'
Your committee therefore report back the resolution offered by Bro. DALE, with
the recommendation that it be not adopted ; and, believing the.t it would be for the
best interests of Masonry thnt no one, who has ·b y violence destroyed his own life,
should be buried with Masonic honors, they offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption :ReaoltJed., That no Lodge in this jurisdiction shall bury with Masonic honon any
Mason who has committed suicide.
All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM C. BELCHER,
HENRY F. WILLU.KS ,
GEORGE F. lllALLETT,

7b the M.-. W.-. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. ALEXANDER G. ABELL
in the case of Bro. WILLIAM M. LARoCHE, sentenced to be reprimanded by Oooidental
Lodge, No. 22, have had the same under consideration, and respectfully report that
the Commissioners found the accused guilty of uttering and publishing the defama·
tory statements set out in the specifications, but did not find him guilty of doing so
m111lcionsly. Bro. ABELL contends that it was done maliciously, and that the accused
should have been more severely punished.
The first question for ns to consider is, was the act of the accused committed
maliciously? Every originator of 11 defamatory statement Is adjudged to do so ma·
licionsly, and every one who publishes such 11 statement Is held to be the originator
thereof, unless he can show that he received it from another. In the present case
the accused Introduced various witnesses to prove that reports were in circulation
and had been communicated to him concerning Bro. ABELL; but when the testi·
mony is sifted and compared with the utterances of the accused as set out in the
specifications, It is seen that they do not correspond. It is not shown that any such
statements were communicated to the accused as those to which he gave utterance.
He mn~t therefore be held to be the originator of those statements, and, as such, to have
uttered them maliciously.
In determining the punishment which ought to be imposed in the present r,11se,
we find the rule therefor laid down in the old Constitutions : " If 11 Mason live amiss,
or slander h'ia brother, so as to bring the Craft to shame, he shall have no further
maintenance among the brethren." The statement~ published by the accused being
as defamatory as it is pl)Ssible for one Mason to utter concerning another, your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resol'IJed, That the action of Occidental Lodge, No. 22, in the case of WILLIAM. M.
LA RocHE, in finding him guilty of having uttered and published the defamatory
statements set out in the specifications, be and the same Is hereby affirmed; that the
accused be and he is hereby adjudged to have published the same maliciously; that
the sentence of reprimand passed upon him be reversed and set aside ; and that he
be and is hereby suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
All which is respectfnlly submitted.
JAS. LAWRENCE ENGLISH,}
GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE,
Committee.
WILLIAM 0. RANDOLPH,

Of the Organization of the Grand Lodge.

.ARTCCLE III.
OF ITS POWEBS A!ID AUTHORITY.

S&OTION 1. The Grand Lodge Is the Supreme Masonic Power and .Authority in
this State, posseSsing all the attributes of sovereignty and government-legislative ,
executive, and judicial-limited only by a strict adherence to the .Ancient Land·
marks of the Order, and by the provisions of its own Constitution and Regulations.
S110. 2. Its legislative powers extend to every case or legislation, not expressly
delegated by itself to the Lodges; and the Constitutions and Regulations, which It
has an Inalienable right to adopt and promulgate at its own convenience, and to
alter, amend, or repeal at its own pleasure, under t'b.e limitations therein Imposed, are
final Bild binding upon all Lodges and Masons within its jurisdiction, until .so altered,
amended, or repealed.
SBO. S. Its executive powers include the granting of dispensations and ohartere
to establish and perpetuate Lodges within this State, and in other territory where no
Grand Lodge exista; the revocation or suspension thereof; the issuing of special dis·
pens:itlons for all purposes permitted by aoy of the provisions or this O•mstltutlon ;
and the exercise, generally, of 1111 such authority as may be necessary to carry it1
own legislation Into complete effect.
Sso. '· Its judicial powers are of two kinds:1st. Original-Includiog the decision of all controversies between any of the
Lodges, or between one of them and a member or mem\Jers of another, or between
members of different Lodges; and the enforcement of discipline upon its own mem·
bers and upon the Lodges under Its jurisdiction: and
2d. Appellat6-Embraclng the revision of all matters or controversy or discipline,
proper for Masonic lnvestlgatiou, which may have arisen in any of the Lodges, and
·
over which it has not retained original j urisdic tlon.

OP lTB TITLB A!ID SBAL.

Sso. 2. It shall l1ave a Seal, bearing such. devices and inscriptions as have heretofore been, or mt1.y hereafter be determined; which shall be aftl.xed to all instrn·
ments lasued by or under its authority.

OP lTS MEMBERS AND THEIR QUALIPlOATlONS.

dress shall be Most Worshipful,) a Deputy Grand Master, a Senior Grand Warden,
and a Junior Grand Warden, (whose addresses Fhall severally be Righi Worshipful,)

OF ITS VOTING AND REPRESENTATION.
8EOTION 1. All questions in the Grand Lodge (except elections of officers,) shall

Urand Tyler,) and each Past Grand Officer present, shall be entitled to one vote.

SEC. 4.. N c. Grand Officer, Past Grand Officer, or Past Master, voting.• or particl·

him.
SEC. 6. When e. Lodge shall be represented by only two of its proper officers,
the officer highest in rank may ca.st two of its three votes.
SEC. 6. When e. Lodge shall·be represented by only one of its proper officers,ir
by a representative, such officer or representative me.y cast all the votes to which lt
is entitled.
Si;io. 7. In all cases of a tie vote, except votes by ballot, the Grand Master,
in addition to his proper vote, may have the casting vote.

.ARTICLE Ill.
OF PROHIBITIONS.

SECTION I. No Lodge shall remove its place of meeting from that named in its
dispensation or charter, unless notice sball have been given &t a •tated meeting that
a resolution for such removal will be offered at the next succeeding one, n<ir unleB!>
such resolution shall have been adopted by the votes of at least two-thlrde of the
members present at such succeeding meeting ; nor shall such removal then take
place until the action of the Lodge shall have been approved by the Grand Lodge or
Grand Master.
SEC. 2. No Lodge in this State shall receive an application for the degrees of
Masonry unless the applicant shall have bee.n a resident within the State during
twelve months, and within the jurisdiction of the Lodge during 11ix monihs, next
preceding the date of his application. Nor shall any Lodge receive· snch applicalid
from any person, who, within twelve months next preceding, shall have been rejected.
by any Lodge, unless by dispensation from the Grand Master, as prO'Vlded in Sec. l,
.Art. I, Part II. .All such applications, as well as those for affiliation, shall be In writ..
ing, signed by the applicant, and recommended by at least two I»embers of the
Lodge, in the forms prescribed in .Art. III, Part VU.
'
SEc. 3. No Lodge shall ballot upon such application (except by dispensaUffi
from the Grand Master, as provided in Sec. 1, .Art. I, Part II,) until it shall have been.
referred to a committee, whose duty it shall be to make strict examination Into the
moral, mental, and physical qualifications of the applicant, and to report thereon at
the next stated meeting, unless further time be granted. No application shall be
withdrawn after reference to a committee, and it shall require an unanimous ballot
to eleet. But if one black ball, only, appear in the ballot.box, the Master, without
declaring the result, may at once order a second ballot, for the purpose of correcting
a possible mistake.
·
SEo. 4. No dispensation shall be Issued to a Lodge to ballot for and confer the
degrees upon a candidate, without reference to a committee as provided in the pre·
oeding section, nor to receive and act upon the petition of a rejected applioani
within less than twelve months after the date of such rejection, unless the application
therefor be made by the Lodge, by an unanimous vote, by ballot; and of tile ~pecia.l
meeting to be holden under such dispensation, and the purpose thereof, the membere
ol the Lodge shall have due notice.
SEC. 6. No Lodge, unless it be otherwise provided in its by-laws, shall have more
than one ballot for the three degrees: but, though an applicant may be elected to
receive them, if, at any time before his initiation, objection be made by any member,

the close of that Communication, shall become a part of the Constitution.
Silo. 3. If the vote in favor of such proposed amendment be not unanimous, but
there be a majority therefor, ft shall lie over for one year, and sball be published with
the proceedings, under the caption of" Proposed Amendments to the Constitution·"
and if, at the next succeeding Annual Communication, it shall receive two-thirds~!
the v~es given thereon, it shall be declared adopted, and from and after the close ol
that Communication, shall become a part of the Constitution.
Szo. '· No vote upon a proposed amendment shall be taken after the election of
the Grand Officers.
Si;:o. 6. All former. written Constitutions of this Grand Lodge are hereby repealed,
as are also all Regulations, or parts thereof, which are repugnant to or inconsistent
with this Constitution; and no Regulation shall hereafter be adopted which shall be
in violation of or inconsistent with any of its provfelons.

The jurisdiction of a Lodge includes all Masons residing nearer t o its place of

REGULA.TION.-By a regulation of the Grand Lodge is meant any resolution, edict,
law, or ordinance of any kind whatever, other than the Constitution, which it may
ado11t.
SusPENBION.-The suspension of a Lodge Is an arrest of its charter and a tempo·
rary prohibition to assemble or work as a legal Lodge, until again authorized so to
do by competent authority ; and the act suspends all its members except those espe·
cially exempted from its eft'ect.
The suspen1ion of the Masier of a Lodge is a temporary deprivation of his otllce,
and prohibits all recognition of him in that capacity, until he be rest ored by compe·
tent authority.
·
The suspension of a Mason is a temporary deprivation of all his rights and privi•
leges as such, and prohibits all Masous and Lodges from holding any Masonic
intercourse, whatever, with him, until he shall be legally restored by the Lodge which
suspended .h im, or by the Grand Lodge.
ExPULSION.-The expulsion of a Mason is the highest penalty known to the Ma·
sonic Jaw. It is an absolute deprivation of all the rights and privilege~ of the Order,
and prohibits all Mason's and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse with him
forever, unless he be restored by the Grand Lodge.

<,}ENERAL REGULATIONS.

I. The practice of dueling being repugnant to the principles of Freemasonry, in
all cases where two brethren resort to this mode of settling their dlspntee, It shall be
the duty of the Lodge or Lodges of which they are members, or within whose jnrlsdiction they may reside, forthwith to expel them from all the righ~ and.privileges of
Masonry; and no brother who may fall in a duel shall be buried with Masonic
honors. [1854.]
2. All bodies purporting fo be Masonic Lodges-held in the United States or any
of their Territories, within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of any State or Terri·
tory, without authority from such Grand Lodge-and all the members thereof, are
declared Illegal. [1864.]
·
S. All Lodges within this State, having concurrent jurled!Qtion with other Lodges,
shall immediately notify such others of all applications for membership or initiation.
[1854.]
4. This Grand Lodge, having recognized the principle that no one should be initl·

ated into the mysteries of our Order, except In the Lodge nearest his place of
residence, (unless by Its permission,) and having, by an established regulation, taken
care to avoid infringing the jurisdictional rights of others, will not tolerate thal\ts
own be Invaded; and It is therefore ordered that no Lodge, subordinate to the Grand
Lodge of California, shall admit to membership any person who, being at the time a
resident of this State, has .received, or claims to have received, the degrees of Ma·
eonry from any source beyond its jurisdiction, without the proper permiBBlon, until
he shall have paid the Lodge to which he applies for membership, the full amount
charged by that Lodge for conferring the degrees, lees the sum paid by him to
the Lodge in which he received them. [1855 and 1857.]
5. Thie Grand Lodge rec()gnizes no degree of Past Master conferred by any au·
thority not holden under a legitimate Grand Lodge-acknowledging only the Order
of that name as it exists in the ceremonies attending the Installation of the Master
elect of a chartered Lodge .; which 0l'der shall be conferred only by a convocation
of Present or Past Masters, not lees t han three in number, who h·a.ve thus regularly
received it. [1855.]
6. All Masonic communication between- the Lodges and Masons of this jurledlc·
tion and those acknowledging allegiance to the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, le hereby
forbidden , while that body shall continue its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of
the jurisdictional tights of the Grand Lodge of New York. [1855.]
7, Such standard of revenue shall be continued hereafter as will afford an excess
over the ·current expenditures of at least one thousand dollars; which excess shall
eaoh yeai be set aside, as an accumulating fund, for the future erection of a Masonic
He.II, and shall not be used for any other purpose. At each Annual Communication,
a Board of Trustees, three in number, she.II be elected, whose duty it shall be Jndi·
cionely to invest all moneys set aside for such fund, and all moneys accrnlng from
the interest on such Investments; and each member of said Board shall execute and

General RegW,ati<mS of the

Grand, Lodge of California..

Ille in the office of the Grand Secretary, a bond in the penal sum of $5,000, to be approved by the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer, and Grand Secretary, conditioned
that he will faithfully perform the duties of his trust. [1866.]
8, .A.11 members of Lodges, the charters of which have been surrendered, who
were In good standing at the date of such snrrender, and whose dues shall have been
paid, are entitled to, and may receive from the Grand Secretary, a certificate to that
elfect. [1858.]
9. No Lodge under this jurisdiction shall be allowed to transact business, other
than the conferring of degrees, with a less number than seven members present.

by the by-laws of the Lodge to which they may apply; or, if they desire to restore
themselves by contribution, they shall pay a sum equivalent to the amount of the reg·
ular dues of the Lodge within whose jurisdiction they reside, during the whole period
of such residence-unless sickness or inability to pay be shown as the reason for
such non-affiliation or non-payment. [1864, 1866.]
17. When It is the Intention of any Lodge to take measures to apply to the Grand
Lodge for the restoration of it Mason who has been expelled, it shall be the duty of
the Master thereof to D'' .1· the members of his Lodge, as far as possible, of the
time when such proposed action will be had ; and to cause to be recorded, in the
minutes of the meeting at which such action shall be had, the fact that snch notification was duly gi,-en. [1864.]
18. The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no woman nor
eunuch; freeborn, being neither a slave nor the son of a bondwoman; a believer in God
and a future existence ; of moral conduct; capable of reading and writing ; not de·
formed or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical conformation, having his
right limbs as a man ought to have ; and able to cvnform literally to what the several degrees respectively require o{ him. [1864.]
19. Whenever any M~son, under sentence of suspension, who has submitted to
the judgment of the subordinate Lodge or whose sentence of snspension has been
